chapter_sentences: [break]Introduction. The religious and mythic elements of German National Socialism often made the Third Reich look like a cult in power. The pageantry of Nazi rallies and their quasi-liturgical nature matched the extraordinary fervor of the huge crowds. Most participants were caught up in an intense atmosphere of collective excitement and self-surrender.
Hitler's undoubted charisma and the careful development and cultivation of the Führerkult since the earliest years of the movement were crucial factors in building Nazi religiosity.

Huge congregations, banners, sacred flames, processions, a style of popular and radical preaching, prayers-and-responses, memorials, and funeral marches were all essential props for the cult of race and nation. They supported the mission of Aryan Germany and victory over her enemies. The messianic figure of Adolf Hitler, the savior of Germany, towered over the entire project. National Socialist ideology was deeply shaped by radical religious ideas.
The belief in a Jewish world conspiracy, supposedly supported by the infamous The Protocols of the Elders of Zion, created an image of a demonic enemy.

Nazi anti-Semitism grew from this apocalyptic demonology. It blamed Jews for all ills, including liberalism, communism, moral corruption, and the collapse of the traditional world. The idea of national regeneration also had an apocalyptic spirit. Only the destruction of Jews could ensure Germany's salvation in a racially pure millennium. Alfred Rosenberg, the main Nazi Party ideologue, was an early promoter of the Protocols.

He established their central place in Nazi philosophy in the early 1920s. Dietrich Eckart, Hitler's mentor in Munich, held a gnostic-dualist view of Jews and their opposing role in German national life. Hitler's belief in a Jewish world conspiracy was a lifelong conviction. It found terrible fulfillment in the Holocaust. In an earlier book, The Occult Roots of Nazism, I traced ideas of racial election, demonology, and the millennium among Austrian German nationalists before the First World War.

That study aimed to show how quasi-religious and even occult ideas could support German identity. They did so in response to perceived threats from liberalism, laissez-faire capitalism, and the rise of subject nationalities at the start of the last century. At that time, traditional groups saw large-scale industry, new metropolitan cities, the growth of capitalist finance, and organized labor as threats. These völkisch Ariosophists offered a defensive ideology of "Aryan" German folk identity.

They presented it as a cure for unwelcome, disruptive challenges to traditional status, custom, and political authority. Against the rise of anthropology and eugenics, these sectarians embraced ideas of race. They stigmatized Jews as the supposed agents and beneficiaries of liberalism and modernity. Their occult notions of racial superiority combined with anti-Semitism and millenarian myths of national regeneration.
This mix found its ultimate expression in the ideology of the National Socialist movement. Multicultural societies face a similar challenge today.

In 1900, white Europeans made up about 35 percent of the world's population. White birth rates have fallen in advanced industrial nations. At the same time, populations in the Third World have exploded. Better medicine, sanitation, and industrialization drove this growth. Today, white Europeans make up just under 10 percent of the global population. Guest workers, immigrants, economic migrants, refugees, and asylum seekers form major population flows.
These groups bring the population surplus of developing countries into lands traditionally settled by white people of European descent.

Advanced industrial economies absorb ever larger levels of immigration. Their political commitment to multiracialism is now an article of faith. Today, the United States and most European nations face a demographic shift against their historic native stocks. The resulting issue of white identity repeats the dilemma of Austrian Germans. They feared a loss of influence in the old Habsburg Empire. Black Sun looks at how "Aryan" racial ideas have survived and returned.

This happened in response to the challenges of the postwar world. More than fifty years after the defeat and disgrace of Nazism and fascism, the far right is again challenging the liberal order of Western democracies. It seeks political space. Radical ideologies feed on the threats of economic globalization, affirmative action, and Third World immigration. The book explores the far edges of right-wing extremist ideology.

Aryan cults, aristocratic paganism, anti-Semitic demonology, Eastern religion, and the occult supply underground beliefs. These beliefs serve individuals and groups. These people fear a loss of status, cultural tradition, and identity. This fear arises in the emerging multicultural societies of the United States and Europe.
The scene begins with a historical review of neo-Nazism in the United States and Britain.

There, Nazism returned as an extreme reaction to communism, liberalism, and especially the desegregation of African Americans and other colored immigrants. In their search for a radical opposing ideology, American and British neo-Nazis supported Hitler and National Socialism against liberalism and the presence of ethnic minorities. Their underground publications praise National Socialism as a racial policy to ensure the global dominance of the white race forever.

However, despite their main focus on colored races, neo-Nazi ideology still viewed Jews as the demonic enemy of white Aryan peoples. They see Jews as the architects of a multiracial world order. This order supposedly dissolves all nations, traditions, and loyalties before the final achievement of Jewish world conquest. The persistence of anti-Semitism in modern racist talk, which mainly targets ethnic groups, shows that the demonology of Nazism endures.

Like Gnostics separated from a higher god in a dark world, American and British neo-Nazis claim that Hitler and Nazism are the only hope for the racial survival of white nations filled with growing ethnic minorities. Anti-Semitism acts as a Manichaean dualist heresy that splits the world into forces of good and evil. Millenarian racial cleansing and the belief in a Jewish world conspiracy are the defining moments of this neo-Nazi religiosity.
[break]From the 1950s to the 1970s, neo-fascist and neo-Nazi groups copied the past.

They used uniformed members, swastika flags, and marches. Fringe political parties stayed the domain of fanatics. Recruitment was strictly limited to people who admired fascism or were convinced anti-Semites. Even when German nationalism became a global ideology of white racism, the history and politics of Nazi Germany remained the main model to copy. This loyalty to history marked the neo-Nazi cults linked to George Lincoln Rockwell and Colin Jordan.

It also marked their successors and followers in the postwar Anglo-American world. Bound by the memory of German National Socialism, Anglo-American neo-Nazis stayed trapped in a nostalgic cult of Hitler worship. Universal condemnation of the Third Reich and the Holocaust blocked any chance of political success. Like the Ariosophists in the early 1900s, political isolation in a hostile, liberal world pushed many neo-Nazi and neo-fascist groups toward occult ideas of ancient Aryan wisdom.
Starting in the 1970s, right-wing extremists repackaged the old ideology of Aryan racism, elitism, and force.

They used new cultic forms that mixed esotericism and Eastern religions. In Austria and Germany, former SS man Wilhelm Landig revived the ariosophical mythology of Thule. Thule was the supposed polar homeland of the ancient Aryans. He created the idea of the Black Sun. This was a substitute swastika and a mystical energy source that could regenerate the Aryan race. He popularized esoteric ideas found in the pre-Nazi völkisch movement and the SS.
These ideas covered Atlantis, the World Ice Theory, prehistoric floods, and secret racial doctrines from Tibet.

He also highlighted Nazi interest in the medieval Cathars and Grail traditions. He presented these as an alternative Germanic religion of dualist heresy. In Italy, Julius Evola's aristocratic elitism and esoteric Aryan-Nordic traditions inspired a whole generation of postwar neo-fascists. When wanted far-right terrorists fled abroad, they carried Evola's ideas to far-right parties and groups elsewhere in Europe.

By the late 1980s, this little-known philosopher had become a major political icon of opposition to democracy and liberalism in the West. Julius Evola's interest in the Indo-Aryan world included the exotic realms of Hinduism and Tantrism. Following James Madole's early adoption of Theosophy and Hindu caste hierarchies, neo-Nazi ideology absorbed Eastern themes in the mystical doctrines of Savitri Devi and Miguel Serrano.

These two are currently popular in the racist underground. Savitri Devi, a French-born Nazi-Hindu prophetess, described Hitler as an avatar of Vishnu. She compared Nazism to the cult of Shiva, which emphasizes destruction and new creation. Adopting the Hindu cycle of the ages, she claimed that mankind is living in the Kali Yuga, a dismal dark age. She argued that only regenerative violence, war, and genocide can end it.
Miguel Serrano, a retired Chilean diplomat and author, blends exotic oriental religion with his Gnostic-Manichaean doctrine of "Esoteric Hitlerism."

Serrano traces the semi-divine Aryans to extraterrestrial origins. He recommends kundalini yoga to repurify "mystical Aryan blood" to its former quality of divine light. His other themes include a Gnostic war against the Jews, the Black Sun, the Hitler avatar, and Nazi UFOs in Antarctica. Neo-Nazism has thereby acquired new myths and meanings for a younger generation. Another revaluation of Nazism came from its demonization in many thrillers and books about Nazi occultism.

These were published in sensational paperback editions during the 1960s and 1970s. In these works, Nazism was mystified and romanticized into a neo-Gnostic religion. It had links to oriental mythology, secret Tibetan doctrines, and demonic inspiration. This effect turned the facts of dictatorship, terror, war, and oppression into a mythological tableau. It removed them from history. Reality soon followed popular literature.

In the early 1970s, satanist groups in the United States flirted with Nazi themes. They saw these themes as symbols of the forbidden, dark side of life. In the 1990s, Nazi satanic cults replaced these experiments in the shock value of Nazism. These cults linked anti-Christian paganism to a transgressive praise of Hitler and the Third Reich. In America, Europe, and Australia, such "darkside" lodges espouse a vulgar Nietzschean worship of force.
They back this with anti-Christian, elitist, and Social Darwinist doctrines. In the 1980s and 1990s, the far right saw a dramatic revival in Europe and America.

This was especially true among alienated white youth and lower-income groups. These groups felt increasingly pushed aside by new high-tech industries. They also felt marginalized by the growing presence of ethnic minorities in their communities. Rapid growth in Hispanic and Third World immigration in the United States fueled fresh fears of racial inundation. Similar immigration from developing countries into Western Europe had the same effect.

The collapse of the Soviet Union and Yugoslavia led to further migrations. Gypsies and East European nationals moved to Western Europe. Free-trade agreements, the collapse of traditional manufacturing, and the export of service jobs abroad via computer communications are stimulating racism and hostility toward liberalism. Globalization is sending huge flows of capital, information, skills, and people across national borders.

The Western world is quickly going through major structural changes. Borders are becoming easier to cross. Skilled workers, economic migrants, refugees, and asylum seekers are moving into advanced industrial countries in growing numbers. As more immigrant groups arrive, traditional national culture faces unfamiliar customs, norms, and religions. At the start of our new century, these cultural trends put great pressure on the idea of the nation-state.

A century later, liberalism and laissez-faire capitalism are again seen as the engines of unwanted and threatening change. Once again, extremist nationalist reactions echo völkisch ideas. They focus on defensive race ideologies to counter threats to national and cultural identity. Some challenged groups turn to racial identity as a last resort. In the United States, the doctrine of Christian Identity mixes heretical Christian dualism with a vicious anti-Semitic theology.

This theology views Jews as the "spawn of Satan." It stigmatizes African Americans, Asians, Hispanics, and all other colored peoples as "mud" races. These groups claim these peoples are diluting and destroying the Aryan race in its traditional white homelands. Here, Nazi demonology and apocalyptic ideas are freely invoked. They are combined with Hitler worship and Third Reich symbolism. This mobilizes violence to support a white racial state. Other groups mix racism with Nordic pagan religions.

They celebrate runes as magical signs of ancestral heritage and mystical blood loyalty. In the United States, Britain, Germany, and the Scandinavian countries, racial pagan groups study runes, magic, and the sinister mythology of the Norse gods Wotan, Loki, and Fenriswolf. The racial interpretation of these esoteric ideas, cosmology, and prophecies reveals these groups' overwhelming anxiety about the future of white identity in multiracial societies.

[break]This book began as a sequel to The Occult Roots of Nazism. It aimed to document how occult Nazi themes survived after the war. As I worked, my view widened greatly. I did not just trace faded fascist mystics and outdated ideas. I actually wrote a new history of modern neo-völkisch groups and ideas in America and Europe. This new völkisch revival is common in the English-speaking world. It shows a reaction to the rise of liberalism and globalization from the 1980s onward.
[break]The original völkisch movement started as a defense of German identity against modernity in the late 1800s.

This neo-völkisch revival does the same for white identity. It defends against multiculturalism, affirmative action, and mass immigration from the Third World. As these neo-völkisch groups focus on identity and ethnicity, many turn to esoteric themes. They explore Aryan origins, secret knowledge, and occult heritage. Their German predecessors did the same. Like the Ariosophists from 1890 to 1945, these new white-pride movements are the most radical response.

Western societies now face deep challenges to their cultural identity. The original völkisch movement led to National Socialism and the Third Reich. So, the rise of a new völkisch movement should worry us. Who knows what politics and societies will emerge by 2030-50 from the growing sense of white marginalization? I know this provocative study of modern racist movements may offend politically correct views. It asks questions that liberal elites prefer to ignore or suppress.

[break]Racist religion carries great risks. When people project their grievances, fears, and anxieties onto "shadow" figures of other races, religious transcendence is stunted and twisted into exclusion and hatred.

Instead of genuine spirituality, we see partiality, separation, and restriction. A rigid self-righteousness leads into the spiritual basement of primitive dualism, where pseudo-salvation depends on eliminating the Other. Projecting religious Manichaeism onto human differences inevitably causes strife and violence. Whenever human groups are viewed as absolute categories of good and evil, light and darkness, both the human community and humanity itself are diminished.

Such degraded religion never leads to light, only to darkness. I hope that understanding the substitute faiths documented in these pages, along with their causes, can help us avoid repeating past conflagrations.
[break]

1. American Neo-Nazism. American neo-Nazism is an exotic import from Europe that has always gone beyond American nationalism. American neo-Nazis see themselves as brothers to all white men in a global movement of racial nationalism.

They remain fixated on Adolf Hitler as the lost savior of the Western world. Yet his German nationalist limits are replaced by their wider vision of a pan-Aryan movement. In this vision, the United States leads as the top white power in the postwar world. American neo-Nazism traces its roots to the early 1950s. At that time, the anti-communist ideology of the Cold War found a nostalgic model in Hitler's attempt to destroy the Soviet Union.

Neo-Nazism quickly labeled liberalism and American Jews as the helpers of communism. This created a violent anti-Semitism based on Nazi models. However, desegregation and the black civil rights movement of the early 1960s provided the lasting political drive for American racial nationalism. The social empowerment of black Americans, forced integration, busing, affirmative action, and equal opportunities led American neo-Nazis to take on a white supremacist role.
When large-scale Hispanic and other Third World immigration began in the 1980s, American neo-Nazism saw itself as the front-line defense of America's survival as a white nation.

The changing ethnic mix of the United States is a deep issue. So is the political unity of an increasingly diverse multicultural society. The path of American neo-Nazism from George Lincoln Rockwell in the 1960s to William Pierce in the 2000s shows how the religious myths of German National Socialism apply to major cultural changes in American demography and identity.

[break]George Lincoln Rockwell, who called himself the Führer of the 1960s, is always identified as the founder of the openly pro-Hitler, postwar Nazi movement in the United States. Rockwell's extravagant praise for Hitler, his violent racism against Jews and blacks, and his use of excess and exhibitionist tactics have given him a lasting place in the folklore of American political extremism.

Disappointed by his earlier political work with old-style far-right groups, Rockwell founded his American Nazi Party in 1959. He adopted a brazen Nazi image, complete with swastika flags, stormtroopers, and open declarations of his intention to gas the Jews. He fantasized that he would become president of the United States by 1973.

He imagined that a Senate and House of Representatives made up of his party's members would support him. His political program was firmly grounded in a policy of "white survival." This policy aimed at the wholesale repatriation of all American Negroes to Africa and the extermination of the Jews. He regarded the Jews as the architects of racial desegregation, national decline, and cultural degeneracy. Rockwell's public appearances mixed clowning with provocation.

Soon after founding the party, Rockwell and his men regularly picketed the White House. They held signs that read "Save Ike from the kikes," "The only communist party in the Middle East is in Israel," "Gas red Jewish spies," and "Communism is Jewish."

In 1961, Rockwell drove a "Hate Bus" through the South. His party was arrested in New Orleans. The bus sides displayed notices like "We do hate race-mixing" and "We hate Jew-Communism." Back in Washington, his stormtroopers drove a bus around the city. It bore the slogan: "Rockwell is right! Who needs niggers?" In Boston and Philadelphia, the party picketed cinemas showing the popular film Exodus, which told the story of Jewish immigrants to Israel after World War II.

They held banners demanding "America for Whites and Gas Chamber for Traitors." Throughout the mid-1960s, Rockwell and his American Nazi Party took part in many protests and disruptions. Charges against stormtroopers included fighting, loitering, vagrancy, and assault. They also faced charges of desertion, criminal defamation, and unlawful possession of firearms. What makes an American Nazi?

Looking at Rockwell's life, we see a mix of religious belief and idealism. These drove a loud program of anti-Semitism and anti-communism, white supremacy, and eugenics. His showy tactics likely came from his parents' background. George Lincoln Rockwell was born on 9 March 1918 in Bloomington, Illinois. He was the eldest son of theatrical performers. His father, George Lovejoy "Doc" Rockwell, was a vaudeville comedian. He had English and Scottish ancestry.

He had a top act on Broadway. He was well known on radio and in the leading theaters of the country. His mother, born Claire Schade, was a young German-French toe dancer. She was part of a family dance team. After his parents divorced, he spent his childhood staying with his mother in rural Illinois. He also stayed with his father on the Maine coast. Regular house guests included Fred Allen, Benny Goodman, and Groucho Marx.

[break]After finishing prep school at Hebron Academy, Rockwell went to Brown University in 1938 to study philosophy and sociology. He soon turned against the liberal, egalitarian tone of social science and his teachers. Later, he believed that liberalism was the "pimping little sister" of communism. His grades were poor, but he served as art editor for the campus magazine, Sir Brown.

[break]His cartoons ranged from humor to comic book horror, featuring images of violence, destruction, and bombings. The prospect of war offered a welcome break from his studies. Eager for action, high-strung, and edgy, Rockwell was influenced by the growing anti-German sentiment. By March 1941, he had enlisted in the Naval Air Corps and quickly earned his wings. He served as a naval aviator flying anti-submarine missions in the South Atlantic and South Pacific throughout World War II.

He commanded naval air support at the Battle of Guadalcanal and during the invasion of Guam in August 1944. He was discharged in October 1945 with the rank of lieutenant commander and several decorations. Meanwhile, he married a girl he had known as a student at Brown.

After leaving the navy, Rockwell spent the first five years studying art. He then took various jobs as a commercial photographer, a painter, an advertising executive, and a publisher in Maine and New York. He showed some promise as a commercial artist and enrolled at the Pratt Institute in New York. In 1948, he won a $1,000 prize in a national art contest sponsored by the National Society of Illustrators. But war interrupted his career again.

In 1950, when the Korean War began, Rockwell returned to active duty. He trained fighter pilots in southern California. His involvement in the Korean conflict created in him a lasting hatred of communism. It also bred a paranoid fear that communism would undermine the United States. Rockwell first became politically involved here in the campaign to elect military hero General Douglas MacArthur as president.

Joseph McCarthy's anti-communist revelations also dominated this time. Rockwell deeply suspected the motives of those trying to discredit him. An old lady in San Diego who worked on the MacArthur campaign showed him some newspapers. She claimed Jews controlled these papers and used them to smear both men. She introduced him to McCarthy's speeches and Conde McGinley's anti-Semitic newspaper, Common Sense,.

This paper contained shocking claims about a secret Jewish-communist plot behind the scenes of twentieth-century history. She also encouraged him to attend a speech by veteran anti-Semite and rabble-rouser Gerald L. K. Smith in Los Angeles. Rockwell was overwhelmed by Smith's emotional exposure of the Jewish conspiracy and its bid for world power. Through further reading in the San Diego public library, he became convinced that a Jewish-communist world conspiracy existed.

Rockwell was staggered by both the apparent size of the conspiracy and the silence of officials and media about it. One autumn day in 1950, in the dark book stacks of the San Diego library, Rockwell experienced illumination and political awakening.

He had always felt that the world was out of joint and that mischief was afoot. But now he felt he held the key to the past and the present. Yet how could he fight against this monstrous and universal plot? Given the apparent enormity of the Jewish world conspiracy, Rockwell now wondered why America had gone to war on the side of the communist Soviet Union. He opposed "Christian Germany, which never had a single highly placed spy in [America], and no plans for conquering the world."

The example of Adolf Hitler and his crusade against world Jewry and communism quickly came to mind. Rockwell believed Hitler had understood the Jewish menace from the outset of his career. He believed the Jews had involved Britain and America in the conflict for their own interests. Early in 1951, Rockwell found a copy of Mein Kampf in a local bookshop. He read it and saw the world anew:

[break]I found abundant "mental sunshine," which suddenly bathed the gray world in the clear light of reason and understanding. Word after word, sentence after sentence, stabbed into the darkness like thunderclaps and lightningbolts of revelation.

They tore and ripped away the cobwebs of more than thirty years of darkness. They brilliantly illuminated the mysteries of the heretofore impenetrable murk in a world gone mad. I was transfixed, hypnotized. I wondered at the utter, indescribable genius of it. I realized that National Socialism, the iconoclastic world view of Adolf Hitler, was the doctrine of scientific racial idealism. It was actually a new religion. George Lincoln Rockwell converted to National Socialism.

In later years, he wrote that future generations would see Adolf Hitler as the White Savior of the twentieth century. He also said they would view the Fuehrerbunker in Berlin as the Alamo of the White race. It took another eight years before he became a vocal Hitler supporter leading the American Nazi Party.

In November 1952, the navy sent him to a base at Keflavik in Iceland. He spent two years there as an F8F Bearcat pilot and reached the rank of commander. He met his second wife, Thora Hallgrimsson, there. She came from a prominent local family and was the niece of Iceland's ambassador to the United States. Rockwell was still deeply absorbed in Mein Kampf. He took his bride to Berchtesgaden, Germany, for their honeymoon.

They visited Hitler's Eagle's Nest with feelings of reverence and fascination. After returning to civilian life, he decided to enter magazine publishing. He hoped to find a living and a place to share his political ideas. He was also active in right-wing groups. He tried to start an American Federation of Conservative Organizations. He tried to move forward by hiding his core Nazi beliefs behind a respectable front. Eventually, he gave up on this strategy.
It failed to attract dedicated racists and anti-Semites. In the winter of 1957-58, Rockwell had a series of recurring dreams that always ended with him meeting Hitler.

This prompted him to go public against what he saw as Jewish power in America. He received financial support from Harold N. Arrowsmith, a wealthy anti-Semite. In Arlington, Virginia, they formed the National Committee to Free America from Jewish Domination. After a maverick campaign for the governorship of Georgia, Rockwell's first chance for confrontation came in May 1958. The U.S. government provided military aid to the Chamoun regime in Lebanon.

This aid was unpopular with Lebanese Arabs but enjoyed the support of the Israelis. On 29 July 1958, Rockwell led a picket of the White House. He protested against Jewish influence on the government. He also organized simultaneous demonstrations in Atlanta, Georgia, and Louisville, Kentucky. Earlier that year, Rockwell had helped found the National States Rights Party. This was a new anti-Semitic and racist party in Georgia.

On 12 October, a synagogue in Atlanta was blown up. The police seized Rockwell's supporters there. Newspapers around the world carried stories implicating Rockwell. Now he and his family were harassed, and his home was attacked. Arrowsmith retreated from the glare of the publicity and withdrew his support. His wife and children soon found the strain too great and returned to Iceland.

Rockwell was left alone by his family and former supporters. He faced a bleak and solitary future in the early months of 1959. One cold March morning in his house at Arlington, he sat alone with a huge swastika banner and a plaque of Hitler. After another "religious experience" that involved a brief state of universal awareness, he became convinced he had to fulfill Hitler's mission. This meant achieving a total, global victory over the forces of tyranny and oppression.
He would become an overt National Socialist and a self-proclaimed devotee of Hitler. He abandoned all thought of working with conservative groups or maintaining respectability.

He proudly displayed his Nazi banner. He recruited a handful of stormtroopers. He issued them grayshirt uniforms and swastika armbands. He mounted a large illuminated swastika on the roof of his house. He founded the American Party, later called the American Nazi Party. Besides the party headquarters at his house at 2507 North Franklin Road in Arlington, Rockwell also maintained a barracks in a run-down farmhouse nearby.
This housed his growing detachment of stormtroopers. After Rockwell chose to openly declare his support for Nazism, he focused all his actions on provoking Jews and society at all.

He saw society as a passive victim. He and his stormtroopers showed off their Nazi uniforms and badges. They missed no chance to shock and anger the public. Starting in 1960, his bold and sensational acts aimed to get maximum press coverage. This was for a fringe group that was considered crazy by others. The group had no more than two hundred members at its peak. Rockwell gave speeches to curious crowds and eager reporters. He stood surrounded by waving American and swastika flags.

He pushed a national and then global plan for eugenics to purify the Aryan race. He constantly called Jews the representatives of Marxism, unchecked capitalism, racial decay, and cultural Bolshevism. He demanded that they be tried and killed by gas. Rockwell forced the media to cover him. He did this by distributing inflammatory leaflets, causing public incidents, and yelling at crowds to provoke violent reactions. The American Nazi Party also had a racist policy toward Black people.

Rockwell rejected all race mixing and desegregation. He called them Jewish tricks to mix the American racial stock. He proposed moving all American Black people to a new African state. The U.S. government would fund this. On 25 February 1962, he spoke as a guest at a major Black Muslim convention in Chicago. He told an audience of more than twelve thousand people that he saw Elijah Muhammad as the Adolf Hitler of Black people.

In private, Rockwell imagined that this deportation plan would follow an upcoming race war and the mass killing of Black people. Rockwell's rise to fame depended heavily on the growing strength of the civil rights movement among American blacks, led by Martin Luther King Jr. In the early 1960s, Black people became more politically aware. Protests, marches, and the Watts and Harlem riots showed their impatience for true equality in American society.

This was a time when liberals worried about the plight of Black people. Measures to end segregation were put in place, and busing white and Black children to mixed schools became common. Rockwell hated all of this. He viewed Black people as a primitive, lazy race who wanted only simple pleasures and a life of irresponsibility. He believed they had been content as slaves, but their problems started after they became more involved in the social and economic life of white people.

Rockwell was convinced that Jews had pushed Black people into a hopeless position of supposed equality with whites. Deeply frustrated by their inability to compete in education and for jobs, Black people had become violent. This fulfilled Jewish plans to stir up the breakdown of the traditional order and the rise of communism.

By constantly emphasizing the threat of increasing Black riots, and combining this with his intense anti-Semitism and anti-communism, Rockwell tried to exploit deep American fears about the apparent disorder of the 1960s. The American Nazi Party carried out a steady stream of protests and disruptions during this period. Jewish youths were beaten, a synagogue in Bridgeport, Connecticut, was bombed, and the word "Jew" was painted on front doors.

In early 1962, Rockwell began planning a large rally to celebrate Hitler's birthday in April. That summer, he attended an international Nazi camp congress in Gloucestershire, organized by British neo-Nazi leader Colin Jordan.

Jordan held the event despite a Home Office ban on his entry to Britain. The group agreed to found a World Union of National Socialists. After his deportation back to the United States, Rockwell picketed the White House in protest. In September 1962, he gave one of his captains, Roy James, a medal for punching Martin Luther King Jr. in the face in Birmingham, Alabama. Several disruptive incidents also occurred in the House of Representatives.

One involved Robert A. Lloyd, who ran into the proceedings wearing blackface and a stovepipe hat. He shouted "Long live Rockwell" and asked to be seated as a Mississippi congressman, mimicking a Black person's speech. Rockwell himself was charged with disorderly conduct and stood trial in New York in June 1966. A Jewish lawyer defended him. The court acquitted Rockwell by upholding the free speech rights he denied to his enemies.
[break]While American groups made headlines, Rockwell tried to give the World Union of National Socialists (WUNS) a philosophical basis.

The WUNS was a federation of about seven national Nazi groups and parties. These groups were in Britain, the United States, Chile, Denmark, France, Argentina, and Australia. Colin Jordan originally led the WUNS when it formed in August 1962. Later that year, Jordan went to prison for public order offenses. Rockwell then took over the leadership. Through the WUNS, Rockwell wanted to show that National Socialism's racial idealism was a program for global Aryan power.

He wanted to place this above the nationalisms of the past. He aimed this message at a younger generation of new supporters. Rockwell believed this ideology was necessary to counter the Jewish world conspiracy. He also believed it was needed to counter the rising tide of colored peoples around the planet. In the spring of 1966, Rockwell started publishing a new WUNS periodical called National Socialist World. He published it from his headquarters in Arlington.
This was a new forum for international Nazi ideology. Rockwell appointed Dr. William Luther Pierce (b. 1933) as editor.

Pierce was new to the neo-Nazi movement. He was a physicist. He studied at Rice University and the California Institute of Technology. He completed his doctorate at the University of Colorado. He then taught at Oregon State University for three years. From the start, National Socialist World built its image as the leading international Nazi periodical. It featured long articles and book reviews. These pieces were ostensibly written for an educated, literate readership.

The magazine used high production standards. It was intended to be a quarterly. Each issue had over a hundred pages. The first issue included a philosophical appraisal of National Socialism by Colin Jordan. It also included an article by George Lincoln Rockwell on the value of vulgar Nazi propaganda. A condensed edition of The Lightning and the Sun by Savitri Devi took pride of place. Savitri Devi was a Hindu-Nordicist.

Her Hitler cult and philosophy of history deeply influenced neo-Nazi intellectuals (see chapter 5). By the winter of 1968, six issues had been published. These covered topics such as Gottfried Feder's twenty-five points of the German Nazi Party. They also included Matt Koehl on Hitler and National Socialist doctrine. And they featured Robert F. Williams on race war in America. The magazine promoted the memory of Hitler and the Third Reich in its articles and book reviews.

It also stressed the future role of the United States in the coming global racial struggle. In a long editorial for the summer 1967 issue, Pierce listed the forces in a war of dominance and survival. Rockwell saw the limits of a movement focused only on publicity stunts and provocation.

He began planning a longer-term strategy for the party. This strategy involved mass organization and electoral campaigning. On 1 January 1967, the party changed its name to the National Socialist White Peoples' Party (NSWPP). He was reversing his vehicle out of a parking lot.

He had just left a laundromat in Arlington. The assassin was John Patler. Patler had edited the party bulletin, The Stormtrooper. He had worked with the National Renaissance Party and Rockwell's American Nazi Party. He then left to start his own group, the American National Party. That group lasted from 1962 to early 1963. Patler later returned to join Rockwell. But he caused friction because of his unstable character and Marxist leanings.

In March 1967, Rockwell expelled him from the party. The reason was that Patler was stirring up dissent between fair and dark-skinned members. Patler was tried for murder. He was found guilty. He was sentenced to twenty years in prison. Rockwell's death gave the U.S. Nazi movement a martyr.

It soon split into several small extremist political groups. These groups were driven by fanaticism, paranoia, and suspicion. The NSWPP had about five hundred members. They split into various factions. Matt Koehl was Rockwell's chief lieutenant and formal successor. He had been a party member since 1963. Koehl kept the party name and the Arlington headquarters. James Warner first led this group. He had been secretary of the parent party in the early 1960s. The other major heirs of Rockwell's party were the National Socialist Liberation Front, the National Socialist Party of America, the National Alliance, and the Christian Defense League. Matthias Koehl Jr. was born on 22 January 1935 in Milwaukee, Wisconsin.

His parents were Hungarian immigrants of German descent. He studied journalism at the University of Wisconsin. Then he enlisted in the U.S. Marine Corps and served two years on active duty. As a schoolboy, Matt Koehl was drawn to anti-Semitism. In New York City, he joined James Madole's National Renaissance Party. In 1957, he helped organize the United White Party in Knoxville, Tennessee.
By 1958, he was the national organizer of the National States' Rights Party (NSRP).

This group agitated against desegregation in the southern states. In 1960, he joined Rockwell's movement. In 1961, he became leader of the Chicago section. In 1963, he joined Rockwell at party headquarters in Arlington. He was appointed corresponding secretary of the WUNS and national secretary of the NSWPP. He also edited and published both the WUNS Bulletin and the party's NS Bulletin.

His attraction to the American Nazi Party came from pride in his German origins. He also admired Adolf Hitler with a devotion bordering on religious adulation. In an early article for National Socialist World, Koehl praised Hitler as an idealist, a visionary, and the creator of a heroic new worldview. He described Hitler as someone who worked for a broad Aryan racial revival beyond the limits of German nationalism. This idea was inspired by the pan-Aryan Savitri Devi.

His swastika was intended to represent "the mission of the struggle for the victory of Aryan man" and a New Order of racial blood-brotherhood. In 1968, Koehl stated that "Adolf Hitler is National Socialism, just as National Socialism is Adolf Hitler."

He described Nazi ideology as a creed and a new faith. He rejected the view that American Nazis were fighting for a historical German phenomenon. These critics had failed to understand "the Truth which Adolf Hitler revealed to the world nearly 50 years ago.… Our goal involves far more than the realization of some superficial political or social scheme. It entails a universal transformation of ideas and things, an upheaval of unprecedented magnitude."

Koehl was impressed by Hitler's claim that humans can live only by higher ideals. He quoted a long passage from Mein Kampf. That passage claimed "the [National Socialist] philosophy of life corresponds to the innermost will of Nature,… until at last the best of mankind, having achieved possession of this earth, will have a free path for activity in domains [beyond]."
