Despite the difficulty of finding the actual perpetrators, authorities found strong evidence that these bomb attacks against Italy's civilian order were part of this strategy.

As police questioned Paolo Signorelli, Franco Freda, Claudio Mutti, and Stefano delle Chiaie, members of Italy's well-known neo-fascist underground, one name kept appearing in their investigations. This was a philosopher who served the terrorists as an inspiration, mentor, and guru. His name was Julius Evola. The official effort to catch the terrorists after the Bologna bombing was thorough.
Several members of the violent Nuclei Armati Rivoluzionari (NAR) fled to London and other foreign capitals to avoid arrest.

Wherever they contacted far-right groups abroad, knowledge of Evola spread. Julius Evola became a cult figure. His books and doctrines received increasing attention and discussion in the periodicals and conferences of the European New Right. He had an elegant, smooth-shaven face, a firm mouth, and an imperious gaze with a flashing monocle. Visual images of Evola began to appear in English, French, and German far-right periodicals during the 1980s.

His unqualified elitist posture and high-flown metaphysical critique of modernity attracted those who felt profoundly alienated from the norms and values of liberal society. More importantly, his esoteric elitism and spiritual authoritarianism offered a sophisticated ideology to right-wing intellectuals. These intellectuals saw Anglo-American neo-Nazism as a crude creed with limited appeal. Julius Evola (1898-1974) is a leading symbol of fascist idealism today.

He admired the Indo-Aryan tradition, where hierarchy, caste, authority, and the state held power over material life. Drawing on the heroic and sacred values of this mythical tradition, Evola promoted a radical doctrine against equality, democracy, liberalism, and Jews. He despised the modern world of popular rule and bourgeois values, as well as democracy and socialism.

He saw capitalism and communism as two sides of the same dark rule of materialism. In the 1930s, Evola was known as a bold and controversial theorist in Fascist Italy. He was also well known in Conservative Revolutionary circles in Germany during the Third Reich. Wounded at the end of the war, he spent the postwar years in a wheelchair in his apartment on the Corso Vittoria Emanuelle in central Rome.

Cut off from practical politics, Evola kept the image of a fascist sage untouched by Mussolini's fall until he died in 1974. A young generation of neo-fascists was strongly drawn to this oracle of violence and revolution. Giulio Cesare Andrea Evola was born in Rome on 19 May 1898.

He came from a noble Sicilian family. He soon rebelled against his strict Catholic upbringing. While studying industrial engineering in high school, he developed a strong interest in the Italian literary avant-garde. Giovanni Papini and Giuseppe Prezzolini dominated this group at the time. He also followed Filippo Tommaso Marinetti's futurist movement in art. At nineteen, he joined the Italian army during the later stages of the First World War.
He served as a mountain artillery officer at the Austrian front on the Asiago plateau in northern Italy.

After the war, Evola found it hard to adjust to settled life. Spiritual restlessness plagued him. He began a quest for self-transcendence. This meant breaking with the bourgeois values of the past. He dismissed futurism as loud and showy. He became the leading representative of the Dada movement in Italy. He gave readings of his avant-garde poetry in the Cabaret Grotte dell'Augusteo. This was Rome's answer to the Cabaret Voltaire in Zurich.
He exhibited his paintings in Rome, Milan, Lausanne, and Berlin. Evola disliked the commercialization of avant-garde art and its shift into rigid convention.

He stopped painting in 1922. He then wrote three transrational philosophical books, which he published during the 1920s. His philosophical idealism of the absolute individual was one way he sought self-transcendence. He did this in a postwar age of shattered values and moral uncertainty. He also became interested in oriental studies. He became a deep student of magic, the occult, alchemy, and Eastern religions. He experimented with hallucinogenic drugs.

He discovered the ancient Theravadin Buddhist text, the Majjhima-Nikaya. In 1923, he wrote the introduction to an Italian translation of the Tao-Te-Ching. He attended meetings of the Italian Independent Theosophical League. Its president, Decio Calvari, introduced him to the study of Tantrism. This especially captured Evola's imagination. He began corresponding with Sir John Woodroffe, a learned British orientalist.

Woodroffe revealed the secrets of this esoteric Hindu school in The Serpent of Power and other books. He published these under his pseudonym, Arthur Avalon. Evola presented his own study of Tantrism and kundalini yoga. He based this on Woodroffe's works and original texts. He titled it L'uomo come potenza [The Yoga of Power] (1925). Tantrism began in India around A.D. 400.

It was a radical Hindu cult. It focused on women, goddesses, and sexual energy. It rejected the usual Hindu practice of abstinence. Tantric rituals celebrated intoxicating drinks, meat, fish, mudras, and ritual sex. Tantrism centers on the idea of breaking all ties or bonds (pasha). People with an animal nature are disqualified. They are enslaved by appetite, lust, custom, and religious conformity. The superior adept (vira) uses taboo and spiritually dangerous practices.

These include orgies and intoxication. The adept raises his consciousness to supreme levels. He unites with the divine female power of Shakti. Shakti animates and inspires the whole universe. This process gives him exceptional knowledge (vidya) and magical powers (siddhis). Tantric doctrine stresses the male god Shiva and his bride Shakti. Their sexual union is personified in ritual intercourse. This act symbolizes the creative impulses of the cosmos.

Male ejaculation of semen is usually discouraged. This channels the energy of orgasm away from creating organic life. It directs that energy toward a powerful ascent experience. Tantrism complemented Western idealism in Evola's search for self-transcendence. Its secrecy and elitism essentially rejected the modern world of rationalism and democracy.

Evola wrote that the knowledge and powers the modern world pursues are democratic. That means they are available at educational institutions to anyone with enough intelligence. Likewise, technology is democratic. An instrument or weapon can be used by anyone with sufficient training. By contrast, the tantric magical powers (siddhis) are always personal and exceptional achievements. Only the few can access them. But Evola also thought Tantrism arose specifically in fifth-century India.

This was a time of spiritual decadence. Men could no longer achieve an otherworldly liberation from the world. Instead, they sought a full-blooded embrace of life's delights. This meant liberty within the world. For this reason, Tantrism was more akin to Western modes of thought. It was also appropriate to the modern age. This age is characterized by density, coarseness, and moral decline. Tantric rituals essentially transformed "poison into medicine" for the strong and liberated individual.

[break]In the 1920s, Evola devoted himself to studying the Western esoteric tradition. Through Theosophical and Masonic circles, he met Arturo Reghini (1878-1946), a Roman occultist who immersed himself in alchemy, magic, and theurgy. Reghini edited two journals, Atanòr (1924) and Ignis (1925). Their contents covered initiate studies ranging from Pythagoreanism to yoga, and from Hebrew Cabalism to Cagliostro's Egyptian Freemasonry.
Evola wrote many reviews and articles on Tantrism, the nature of woman, and Rudolf Steiner, as well as an essay on Dionysius.

A circle soon gathered around Reghini and Evola. Giovanni Colazza and Duke Giovanni Colonna di Cesarò brought a strong anthroposophical influence to the group. The group adopted the name UR. Close to it were Guiliano Kremmerz (1861-1939), founder of the Fraternity of Myriam, which had an interest in sex magic, and an Indian alchemist, C. S. Narayana Ariar Shiyali. Between 1927 and 1929, the group published Ur, renamed Krur in 1929.
This monthly journal featured essays and rituals, including many of Evola's magical studies. Arturo Reghini wanted to renew the classical tradition in a fiercely anti-Christian, pagan spirit.

He strongly influenced Evola between 1924 and 1930. He introduced Evola to the traditional texts of alchemy. They saw alchemy's symbolism as a universal key to the macrocosm of the universe and the microcosm of man. After presenting an initial study of alchemy in Krur, Evola published his book La tradizione ermetica [The Hermetic Tradition] (1931).

This book treated hermeticism as an ancient pagan tradition. Evola believed that the hidden symbolism of hermetico-alchemical cosmology described a heroic, pre-Christian worldview. In that world, a warrior aristocracy reigned supreme. Evola cites the "tree" as a symbol of knowledge and immortality. In a heroic myth, a person who fails while trying to win the powers of the tree simply has more courage than luck. He can try again and regain his dignity.

But in a postheroic religious era, he has sinned. His action is a sacrilege and is damned. Evola saw alchemy and hermeticism as an occult survival of the "Royal Art." This was a universal secret science of human and natural transformation based on heroic concepts. It is now buried beneath pusillanimous Christian priestcraft. Evola's political thought was anti-democratic and anti-modernist.
This stance came from his readings of Plato, Nietzsche, and Oswald Spengler. Spengler wrote the famous work The Decline of the West (1918-22).

Evola later translated this book into Italian. However, Reghini was a more immediate influence. Both men saw the Roman patrician world and the imperial constitution as close to their ideal state. This strict hierarchy reflected a higher, transcendental, and absolute order. Christianity's leveling, egalitarian universalism negated this political order. It ultimately dissolved it. This process heralded the disorder of the modern world. In 1924, Reghini wrote in Atanòr.

He noted that fifteen years earlier, he had predicted the rise of an Italian regime based on the ancient world. He welcomed Fascism. In 1923, a member of an order dedicated to this revival presented the fasces to Mussolini. The fasces is a bundle of rods containing an Etruscan bronze axe. This axe symbolized the magistrate's power in ancient Rome. The Group of UR also performed rituals. These rituals aimed to inspire the Fascist regime with the spirit of imperial Rome.

[break]Evola started writing political journalism in 1925. His articles criticized Fascism for being too close to the church, for the careerism of its officials, and for relying on the bourgeoisie and the masses. Evola wanted to change Fascism to fit his ideas of spiritual aristocracy and monarchy. These attacks peaked when he published his book Imperialismo Pagano [Pagan Imperialism] in 1928.

In it, he praised the ideal of ancient Rome, condemned all Christian churches, and attacked the secular universalism of both American democracy and Soviet communism. Mussolini was impressed and interested enough by these ideas to write a journal article responding to Reghini's call for Fascism to start an era of "pagan imperialism."

However, given Italy's political reality, Mussolini could never afford to take an anti-Christian path. The regime aimed to sign a concordat with the Catholic Church. This goal led to the Lateran Treaty of 1929 with the Vatican. This outcome dashed the Group of UR's hopes of influencing the new order. Evola built his anti-modernist political doctrine on his studies of oriental and esoteric subjects.
Through Reghini, he found the work of René Guénon (1886-1951), a French orientalist.

Guénon argued for a primordial Tradition. This Tradition is implicit in the universe's metaphysical structure. It is also reflected in the authentic religious traditions of East and West. Guénon grew up in a Catholic family. He studied philosophy in Paris. Then he immersed himself in the French occult revival at the turn of the century. He had a passing interest in Theosophy and Freemasonry. He was especially receptive to Advaita Vedanta.

Vivekananda was making this school better known in the West. Guénon studied Indian philosophy under Hindu teachers. In his books, A General Introduction to the Study of Hindu Doctrines (1921) and Man and His Becoming According to the Vedanta (1925), Guénon described the ultimate reality according to Vedanta.

This metaphysical unity lies beyond reason or discursive thought. One can grasp it only from an inward-directed point of view. This grasp is a suprarational intellectual intuition. Through this intuition, the Self (Atman) communicates with the ego. Guénon believed that Hindu Vedanta held a "primordial Tradition."

Its transcendent truths also lived in true Islam and medieval Catholicism. The modern West had lost almost all contact with this Tradition. In his key work of pessimism, The Crisis of the Modern World (1927), Guénon showed how the West fell into spiritual decline after the Middle Ages ended.

Materialism took over all life. Art and culture chased only surface things. Thought and science got lost in endless analysis, division, and multiplicity. Western life focused entirely on "becoming." This brought a focus on rational means, speed, and technical efficiency. "Humanistic" ideas about man's importance and consciousness replaced all transcendent references. This created a flawed cult of individualism. It also centered on social and political freedom.

Guénon saw this decline as the fulfillment of the Hindu Puranic divisions of time. The four yugas, each getting shorter, matched the golden, silver, bronze, and iron ages of classical times. The West had been in the fourth age, the Kali Yuga or "dark age," for over six thousand years. Evola felt a strong connection with Guénon's esoteric pessimism.

In this brief outline, he found all the reasons for the decay of a primordial heroic world. That world was based on sacred authority and metaphysical absolutes. He praised Guénon's harsh attack on the empty relativism and chaotic liberalism of the modern world. He immediately began work on his own anti-modernist text, Rivolta contro il mondo moderno [Revolt against the Modern World] (1934).

This remains his best-known and most important book. In it, Evola described a metaphysical Aryo-Vedic tradition. This tradition allegedly governed the religious and political institutions of archaic Indo-European societies. He traced the growth of golden age myths. These myths relate to polar symbolism and the Arctic origin of the white Aryan race. He did this through ancient Indian, Iranian, Greek, and Amerindian texts. He acknowledged Bâl Gangadhar Tilak, a Brahman scholar.

He also acknowledged Herman Wirth, an amateur prehistorian of an Atlantis culture. Wirth later became director of Heinrich Himmler's Ahnenerbe. The sacred nature of regal authority defined this traditional world. So did the mystery of ritual, initiation, and consecration. The divine origins of patrician rule, chivalry, and a rigid caste hierarchy also defined it. This world stood in total opposition to the secular, individualistic, and liberal concerns of the modern world.

Like Guénon, Evola accepted the Hindu cycle of the ages. He equated the modern world with the dark age, or Kali Kuga. In this age, all tradition is forgotten. Disorder is widespread, and society is degenerate. Evola's view of history and political theory rested on a basic "doctrine of two natures," or "primordial Tradition."

This doctrine separates the metaphysical order from the physical one. It divides the immortal world from the mortal one. It sets the higher realm of "being" apart from the lower realm of "becoming." It places the dominant, virile principle of spirit above the lower, feminine domain of matter. For Evola, the power of spirit in Traditional societies was clear in their strict hierarchy of functions. This hierarchy still existed in the caste system of Aryan-Hindu society.

Lower functions dealt with mere matter and organic vitality. Higher functions were increasingly ruled by spirit. In the Hindu caste hierarchy, slaves or workers (sudras) were below the bourgeoisie or merchants (vaisyas). Above them stood the warrior nobility (kshatriyas). All these groups were subject to the spiritual authority of the priests (brahmins). This order, where powers of the spirit matched caste, existed in all Traditional societies.

Evola points to its presence in Plato's Republic, in ancient Iranian society, and in the social divisions of peasants, burghers, nobility, and clergy in the European Middle Ages. The priestly caste sat at the top of the social hierarchy. In the world of early Tradition, this was not a professional priesthood but royalty itself.

Evola believed that the roots of authority had a metaphysical nature. All earthly power came from spiritual authority. Evola quoted the Aryo-Vedic Laws of Manu. He claimed that in societies still based on Tradition, the ruler was not a "mere mortal." Instead, the ruler was "a great deity standing in the form of a man." The Egyptian pharaoh was seen as a manifestation of Ra or Horus. The kings of Rome were incarnations of Zeus. The Assyrian kings were incarnations of Baal.

The Persian shahs were incarnations of the gods of light. Kings and the patriciate performed sacred rites. These rites linked the human world with the gods. They formed a "bridge" to the supernatural realm. Holding and practicing these sacred rites defined the priestly caste. This caste also led the state. The state held the current of divine power.

"The supernatural element was the foundation of the idea of a traditional patriciate and of legitimate royalty: what constituted an ancient aristocrat was not merely a biological legacy or a racial selection, but rather a sacred tradition." Evola closely linked the doctrine of caste to his view of history as a process of decline.

He based his cyclical view of history on the Puranic divisions of time. Evola asserted that civilization inevitably declined from the Satya Yuga, or golden age. In that age, the primordial Tradition was observed and upheld. Civilization then passed through the Treta and Dvapara Yugas. These ages were successively shorter and more decadent. This decline continued until the onset of the Kali Yuga, or dark age. In the Kali Yuga, the Tradition is wholly forgotten.
Social disorder, spiritual alienation, and violence characterize this wretched epoch.

These traits lead to a point of cataclysmic dissolution. At that point, the next Satya Yuga begins its redemptive cycle. Evola recognized that this prehistoric account of a golden age and subsequent decline hardly accorded with Darwin's evolutionist ideas. He insisted that ancient testimonies and writings from all great world cultures make no mention of bestial cavemen. Instead, they describe "more-than-human" beings in a better, brighter, and superhuman ("divine") past.

He speculates that the absence of fossil remains of a superior primordial mankind might indicate its existence prior to materialization. Evola ultimately dismisses evolutionism as a science typical of dark-age myth. This myth derives the higher from the lower and man from animal. It does so in total ignorance of Tradition. Evola presents a broad view of prehistoric cycles of civilization that match the four traditional yugas.

The remote prehistoric epoch of the golden age was a real place in the Arctic. This explains the many polar myths of origin. A spiritual disaster coincided with a catastrophic tilt in the earth's axis. This forced a primal Hyperborean, or extreme northern, race to migrate. The first wave moved toward North America and the northern regions of Eurasia. The second wave moved toward a now lost continent in the mid-Atlantic.

Using occult ideas from Helena Blavatsky's Theosophy, Evola speculated that a large Atlantean group mixed with aboriginal Southern races. These included proto-Mongols and proto-Negroes who may have originated in the lost continent of Lemuria. Following the doctrine of two natures, Evola tended to see spirituality as the prior determinant of a culture, rather than its ethnic or racial population.

However, because certain races carried Southern spirituality, they were identified as decadent factors. The first wave of Hyperborean emigration remained wholly Nordic. The Western civilization of Atlantis absorbed many Southern-Lemurian traits. This gave rise to a dichotomy. One side is solar, male, or Uranian spirituality, found in Northern-Atlantic races. The other is lunar, female, or Demetrian spirituality, found in mixed Southern-Atlantean races. Evola took Bachofen's idea of matriarchy.

He did not see it as an early stage in a linear evolution. Instead, he viewed it as an independent Southern world. This world was home to other races. These races eventually clashed with Northern-Atlantic traditions. This Southern "mother-culture" was later defined by Asiatic-Mediterranean goddesses of life. Examples include Isis, Ishtar, Cybele, and Demeter. These goddesses subordinate the male, solar principle. Images like the child on the lap of the Great Mother also fit this pattern.

Virile spirituality is different. It is implicit in intelligible essences. It appears in gods of war, sky, and the sun. The "mothers" preside over a telluric and cthonic world. This world consists of earth, darkness, and moon. The maternal principle holds that we are all children of the earth. This culture encouraged collectivist social structures. It promoted ideals of sharing, brotherhood, and equality. Evola saw these "lunar" themes of peace and community as typical of Demetrism.

This represents the second silver age, or Treta Yuga. In that age, a priestly caste ruled without virile, regal authority. Evola found further evidence of this feminized spirituality in ancient cults of emasculation. He also saw it in priests wearing robes that resembled female attire. Evola's dualism of male and female spirituality owed an even greater debt to the young Jewish philosopher Otto Weininger (1880-1903). His famous book Geschlecht und Charakter
[break][Sex and Character] (1903) set out a metaphysical view of the principles of male and female sexuality.

Weininger glorified higher reason, Platonic truth, and Kantian imperatives. He rejected the fallen, mundane sphere of matter and nature. Only man aspires to the eternal life of the spirit. Woman embraces the lower life of the earth and the senses. Man may choose between a life that ends with physical death, or a life where death means a return to complete purity. Woman, on the other hand, is part of the material world. She lacks any higher spirit. She knows nothing of logic and morality.

She has no ego or individuality. She leads a purely sexual, impersonal existence. Man is a subject. Woman is an object. Her only desire is to be formed and given meaning by male attention and sexual coitus. Ontologically, she is a nullity. Her existence simply guarantees the continued reproduction of the material, sensate world. Evola's celebration of virile spirituality was rooted in Weininger's work. This work was widely translated by the end of the First World War.
[break]Evola traced the development of Northern-Atlantic heroic spirituality among the ancient Aryans of India and Iran.

He noted that in India, the term arya was a synonym for dvija, meaning "twice-born" or "regenerated." However, he observed that India eventually took a contemplative path. It abandoned the regal and solar path of a spiritual patriciate. Evola blamed the rise of a professional brahmin caste on the decay of the original dynasties. These dynasties had led the Aryan conquest of India. The Aryan worldview in India broke down after Brahman (God) was identified with all nature in a pantheistic sense.

This reflected the spiritual influence of Southern races. In Iran, heroic spirituality led to the warrior cult of Ahura Mazda. It also produced the Aryan ethic of truth and loyalty. Furthermore, it shaped the view of the cosmos as an order maintained through sacred rites. Some decline caused by lunar naturalism and decadent priestcraft led to a solar reaction in the doctrine of Zarathustra. Evola compared this to Buddha's reforming role in decadent Hindu India.

Mithraism then started a new heroic cycle of Aryan, solar spirituality. This cycle opposed all telluric cults of earth and darkness. Once Mithraism declined in Iran, Evola saw its later revival in the Roman Empire. He viewed this as a spiritual path that the West might have followed instead of Christianity. Carl Gustav Jung shared this speculation. In Western history during the current Kali Yuga, Evola praised the Roman Empire.

He saw it as a major effort to reverse the decay of the Mediterranean South. He also saw it as a way to build a unified state based on heroic Aryan-Western spirituality. Evola guessed that Rome's new strictness and rise came from prehistoric immigrant groups. These were "reindeer" and "battle-axe" peoples from Hyperborea. They formed regenerative cores among the original races of the pre-Roman Italian peninsula. These original groups included Etruscans, Sabines, Sabellians, Siculians, and others.

The original peoples who worshipped lunar, female gods usually formed the lower class of plebeians. They lived beneath a patriciate that valued authority and imperium. Roman spirituality then lacked emotional intensity and mysticism toward the divine. Its main virtues were duty, loyalty, heroism, order, and dominion. The revolt of the Roman patriciate against the foreign Tarquin dynasty in 509 B.C. was a representative event.

So were the fall of Capua and the destruction of Carthage in 146 B.C. These events showed Rome's methodical removal of centers of earlier Southern influence. As Rome rose to imperial power, the strong idea of a divinely ordered state replaced all earlier priestly and Demetrian forms of society. The patriciate performed sacred rites under precise law, and all society was subject to strict paternal rights.

Continuing his theme of Northern and Southern spirituality, Evola saw Rome maintain its heroic Aryan-Western culture of hierarchy and state. It did this by constantly rejecting Dionysian and Aphrodistic influences, such as the banning of the Bacchanalia. Roman suspicion of mystery religions of Asian origin and Pythagorean philosophers was also rooted in a spiritual antipathy toward Demetrian throwbacks.

Its famous civil wars, involving figures like Pompeius, Cassius, and Anthony, were contests with Southern revisionism. Through its single-minded dedication to heroic civilization, "Rome shifted the centre of the historical West from the telluric to the Uranian mystery, from the lunar world of the Mothers to the solar world of the Fathers."

By the time of Augustus, the imperial cult had effectively restored the spiritual "genius" of the emperor as a bridge with the supernatural realm. Roman universalism seemed to stretch to the limits of the known world. Evola saw the rise of Christianity as a process of decline unlike anything before. The Christian ideal of a religion open to everyone, regardless of race, tradition, or caste, dissolved Roman order and hierarchy.
By placing simple faith above heroic and initiatory spiritual growth, Christianity appealed to the common people.

It promised salvation from subjection, the world, and even death. Christian egalitarianism, based on brotherhood, love, and collectivism, fought against all Roman ideas of duty, honor, and command. The Christian God was not the god of the patricians. That god was invoked while standing upright and carried before the legions.
Instead, the Christian God was a crucified god-man. People prayed to him in a spirit of sin and atonement.

The spread of Christianity marked a shift from the masculine to the feminine. It moved from the solar to the tellurian. It replaced martial aristocratic values with mystical plebeian sentiment. Evola detected the revival of female, lunar spirituality in its myths. These myths featured a sacrificed and regenerated agricultural god and the Virgin birth. Its iconography of Mother and Child showed this too. Nevertheless, Evola believed Christianity was only a symptom of decline.

He held that the Roman heroic cycle was already exhausted in ethnic chaos and cosmopolitan disintegration. Evola's "Northern" bias led him to see the German peoples as a strong force against Christianity's female culture. As descendants of Northern-Aryan racial stocks, the Germans kept their prehistoric purity outside the cosmopolitan late Roman Empire.

Their Norse myths and tribal ethos held traces of the primordial Tradition. The god Wotan-Odin granted victory, possessed esoteric wisdom, and had secrets he did not give to any woman. He led the dead heroes. The oldest Nordic stocks saw Asgard in the far north as the home of the gods. This ancestral memory linked them with the Indo-Aryans in the East. At the end of the Roman cycle, the German tribes were initially a barbarian force of destruction.

They brought warrior leadership, fealty, and freedom into the medieval European political order. While laying the basis of feudal caste society, these values represented solar spirituality against the feminizing Church.

Chivalry upheld the hero over the saint and the conqueror over the martyr. Loyalty and honor were the highest virtues. Cowardice was a greater evil than sin. Evola saw the quest for the Grail and the Crusades as symbols of a solar tradition within Christian civilization. In the medieval struggle between popes and emperors for precedence, Evola identified the Ghibelline dynasty of Hohenstauffen emperors (1152-1272) as the Germanic champion of "sacred regality" in a revived Holy Roman Empire.
[break]Evola viewed the Italian communes of the Renaissance as early adopters of a secular, anti-traditional idea of society.

This idea rested on economic and mercantile factors. It led to Jewish trade in gold. It also drove the rise of banking and capitalism. Evola praised Dante's condemnation of the Lombard cities' revolt. He also supported the principle of self-government. The Hohenstauffen emperors fought over Italy. They did not seek German expansion. Instead, they fought "against the rebellious race of merchants and burghers in the name of honor and spirit."
Evola found it highly significant that the Renaissance began in Italy. This was not because of its Roman heritage. It happened because Italy was the constant site of conflict between North and South.

It was also the site of conflict between solar and lunar spirituality. In his view, the Renaissance was not a revival of classical civilization. It was only a borrowing of classical decadent forms. These forms served a wholly new spirit of atomization and independence.

Emperors once ruled by nobility and supernatural authority. The new political ideal appeared in Machiavelli's Prince. In this work, an individual can only rule in his own name. He must use cunning, violence, and diplomacy to do so. Evola saw Renaissance humanism as the start of modern thought.

It focused only on the human side of arts, philosophy, and science. Humanism embraced individualism. It did this by rejecting the transcendent world. It glorified the "self" as a false center. The Reformation opposed Rome because of its hierarchy and dogma. These were remnants of Tradition. The Reformation made individual conscience the only authority in religion. Private interpretation of the Bible stressed critical judgment and human reason.

This would eventually challenge all authority and metaphysical reality. Rationalism joined forces with empiricism and experimentalism. Together, they created modern science. Its only object was the material world. Science deals only with the physical dimension. It seeks mathematical relations, laws of consistency, and the calculation of outcomes. Science uses a uniform standard of truth based on "soulless numbers." It ignores quality and symbol. This helped lower social orders rise.

It did so by degrading and democratizing the idea of knowledge. Science denies all transcendence. It tries in vain to compensate the human spirit. It offers power over material objects, titanic technology, and huge industries. Evola traced the ongoing decline of the Kali Yuga in European politics.

Emperors stopped seeking imperial consecration. Frederick III was the last emperor crowned in Rome in 1452. Kings and princes began to claim absolute power. This subverted the universal ecumene with the idea of the national state. Free cities and republics asserted their independence. They did this against imperial authority and against the nobility. The principle of a common body of law declined. Chivalry decayed into a defense of temporal and territorial ambition.

Raison d'état destroyed the foundation of Christendom and European unity. It did so through wars of kings against emperors, alliances with the sultan, and the rise of territorial princes who were virtually independent from the empire. Royalty became increasingly secular. It was divorced from its former spiritual authority. With the Reformation, states themselves began to act as schisms from superordained authority.

In Catholic states during the Counter-Reformation after the Council of Trent, the assertion of the "divine right" of kings was no more than an empty formula. It concealed the spiritual vacuity of kingship divorced from authentic universalism. Evola viewed the rise of national monarchies as a middle step in the cycle of decline.

These monarchies first claimed absolute power. Then, individuals challenged them. These individuals demanded freedom based on their own free, sovereign autonomy. Moving away from the sacred center weakened the principle of hierarchy. The fall of supernatural authority allowed lower social groups to emerge, revolt, and gain freedom. The breaking up of the European imperial order predicted the rise of merchant classes. It also predicted ideas of popular sovereignty and the French Revolution.

In that revolution, authority and law are legitimate only as the will of citizens. This principle of authority from below became the basis of democracy and liberalism in modern bourgeois states. A later stage of this push for equality led to the collectivism of mass consumer society or communism. America and Soviet Russia typified this stage. As this decadent decline in the Kali Yuga progresses, matter rules over form. Leveling happens on every level.

Anti-traditional values of secular humanism, hedonism, and utilitarianism dominate. Evola's idea of involution, or regression through the cycle of ages, matched the law of the regression of castes. Once the sacred rule of the mythical golden age is lost, power falls to the second warrior caste.

In Europe, this caste is represented by national monarchs and absolute sovereigns. Over time, the aristocracy decays. Power then shifts to the third caste, the mercantile class. The Italian communes, merchants, and Jewish bankers of the Renaissance eventually led to capitalist oligarchs and middle classes. These groups consolidated their power by using liberal and democratic ideologies. They drove bourgeois revolutions in the nineteenth century.
By the start of the twentieth century, organized labor and communist revolution tried to transfer power to the fourth caste of slaves.

This move reduced all values to matter, machines, and the reign of quantity. This cycle of castes extended to the international arena. Evola saw the First World War as a global struggle between the third caste, the Entente democracies, and the remaining forces of the second caste, the feudal and aristocratic Central Powers. The Second World War began with the anti-democratic and authoritarian regimes of Germany and Italy challenging the plutocracies.

They did so in the name of fascist collectivism. Eventually, this war became a crusade of democracy. Democracy allied with the fourth caste of the Soviet Union. They fought against a "regression" to warrior castes. The result was the division of Europe. America and Russia became the dominant mass societies. They were united in their crude materialist and utilitarian civilization. Evola viewed race as a spiritual concept tied to spirit and tradition.

He used the phrase "a man of race" to mean "a man of breeding," carrying aristocratic connotations. Evola developed a three-part racial theory involving body, mind (religion and adherence to Tradition), and soul (character and emotions).

In this view, the inner determined the outer forms. Discussing Arthur de Gobineau's racial ideas, Evola argued that races declined only when their spirit failed. Evola actually rejected Alfred Rosenberg and other biological racists in the Third Reich. He implied that their physical anthropology relied on reductionist and materialist science. Evola's interpretation of the word "Aryan" was similarly idealistic. In his book on Buddhism, he translated arya to mean aristocratic or high caste.

He also described it as illuminated in a spiritual sense and linked it to the Nordic, light-skinned Aryan conquerors of India. It will be recalled that Evola's ideal of the "Aryan-Roman" race was defined by its sacral and aristocratic quality. Mussolini adopted Evola's ideas as the official Fascist racial theory in 1938. At that time, Italy enacted its own racial laws, which were distinct from those of Nazi Germany. Evola's anti-Semitism was also metaphysical.
He saw Jewry as a symbol for the rule of money, individualism, and economic materialism in the modern world.

Otto Weininger's influence is clear here. Weininger defined Jewishness (Judentum) as an "intellectual tendency" or "psychic constitution." This trait appears in all individuals and races. However, it finds its fullest expression in historical Jewry. Weininger claimed that Jews resembled women in their metaphysical essence. Like women, he said, Jews had neither a soul nor a need for immortality.

He pointed to the Jewish contribution to science as an urge to deny all transcendence through a mechanistic-materialist worldview. Weininger argued that the Jewish devaluation of all higher meaning was evident in their support of Darwinism and man's descent from the apes.

It was also evident in their support of Marxism and the economic interpretation of history. He stated that Jews lack all conviction. They are ambiguous and endlessly flexible. Significantly, they have no desire for property. They prefer coin and mobile capital so they can quickly change direction for gain. Weininger viewed the modern age, with its increasing emphasis on business and journalism, as a social universe in the image of the Jews.

[break]Otto Weininger's critique of the "psychic constitution" of Jewishness was central to Evola's anti-modernist idealism. Evola saw the harmful Jewish influence in early modern Europe through rational calculation and banking.

Starting in the ghettos, trade with gold and interest eventually conquered and reshaped the world. But the Jews were not the only pioneers. Evola followed Karl Marx and Werner Sombart in seeing a revival of the "Hebraic spirit" in Protestant puritanism, rationalism, and capitalism. The Jews had only used humanism and the Reformation to create the secularized, scientistic, and mechanistic world of modernity.

However, it was the "Jewish spirit [which] destroys everything through rationalism and calculation, leading to a world consisting of machines, things and money instead of persons, traditions and fatherlands." Much later, in 1970, Evola described Hitler's fanatical anti-Semitism as a paranoid idée fixe with tragic consequences. He called it a stain on the reputation of the Third Reich that would be hard to remove. Evola's anti-Semitism also attacked real Jews.
He quoted the Protocols of the Learned Elders of Zion, a famous text of Jewish conspiracy theory.

Evola saw the Jewish press and finance as tools to spread the liberal virus. This virus would destroy the monarchical and aristocratic parts of Western culture. Evola wrote a preface and an essay for the Italian edition of the Protocols. The essay was titled "The Authenticity of Protocols as Proven by Jewish Tradition." It repeated modern anti-Semitic slurs and lies. He found plenty of evidence for the harmful influence of individual Jews in American banking and industry.

He also saw this influence in the Russian Revolution. Jews were always at the front of modern ideas. These included Sigmund Freud and psychoanalysis, Albert Einstein and the theory of relativity, and Emile Durkheim and the "sociology" of religion. Under stress, Evola wrote vicious anti-Semitic journalism. After the murder of his friend Corneliu Codreanu (1899-1938), the leader of the fascist Romanian Iron Guard, Evola attacked "the Judaic horde."
He described a possible communist takeover in Romania as "the filthiest tyranny, the talmudic, Israelite tyranny." Evola found Italian Fascism too compromising.

He then sought recognition in the Third Reich. He lectured there frequently from 1934 onward. National Socialism opposed liberalism and "Jewish culture." Yet Evola disliked Nazi populism, plebeian culture, and nationalism. He saw these as signs of modernity. Nazi racism rested on biological materialism. The Führer principle also ignored all transcendent reality. Under this principle, Hitler drew his legitimacy from the Volk. Evola praised the SS.
He saw it as a tool for the state, hierarchy, racial heritage, and a new warrior elite.

SS authorities rejected Evola's ideas. They viewed them as supranational, aristocratic, and thus reactionary. Evola found his closest allies among the Conservative Revolutionaries in Germany and Austria. These included Edgar Julius Jung, Wilhelm Stapel, and Othmar Spann. Several of his books were translated into German. Many of his articles appeared in German conservative and right-wing periodicals between 1928 and 1943.

In August 1943, Evola met with the deposed Mussolini. This meeting took place at Hitler's field headquarters in East Prussia. Evola was involved in the short-lived Republic of Salò. He fled Rome before the Allies in late 1943. He spent the rest of the war in Vienna. He worked with fascist leaders across Central Europe. He performed liaison services for the SS. He helped recruit a pan-European army to defend the Continent against Soviet and American invaders.

An air raid severely injured him on 12 March 1945. He was permanently paralyzed in both legs. After returning to Italy, he lived in Rome. He became the guru of the neo-fascist right. He died in 1974. How did Evola's grand mythological ideas and deep pessimism lead to neo-fascist action and violence? In the early 1950s, Evola turned his writing toward practical politics. His journalism and his pamphlet Orientamenti

[break][Orientations] (1950) pushed the "legionary spirit" and "warrior ethic." They also outlined how to keep ideals, elites, and order alive. They did this by having the neo-fascist party, the Movimento Sociale Italiano (MSI), along with the police and army, take over the state. In his book Gli Uomini e le Rovine [Men Among the Ruins] (1953), he restated his doctrine.

He framed it as counter-revolution. He argued that the state stands above the economy. He called for an anti-bourgeois, warrior's view of life. By the time Evola wrote Cavalcare la Tigre [Riding the Tiger] (1961), he had lost hope in these fixes.

The postwar economic boom and consumerism were wiping out what was left of tradition, hierarchy, and order. Evola's critique was harsh. He said nothing in this final stage of the Kali Yuga deserved to survive. Evola presents the ideal of the "active nihilist." This person is ready to use violence against modern decay. What did this mean in practice?

Evola claimed to stand above all political parties. Yet he strongly influenced young right-wing Italians. These young people had given up hope that Italy would return to the mainstream of liberal development. Many compared their fate to Dante. Dante had lamented the passing of the Ghibelline order. Young postwar neo-fascists sat at Evola's feet. They listened to this oracle of aristocratic values and war with modernity. Giuliano Salierni was a young MSI activist in the early 1950s.

He recalled Evola's call for violence. Pino Rauti, one of Evola's closest disciples, founded the neo-fascist Ordine Nuovo (ON) in 1956. ON ideology was full of Evolan terminology. This included aristocracy, hierarchy, elite rule, political soldiers, and warrior asceticism. Its strategy matched Evola's initial postwar ideas. These ideas called for strengthening the state. This included seizing power through police, armed forces, veteran groups, and youth organizations.

Giorgio Almirante, the MSI leader, hailed Evola as "our Marcuse - only better." This alluded to Herbert Marcuse, a Frankfurt School veteran. Marcuse was the doyen of the 1968 student revolutions. Violence in Italian neo-fascism grew worse with many bomb attacks and massacres. This started with the Piazza Fontana explosion in Milan in April 1969.
In 1971, Adriano Romauldi, a leading young neo-fascist, named Evola the intellectual hero of militant right-wing youth in Italy.

He did this "because the teaching of Evola is also a philosophy of total war." By 1975, the far-right underground used a leftist strategy to attack the state itself. They murdered officials and robbed ministries. The trend toward violence continued. By the late 1970s, a cult of action replaced ideology. This elevated combat to an existential duty.

Neo-fascist terrorists like Franco Freda and Mario Tuti often reprinted and cited Evola's two most militant tracts, Metafisica della guerra (1935) and Dottrina ariana (1940). They praised "heroic" and "exemplary" action without an instrumental purpose. Inspired by these ideas of metaphysical struggle, the underground bulletin Quex (1978-81) glorified Corneliu Codreanu's "legionaries" and "fulfillment in heroic death."

It did this in the same breath as Evola's "luminous forces against all tellurism and chaos." The name Quex comes from Hitlerjugend Quex, a Nazi youth hero. Groups like Movimento Revoluzionario Popolare, Terza Positione, and Nuclei Armati Rivoluzionari then unleashed a surge of black terrorism in Italy. This continued until most militants were captured or killed, and a few fled abroad. In late 1980, a group of fugitives from Nuclei Armati Rivoluzionarice (NAR) arrived in London.

There, they contacted Britain's far-right National Front (NF). Roberto Fiore, a close associate of the imprisoned Mario Tuti, was part of this group. So were Massimo Morsello and his wife Marinella Rita, as well as Amadeo de Francisci and Stefano Tiraboschi. A Rome court later convicted all of them in absentia for NAR terrorist offenses involving armed conspiracy. Roberto Fiore, inspired by Evola and Codreanu, had a catalytic influence on the NF's new ideological direction.

The NF had seen dramatic increases in membership and success at the polls during the strife-torn 1970s. However, its support then drained to the new Conservative government of Margaret Thatcher. That government vigorously addressed industrial unrest, rising crime, and weak immigration control. This weakening and isolation of the NF had a radicalizing effect on its leaders and their ideology.

A younger generation of university-educated NF activists felt the party lacked theoretical sophistication. Nick Griffin, Derek Holland, and Patrick Harrington represented this group. They believed the NF's mixture of reaction, concern over law and order, and the immigrant threat to jobs and homes was too soft. The older NF leaders, John Tyndall and Martin Webster, were tainted by British neo-Nazism. In contrast, the young men embraced the ideals of Italian neo-fascism.
[break]Roberto Fiore and his colleagues helped the NF create a new militant elitist philosophy.

This philosophy rejected electoral strategies. Instead, it focused on educating and training a fanatical, quasi-religious "New Man" in select groups for a national revolution. By 1983, this group - led by Griffin, Holland and Harrington - had split off to form the NF "Political Soldier" faction. Groups similar to Iron Guard legionary "nests" became the basic organizational unit. Training seminars were held at the Hampshire country house of Rosine de Bounevialle.

She was the publisher of the Catholic anti-Semitic magazine Candour, which A. K. Chesterton originally founded. Fiore backed the "Political Soldiers" as they published a new journal, Rising (1982-85).

This journal emphasized the spiritual and cultural basis of a new social order. A revival of the countryside and a return to feudal values reflected Codreanu's prewar attack on the decadence and materialism of urban life. Nationalist communes were planned in upland areas of Britain. Archaic woodcut art placed knights and rural idylls next to consumerism and modernity. The group discussed Evola's most militant tract.

They focused especially on his call for a "Great Holy War" fought for personal spiritual renewal. This paralleled the physical "Little Holy War" on a material plane against national or ideological enemies. Like the hero of the Bhagavad Gita, Christian Crusaders, ancient Norse warriors and Roman legionaries were all united in the Aryan struggle for self-transformation and a nobler reality.
A paean to Franco Freda, Italy's most notorious neo-fascist terrorist, gave some indication of this struggle. Derek Holland published The Political Soldier in 1984.

He wrote it as a manifesto for the new National Front elite. They believed in racial nationalism. They wanted to fight "the forces of Evil swamping the entire globe in an ocean of Filth, Corruption and Treason." Only the Political Soldier could fix the global dark age. He could also fix the National Front's past failures. Holland called this figure a "New Type of Man." He pointed to Codreanu's Legionary Movement in Romania. This group, the Iron Guard, had a cult of death.

Holland saw it as the best example of political soldiery in the twentieth century. He quoted it as "[Men] willing to sacrifice anything and everything for the victory of their Ideal." He also cited Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards. He called them fanatical, spiritual warriors. They had a similar contempt for death. Evola's anti-modernity and warrior ethics of the "Holy War" influenced the National Front "Political Soldiers." Like their Italian models, they embraced pro-Islamic positions.

They publicly supported the anti-Western, national revolutionary regimes of Muammar Qaddafi and Rûhollâh Khomeini. These leaders ruled Libya and Iran. By the end of 1989, Nick Griffin, Derek Holland, and the Italians left the National Front. They formed the International Third Position (ITP). Evola's ideas reached far beyond this Anglo-Italian revolutionary nationalist group. From the late 1970s, neo-fascist thinkers tried to bring the New Right's ideas into mainstream society.

In 1969, GRECE (Groupement de recherche et d'études sur la civilisation européenne) was founded in Paris. Soon after, new glossy magazines like Elements, Totalité, Vouloir, Diorama Letterario and Elementi appeared in France, Belgium, and Italy.

These magazines challenged liberal and egalitarian beliefs. They rejected the market and utilitarianism in favor of a higher spiritual view of life. They praised organic community over capitalist society and its abstract, quantitative relationships. They used racial origins, differences, and identity to fight egalitarian and multiracial ideas. Once again, Roberto Fiore and the Italians in London helped spread this intellectual discourse in Britain. Fiore was a close friend of Michael Walker.

Walker was a former NF organizer in central London. He started publishing the journal National Democrat in late 1981. In spring 1983, he renamed it The Scorpion. As a linguist and translator, Walker was well suited to edit a New Right magazine in Britain. This magazine offered readers articles on nationalism, anti-egalitarianism, and the Conservative Revolution.

These articles were written by Robert Steukers, the Belgian editor of Vouloir, and by Alain de Benoist and Guillaume Faye of GRECE. Evola's ideas fit well into this new radical discourse. He argued for tradition over progress, hierarchy over equality, rule from above over democracy, and aristocratic values over plebeian ones.

Evola also despised America. He saw it as the most advanced center of Western alienation from Tradition. This view matched a widespread mood of anti-Americanism in the 1980s. Both the left and the right condemned the cultural colonization of Europe. They blamed U.S. multinationals, Hollywood films, American television soaps, and the rapid rise of American-style consumerism. McDonald's hamburgers and Coca-Cola became key symbols of banal American mass culture.

This culture penetrated the postwar vassal states of Europe. Widespread opposition to the United States stationing Pershing and Cruise missiles in Europe also fueled these anti-American sentiments. People feared that Europe would be sacrificed in any nuclear exchange between the superpowers. Michael Walker introduced Evola's life and work to a wider English readership in The Scorpion between 1984 and 1986.

He placed Evola's spiritual theory of race, his anti-modernity, and his views on Jewish influence within a "superior, heroic and aristocratic conception of existence." The magazine devoted its entire summer 1984 issue to attacking the secular, liberal notion of American statehood.

This notion was divorced from any ethnic roots or culture. One article translated Evola's 1945 essay "American 'Civilization.'" That essay saw America as the final stage of European decline. It descended into the "interior formlessness" of vacuous individualism, conformity, and vulgarity. All of this occurred under the universal aegis of money-making. A mechanistic and rational philosophy of progress combined with a mundane horizon of prosperity.

This combination transformed the world into an enormous suburban shopping mall. Evola's ideas on a unified Europe's need for a spiritual and supranational basis extended this anti-American theme. Europe could challenge both superpowers for global hegemony only by opposing the current Westernization of the world. Through these articles, Walker presented Evola as the champion of a European spiritual and national revival.

This revival stood against the liberal, multiracial quagmire of the United States. Julius Evola's international export added a vital strand to the contemporary radical right in the Anglo-American world and elsewhere. Once Evola embraced the mythic ideology of cultural decadence and rebirth, he linked self-transcendence to the higher, timeless spirituality of a lost world.

He believed this world could only be reborn through catastrophic change. Evola's studies in Tantrism, oriental religions, and the Western esoteric tradition also opened new intellectual horizons. They widened access to fascist idealism. His works on Zen and Taoism were matched by translations of Pascal Beverley Randolph's Magia sexualis and several of Gustav Meyrink's occult novels. His dualist metaphysics of sex, derived from Otto Weininger, provided a key to world religions and occult doctrine.

This doctrine highlighted the abyss of emancipatory, collectivist politics based on lunar spirituality. His notion of the "Jewish spirit," also from Weininger, has influenced Miguel Serrano's "Esoteric Hitlerism." Evola's aristocratic world of Tradition, dressed in the exotic colors of Hyperborean and Eastern mythology and set against the "Jewish spirit," gives a mystical edge to reactionary talk.

It is drawing new readers. His strict New Age spirituality speaks to people who fully reject the leveling world of democracy, capitalism, multiracialism, and technology at the start of the twenty-first century. Their sharp sense of cultural chaos finds strong relief in his ideal of total renewal. In 1998, many publications and conferences marked the anniversary of Evola's birth.

Inner Traditions, a major U.S. New Age publisher, has released English editions of eight of Evola's main books. The right-wing Arun-Verlag has published several titles in German. Kshatriya, a Viennese intellectual right-wing journal focused on Evola and Codreanu, offers a space for Russian, German, and Hungarian Evolans. Black Metal music has also embraced Evola. Michael Moynihan, a right-wing U.S. industrial musician, has translated Men among the Ruins.

4. Imperium and the New Atlantis. For more than thirty years, James H. Madole (1927-1979) regularly shouted at passers-by on crowded New York City streets.

He urgently called for a fascist revolution in the United States. His style resembled open-air revival meetings and evangelical preaching. He stood flanked by his own stormtroopers. They wore uniform black caps, gray shirts with lightning-bolt armbands, and black trousers. Madole always wore a close-fitting suit jacket with all three buttons fastened. He also wore a ridiculous motorcycle crash helmet over his thick horn-rimmed glasses. The plump, middle-aged Madole stood on a pulpit-like rostrum.

It was decorated with the lightning bolt symbol of his National Renaissance Party. He emphasized his speeches with staring eyes, wild grimaces, and striking melodramatic poses. Throughout the 1960s and 1970s, the National Renaissance Party frequently made headlines. They provoked violent protests and riots in New York districts heavily populated by Jews and blacks. There, Madole carried his missionary message of white supremacy and Aryan renaissance. Madole was clearly a fanatic.

People could easily dismiss him as a wild eccentric. He pursued a hopeless political campaign on the edges of postwar American society. However, his campaign strategies, organization, and philosophy of Aryan renewal mark him as an early and important figure in the development of esoteric fascism. His ideas were full of the fantastic mythology of science fiction. They also drew on occult notions from Theosophy. He attacked Christianity.
He held up the hierarchical caste society of Vedic India as the model for his "New Atlantis," the future fascist state of America.

Ultimate authority would rest with philosopher-kings. These leaders were selected and trained for rulership from childhood. His street-fighting stormtroopers, known as the Security Echelon, were meant to be the living example of a new military caste of Aryan warriors. Madole also anticipated later fascist "Third Way" movements. He rejected both capitalism and communism.

In his opposition to the plutocracy and imperialism of the United States, Madole even sought alliances with Arab and black nationalists. He encouraged them to hold joint meetings with the National Renaissance Party. By the mid-1990s, fascist and neo-Nazi groups celebrated Madole as the "father of post-war occult-fascism." James Hartung Madole was born in New York City on 7 July 1927.

Two years later, his parents separated. His mother raised him in Beacon, New York. She held strong anti-Semitic views. In high school, the lonely boy developed a deep interest in science. He built a laboratory at home. There, he ran experiments in chemistry and astronomy. As a young man, Madole saw the scientist in Faustian terms. He viewed the scientist as a semi-divine sage seeking mastery over the earth and the universe. He believed science was the only valid basis for culture.

He thought society should be ruled by scientists. This naive belief in the power and certainty of science grew stronger. Madole loved science fiction. This genre had a strong grip on the American public. It spread through mass-circulation magazines and pulp fiction in the 1930s and 1940s. Science fiction often highlighted the elitist pretensions of the heaven-storming scientist. Its fantasy stories often described magical lands and authoritarian utopias on alien planets.
[break]The elitism of science and science fiction (SF) led Madole to fascism as a political philosophy.

In his late teens, Madole looked for SF fans with fascist views. This is how he met Charles B. Hudson. Hudson was an SF writer and a veteran American fascist from before the war. He was a main defendant in the famous Sedition Act trials of 1941-43. Hudson was a short, plump, bald man with a fanatic temperament. In the 1930s, he built a following of Midwestern fascists. He did this with his bulletin, America in Danger. He worked closely with Weltdienst. This was the Nazi German press agency.

Lieutenant-Colonel Ulrich Fleischhauer ran it in Erfurt. It operated under the auspices of Alfred Rosenberg. The agency tried to build overseas support for the Hitler regime. It did this by creating an anti-Semitic international. It promoted a global ideology of resentment. Hudson was an obsessive conspiracy theorist.

He filled his bulletin with references to the "hidden hand." He blamed the Jews for every disaster in American history, from the assassination of Lincoln to the Johnstown flood. His favorite phrase, "Judeo-Socialistic-Communistic Nu-Deal Organized-Jewry-Finance World-War I," summed up all the dangers he saw in modern liberal society. He later shortened it to the "synagogue of Satan." By 1940, Hudson's bulletin and his Omaha base served as major outposts in the Midwest.

They spread defeatist and appeasement propaganda in favor of the Third Reich. He promoted the pro-Nazi views of John B. Snow, James True, Colonel Eugene Sanctuary, and Congressmen Jacob Thorkelson and Clare E. Hoffman. He also supported the charismatic radio priest, Father Charles E. Coughlin. He backed Mrs. Leslie Fry, a Russian-born promoter of the anti-Semitic Protocols of the Elders of Zion. He also supported Mrs. Elizabeth Dilling, a communist-obsessed agitator and lecturer.

[break]By the time Madole met Charles B. Hudson at the end of World War II, Hudson had become notorious. He had been indicted for sedition after Pearl Harbor and the start of war with Japan and Germany.

Many of his associates were tried, convicted, and imprisoned. Hudson, however, remained free. He continued to sell anti-Semitic and anti-communist literature. In 1945, Madole formed the Animist Party. This was a right-wing political movement based among science fiction fans. Hudson's influence helped Madole gain support from several "America First" and patriotic groups that survived from before the war. Madole soon attracted the attention of Kurt Mertig, another patriot.

Mertig had led the Citizens Protective League before the war. He was a German American shipping executive for the Hamburg-American Line. He had fat jowles and a heavy accent. Together with Louis Zahne, a brusque Prussian and former member of the Friends of the New Germany, Mertig held weekly mass meetings.
The Friends of the New Germany was a precursor to the German-American Bund. These meetings were for Americans and Germans at the Turnhalle in Yorkville, New York, during the early 1940s.

Mertig gave anti-Semitic, anti-war, and pro-German speeches. These speeches made it clear that the League was a Nazi front. In 1943, the Army Exclusion Board ordered Mertig removed 300 miles inland as a security measure. In 1949, the elderly Kurt Mertig founded the neo-Nazi National Renaissance Party.

Its headquarters were in Yorkville. The party took its name from Hitler's Political Testament. In that document, the Führer proclaimed that his death would bring about "the seed of a radiant renaissance of the National Socialist Movement." Mertig sought a successor. He was impressed with Madole. Madole was barely twenty-two years old. He had already shown strong oratory skills in the Animist Party and the Nationalist Action League.
Shortly after joining Mertig, Madole took over the National Renaissance Party (NRP).

He held this position until his death thirty years later. The party thus had roots in the prewar German-American Nazi fronts of Yorkville. This area had a predominantly German population. Between 1937 and 1941, these streets regularly saw parades of Fritz Kuhn's "Bund Boys." They marched under their ominous swastika standards. The NRP became Madole's lifelong career. It was the vehicle for his radical ideas of Aryan renaissance and occult fascism.
[break]Madole started as a Nazi enthusiast.

He first used the swastika as the party flag. Later, he replaced it with the fascist symbol of a lightning bolt inside a circle. In his party bulletin, he stated that "what Hitler did in Europe, the National Renaissance Party intends to do in America." The NRP proposed to abolish Congress and replace it with elite rule. It sought to protect the Aryan race from racial contamination by deporting non-white groups. It also planned to destroy communism by eliminating Jews.

During the 1950s, Madole led the NRP down new paths of fascist development. This involved a "Third Way" stance that rejected both capitalism and communism. The NRP moved away from its earlier radical right-wing views of anti-Semitism and anti-communism. It changed its view of the Soviet Union. Madole was influenced by American fascist intellectuals Francis Parker Yockey and Frederick Charles Weiss. Both men supported a pro-Soviet position against the United States and world Jewry.
[break]Francis Parker Yockey (1917-1960) worked as a legal assistant for the Allied prosecution at the Wiesbaden "second string" war crimes trials in 1946-47.

He resigned in disgust because he saw Allied hypocrisy. While in Ireland, he wrote Imperium (1948). This large book describes Western heritage and destiny from a Spenglerian point of view. Yockey then contacted a national bolshevist (pro-Soviet) neo-Nazi circle in Germany led by Alfred Franke-Grieksch. He went to London to push the English Mosleyites of the Union Movement toward this neutralist, anti-American direction.
In 1949, Yockey founded the anti-Semitic European Liberation Front there.

He published The Proclamation of London as its manifesto. After falling out with Mosley, Yockey traveled in Europe. From the early 1950s until his suicide in FBI custody in 1960, he acted as an active neo-fascist agent across Europe and the United States. He built close links with several far-right groups. He kept his pro-Soviet bias to support his anti-American and anti-Zionist beliefs. Yockey's analysis of Russia in Imperium was more favorable than his view of America.

In 1952, he wrote approvingly of Stalin's anti-Zionist campaign in Czechoslovakia for the NRP press. Authorities suspected he visited East Germany, the Soviet Union, and even Cuba. Yockey was born on 18 September 1917 in Chicago.

He came from a wealthy upper-middle-class family of Irish and German descent. He grew up in Ludington, Michigan. He attended the Foreign Service School at Georgetown University and Northwestern University. In 1941, he graduated with a law degree from Notre Dame University. He felt a deep attraction to European traditions. His parents had lived in Paris before the First World War. He felt repelled by the mediocrity of American culture and democracy.

Early on, he fell under the spell of Oswald Spengler. Spengler's widely translated magnum opus, The Decline of the West (1918-22), explained the growth and decay of civilizations according to organic principles.

In the late 1930s, Yockey joined several domestic pro-German and fascist groups. In 1939, he spoke at a gathering of William Dudley Pelley's Silvershirts. Mrs. De LaFayette Washburn tipped him to lead the National Liberty Party. While serving in the U.S. Army in 1942-43, Yockey kept his Silvershirt contacts. People suspected him of Nazi sympathies. In November 1942, he went AWOL from a Georgia camp.

He then undertook a Nazi intelligence mission in Texas and Mexico City. He later got a medical discharge by feigning mental illness. In 1944-45, he took legal appointments in Detroit. He then worked for eleven months on the War Crimes tribunal in Germany. After five months in the States, he settled at an inn in Brittas Bay, Ireland. There, he wrote his six hundred-page political opus. Imperium despises democracy, equality, and the ideas of 1789.

Its central theme is a metahistorical anti-Semitism. Spengler's The Decline of the West suggests this theme. In his large book on the cycles of history, Spengler contrasted two souls. The Western Faustian soul has dynamic energy in limitless space as its main symbol. The Magian soul belongs to Babylonian-Semitic culture. Algebra, mosaics, and arabesques typify this culture. So do the sacraments and scriptures of Jewish and Christian religions.

Spengler described Jews as a leftover fossil of the earlier Magian civilization. They were stranded in urban ghettos among the settlements of medieval Europe. Landless, cynical, and mercantile, Jews represented the final stage of an earlier civilization. This civilization was quite alien to the young Faustian culture of the West. Europe only became intellectual and cosmopolitan in the eighteenth century. Then, Jewry felt at home.

From that point on, Jews contributed greatly to the acceleration of modernity. They did so through commerce, art, and philosophy. However, their contribution was critical and destructive of the native Western spirit. Yockey used these Spenglerian ideas in his analysis in Imperium. At the moment the West should have been moving toward the final stage of an empire, Jewry acted as a fateful form of "cultural distortion."

Remembering their past oppression, Jews vengefully used new cultural forms like money thinking, rationalism, materialism, capitalism, and democracy. They used these tools to destroy Western traditions and the authority of its old elites.

From then on, Jews remade the modern world to fit their own image and interests. Yockey describes the large-scale Jewish immigration to the United States starting in 1880. This brought about 5 to 7 million immigrants from Eastern Europe. He calls the Democratic victory under Franklin D. Roosevelt in 1933 "The American Revolution of 1933." [break]She was born Maximiani Portas on 30 September 1905 in Lyons. She grew up there in comfortable circumstances. Her mother, Julia Nash, came from Cornwall.
