She considered its Indo-European pagan gods and beliefs undefiled by Judeo-Christian monotheism. Maximiani Portas traveled to India to find the Aryan heritage. In doing so, she retraced the intellectual path of many European philosophers and philologists. These thinkers began looking for the origins of humanity in India from the mid-eighteenth century onward. During the Middle Ages and the Renaissance, European scholars generally accepted the biblical creation story in the Book of Genesis.

This account traced the descent of all races from Adam and Eve in the Garden of Eden, and then from Noah and his sons, Shem, Ham, and Japhet. However, the discovery of the Americas and many previously unknown aboriginal peoples put increasing strain on this biblical explanation. During the Enlightenment, the philosophes expressed the anti-clerical and anti-biblical mood of a rational age.

They rejected the old Hebraic account of human origins in favor of a more exotic yet universal source. India provided the location for this source. This gave a background to the quest for a new Adam. The subsequent development of this post-biblical theory of human origins gave rise to the Aryan myth in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. It exercised a powerful and fatal influence on Nazi racial doctrine. In his highly influential essay Über die Sprache und Weisheit der Inder
[break](1808), the German Romantic thinker Friedrich Schlegel (1772-1829) praised Sanskrit.

As a philologist, he admired its beauty, age, and philosophical clarity. In the book's final part, he shared his anthropological ideas. He claimed a new masterful race formed in northern India. This group then marched down from the roof of the world. They founded empires and civilized the West. Schlegel believed all famous nations with high cultural achievement came from one stock. He argued their colonies were all one people. This people ultimately derived from an Indian origin.

He wondered why people in fertile Asian areas moved to the harsh north of Scandinavia. He found an answer in Indian legends. These legends spoke of the miraculous and holy mountain of Meru in the Far North. Indian tribes moved north not out of necessity. They moved because of "some supernatural idea of the high dignity and splendor of the North." The language and traditions of Indians and Nordics proved they formed a single race.
[break]By 1819, the new theory of the origin of gifted white European races was complete.

This happened when Friedrich Schlegel applied the term "Aryan" to this as yet anonymous Indic-Nordic master race. The word came from Herodotus's Arioi, an early name for the Medes and Persians. French and German authors had recently used it to name these ancient peoples. Schlegel's new usage caught on. He linked the root Ari with Ehre, the German word for honor. Philologically, he was quite correct. One also finds the same root with a similar meaning in the Slavic and Celtic languages.

However, the anthropological implications of the new word for the ancestral European race were much more exciting and flattering. As Aryans, the Germans and their ancient Indian ancestors were the people of honor. They were the aristocracy of the various races of mankind. Friedrich Schlegel was neither an extreme German nationalist nor an anti-Semite. Nevertheless, his ideas in due course stimulated the boldest ideas about Aryan supremacy among German, French and English scholars.

[break]In the first half of the nineteenth century, famous and obscure German philosophers and philologists worked hard to develop and refine the Aryan myth. Julius von Klaproth, who coined the term "Indo-Germanic," Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel, Jacob Grimm, and Franz Bopp added many more speculations. In 1820, the geographer Karl Ritter described Indian armies breaking through to the West across the Caucasus.
Grimm, the creator of the famous dictionary, had a lasting influence on literary and historical textbooks.

He described the arrival of the Greeks, Romans, Celts, and Germans in Europe as successive waves of immigration from Asia. However, these accounts did not yet set the Aryans against the Jews. The outlines of Aryan-Semitic dualism first appeared in 1845. Christian Lassen (1800-1876), a student and protégé of the Schlegel brothers, contrasted the Semites unfavorably with the Indo-Germans. He depicted the Semites as unharmonious, egotistical, and exclusive.

His focus on biology, the triumph of the strongest, the youthful and creative nature of the most recent species, and the superiority of whites provided the basic ingredients for all later thinking about the master race. The famous composer and author Richard Wagner (1813-1883) soon combined these notions with virulent anti-Semitism. Wagner enjoyed an enthusiastic mass following in Germany and Austria.

[break]Standard encyclopedias and textbooks in France, England, and Germany have included entries for "Aryans" and "Indo-Europeans" since the late 1860s. Therefore, it is not surprising that Maximiani Portas adopted a racial Manichaeanism based on an Aryan-Semitic dualism. However, her ideas about the original Aryan homeland relied more on European romanticism and native Indian scholarship than on modern theories by German racist and nationalist authors.

She did not seek the heirs of the pristine race in northern Europe. Instead, she traveled to India, "that easternmost and southernmost home of the Aryan race." In this respect, her thinking was quite traditional. Max Müller, for example, believed that the purity with which Hindus preserved the Aryan language and religion showed that those Aryans who migrated to India were the last to leave their highlands in Central Asia.

Maximiani Portas's enthusiasm for Aryan Indians was thus firmly grounded in the Aryan myth as it had developed in Europe since the time of the German Romantics. Her ideas about where the Aryans came from came straight from the books of Bâl Gangadhar (Lokmanya) Tilak (1856-1920).

People widely called him "the father of Indian unrest." After finishing his education at Poona University, Tilak turned down a job in government service. He devoted himself to the cause of national awakening. In addition to his radical political work, Tilak was a skilled scholar of ancient Hindu sacred texts. As an Indian nationalist, he had a special interest in the Vedas. He saw them as the earliest document of the Aryan Indians and the oldest writings in human history.

During a short prison term for sedition in 1897-98, Tilak focused on studying the Vedas. He then published his main statement on the age and original location of Vedic civilization, The Arctic Home in the Vedas (1903). Tilak used astronomical statements in the Vedas to conclude that the Aryan ancestors of the Vedic writers lived in an Arctic home.
This was during inter-glacial times between 10,000 and 8000 B.c. They enjoyed a level of civilization higher than both the Stone and Bronze Ages.

The start of the last Ice Age destroyed their homeland. As a result, the Aryans moved south. They wandered across northern Europe and Asia from 8000 to 5000 B.c. They looked for land suitable for new settlements. Tilak believed many Vedic hymns date to the early part of the period between 5000 and 3000 B.C. At that time, Aryan bards had not yet forgotten traditions from their former Arctic home.

From 3000 to 1400 B.C., later Vedic texts, including the Brahmanas, were written. During this time, Arctic traditions were gradually misunderstood and lost. On Aryan strength, Tilak concluded that "the vitality and superiority of the Aryan races, as disclosed by their conquest, by extermination or assimilation, of the non-Aryan races with whom they came in contact …is intelligible only on the assumption of a high degree of civilisation in their original Arctic home."

[break]Tilak's ideas about Aryan origins in the Arctic, along with the standard Aryan myth, strongly shaped Maximiani Portas's view of India, its culture, and its people. She believed the Aryan invasions of India happened over a long period during the fourth and third millennia B.C. Like many European scholars, she saw the Aryans as gifted barbarians.

Their skill in horsemanship and use of wheeled chariots let them dominate the Dravidians and other dark-skinned groups they met in the more advanced Indus civilization in northwest India. The Vedas allowed scholars to reconstruct much about these light-skinned proto-Nordic invaders. After entering northern India through the passes in the Hindu Kush mountains, the Aryans settled the Punjab.

They then slowly moved along the river courses throughout the Gangetic plain of northern India. At first, they lived as seminomadic pastoralists who relied on cattle. The cow was a very valuable item and often an object of veneration. Vedic hymns describe the Aryans as a vigorous warrior aristocracy. They cared more about fighting than about agriculture. Battle, chariot racing, drinking the intoxicating soma, music making, and gambling with dice brought great prestige and pleasure.
[break]Maximiani Portas cared most about the Hindu caste system.

She saw it as the model for racial laws. These laws aimed to separate different races and keep Aryan blood pure. The Aryans were fair-complexioned. When they first invaded India, they already had three social classes: warriors or aristocracy, priests, and common people. The Aryans looked down on the dark-skinned, flat-nosed people of Dravidian and aboriginal stock whom they conquered. They called these people Daysus. This word meant "squat creatures," "slaves," and even "apes."

A stricter caste system grew out of this encounter. The Aryans feared the Daysus. They also worried that mixing with them would erase Aryan identity. The Sanskrit word for caste is varna. This word actually means color. It formed the basis of the original four-caste system. This system included the kshatriyas (warriors and aristocracy), the brahmins (priests), and the vaishyas (cultivators).

The fourth caste, the sudras, were the Daysus and those of mixed Aryo-Daysu origin. Maximiani Portas revered the Aryan race. She valued its racial purity as the peak of physical perfection. She also admired its beauty, intelligence, willpower, and thoroughness. She saw the survival of the light-skinned Brahman minority as a living tribute to the Aryan caste system. This minority survived among many different Indian races for sixty centuries.
[break]Maximiani Portas saw Hinduism as the keeper of the Aryan and Vedic heritage through the centuries.

She viewed it as the very essence of India. In her view, Hinduism was the only surviving example of an Indo-European paganism that was once common to all Aryan nations. She wrote, "If those of Indo-European race regard the conquest of pagan Europe by Christianity as a decadence, then the whole of Hindu India can be likened to a last fortress of very ancient ideals, of very old and beautiful religious and metaphysical conceptions, which have already passed away in Europe.

Hinduism is thus the last flourishing and fecund branch on an immense tree which has been cut down and mutilated for two thousand years." She imagined that Indian society could show how the world would look around A.D. 8000, once the New Order of Nazism had prevailed for six thousand years. Years earlier, while visiting Palestine, she decided to honor the pagan gods and oppose the Judeo-Christian legacy of the West.
Now, seeing herself as a pioneer of Nazi ideals in the East, she resolved to do everything she could to preserve Hindu traditions against Christianity and all other philosophies of equality.

Maximiani now considered India her home. From 1932 until mid-1935, she traveled extensively throughout India. Then, from July to December 1935, she lived at Rabindranath Tagore's ashram in Shantiniketan, near Bolpur in Bengal. This place was known for its diverse membership. The low cost of living there outweighed her dislike of its liberal spirit and the presence of German Jewish émigrés. She learned Hindi and perfected her Bengali.

In 1936, she taught English and Indian history at Jerandan College, not far from Delhi. She also worked in a similar role at Mathura, the holy city of Krishna. As she became more involved in Hindu life and customs, she adopted the Hindu name Savitri Devi. This name honored the female solar deity. We will use this name for her in this account. She vividly describes the colorful diversity of India in L'Étang aux lotus [The Lotus Pond] (1940).

This book records her early impressions of the country from 1934 to 1936. The political institutions of late British rule directly shaped Hinduism's future in India. These institutions created quotas for representation in state legislatures based on the size of each religious group. Several Hindu political organizations gained major prominence during the interwar period.

The Hindu Mahasabha and the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) were notable examples. They addressed the problem of declining Hindu influence. They also sought conversions among non-Hindus and the return of former apostates. Savitri Devi's Aryan-Hindu enthusiasm now interacted with this militant expression of Hindu nationalism. After settling in Calcutta in late 1936, she discovered the Hindu Mission there. She immediately offered her services to it.
[break]Savitri Devi told her president, Srimat Swami Satyananda, that she was an Aryan pagan.

She regretted that Europe had converted to Christianity. She wanted to stop the last country that honored the Aryan gods from falling under Jewish spiritual influence. She also said she was a devotee of Adolf Hitler. She believed he led the only movement in this Aryan pagan spirit against Western Judeo-Christian civilization. Satyananda was interested and impressed by the young Greek woman. He noted her intense eyes, outspoken manner, and fluent command of Hindi and Bengali.

He shared the interest in Hitler that many educated Hindus held. They admired his Aryan mythology and his use of the swastika, the traditional sign of fortune and health. He told her he considered Hitler an incarnation of Vishnu. He saw Hitler as an expression of the force that preserves cosmic order. In his view, Hitler's disciples were the spiritual brothers of Hindus. With this clear meeting of minds, Satyananda hired Savitri Devi as a lecturer.

Her duties included speaking at the Mission headquarters in Calcutta. She also traveled to give lectures throughout Bengal and the neighboring states of Bihar and Assam. Savitri Devi's pro-Nazi views led her to the Hindu Mahasabha, a nationalist Hindu party. After Germany invaded Czechoslovakia in March 1939, the Mahasabha took a strong pro-German stance. It saw a close match between the Aryan cult of Nazism and Hindu nationalism. One Mahasabha spokesman declared:

[break]Germany's serious idea of reviving Aryan culture, its praise of the Swastika, its support for Vedic learning, and its strong defense of Indo-Germanic civilization are welcomed by religious and sensible Hindus in India with joyful hope. Germany's fight against the enemies of Aryan culture will make all Aryan nations in the world realize the truth and awaken Indian Hindus to restore their lost glory.
[break]While moving in these circles, Savitri met Asit Krishna Mukherji, a Hindu publisher with strong pro-German sympathies.

He edited and owned The New Mercury. This was a fortnightly National Socialist magazine. The German consulate in Calcutta supported it. It ran from 1935 until 1937, when the British government suppressed it. She had already noticed this publication during her earlier travels around Bengal. It was the only Nazi paper in India. She read its contents with great interest. Mukherji's editorial line was openly pro-German and pro-Nazi.

Yet he also stood for a pan-Aryan racism with a strong Indian element. The articles ranged from Hitler's views on the nation and architecture to translated excerpts of Mein Kampf. They also included studies on the original Aryans, the origin of the swastika, and the Arctic homeland of the Aryans. In 1938, on the eve of his departure for a new assignment, the German ambassador, Baron Eduard von Selzam, wrote a secret communiqué to all German legations in the Far East.
He stated that no one had rendered services to the Third Reich in Asia comparable to those of Sri Asit Krishna Mukherji. Mukherji admired the growing power and influence of the Third Reich.

He was deeply impressed by the Aryan ideology of Nazi Germany. This ideology included a cult of Nordic racial superiority, anti-Semitism, and race laws. He approved of the German focus on the Hellenic ideal of physical strength and beauty. The Olympic Games in Berlin in the summer of 1936 displayed this ideal well. He recognized the Nazi flag as a close relative of the Pan-Hindu flag. The Nazi flag features a black swastika on a white circle on a red background.

The Pan-Hindu flag bears ancient Aryan symbols: the swastika, the lotus, and the sword. He also saw parallels between the martial spirit of the Third Reich and the old Hindu warrior tradition of the Marathas and other Indian groups.

He saw parallels between M. S. Golwalkar's RSS Hindu youth formations and the Hitler Youth. The Hitler Youth had been his inspiration. Just as Hindu nationalists protested against colonial rule, Germany marched in defense of Aryandom. Germany had already challenged Britain and France. These were its sworn enemies. Germany demanded an end to the ignominious Versailles settlement. It also sought the leading position in Europe. Savitri Devi's meeting with Mukherji was a turning point in her life.
She had finally found a pan-Aryan activist who shared her belief in the Aryan revival of India.

He became her husband. When war broke out in September 1939, her status as a Greek passport holder in Calcutta became a problem. As a Hindu Mission lecturer, British authorities knew her as an alien with Nazi sympathies. She faced a real risk of deportation or detention. In early 1940, Mukherji proposed they marry so she could become the wife of a British subject and stay free. She claims it was not a romantic match.

It was based on their friendly relationship and shared ideals. The wedding date coincided with news of the British evacuation from Dunkirk and the likely fall of France. Wearing her best gold and scarlet sari, Savitri Devi married Asit Krishna Mukherji in a Hindu ceremony on 9 June 1940 in Calcutta. She spent the rest of the war happily expecting an Axis victory. She also expected India to be divided between Germany and Japan.

Her husband engaged in espionage for the Japanese in India and Burma. By the end of the war, Savitri Devi had blended many Hindu ideas into a form of National Socialism that glorified the Aryan race and Adolf Hitler.

First, she adopted the Hindu cycle of ages from the Vishnu Purana. This text is one of the ancient legends in popular Hindu scripture. This cyclical doctrine says four ages, or yugas, of decreasing length mark the world's decline. It moves from a golden era to the total decay of the dark age, or Kali Yuga. This pessimistic view of entropy and exhaustion fit her strong hostility toward liberalism, democracy, and modernity.

She was deeply convinced the world entered that dark age around 3000 B.C. The religious prominence of Jewry, its universalistic successor in Christianity, and above all the modern world and the rational ideas of 1789 - freedom, equality, and brotherhood - were only signs of its accelerating degeneration. She developed her own doctrine of Men in Time, above Time, and against Time to counter the bleak cosmology of the Kali Yuga.
These three types of historical figures showed three distinct responses to the bondage of Time within the cycle of the ages.

Men in Time were the essential and most active agents of the Kali Yuga. Their egoism, violence, and drive for power typified the Dark Age and all its ups and downs. She identified Genghis Khan (1157-1227) as a leading example of the Man in Time. This medieval Mongol chieftain achieved lightning victories that gave him brief dominion across Eurasia in the thirteenth century. Men above Time belonged properly to the undisturbed perfection of the Satya Yuga, or golden age.

As unworldly mystics and sages, their divine revelation ideally shone upon an ordered realm that knew no strife. She believed the solar mystic and Egyptian pharaoh Akhenaton (c. 1370-1340 B.C.) was an eminent Man above Time.

Men against Time combined the qualities of the other types, lightning and sun. They acted with ruthless violence to restore the conditions of the coming golden age at the end of the dark age. These martial heroes were the saviors of the cycle of the ages. Through war, revolution, and annihilation, they worked to redeem the world from the thrall of the Kali Yuga and start a new time cycle. She connected these ideas to the theistic Hindu concept of the avatara (avatar).
This is a deity, usually Vishnu, who descends to earth in a human, superhuman, or animal form. This mediator between God and people developed from the non-human gods of the Vedic period.

The origin of the avatar concept is unclear. Scholars have traced early forms to Aryan Iran in the Bahram Yasht, a Zoroastrian text. This text may even show signs of Chinese influence and mythology. However, the concept plays a much larger role in post-Vedic Hindu thought, found in the epics and the Bhagavad Gita, than in any of these other beliefs. Both the Ramayana and the Mahabharata describe the avatar descending as Rama and Krishna.

These two figures reappear as the favorite incarnations of Vishnu. In the Puranas, these avatars also appear between ages as yuga avatars. The Kalki avatar appears as the tenth and final incarnation of Vishnu. In a way similar to Judeo-Christian apocalypse, he arrives on a white horse, carrying a sword. He comes to defeat the dark age and begin a new golden age. Savitri Devi believed Adolf Hitler was the greatest Man against Time in all recorded history.

She saw him as the divinely appointed leader of the Aryan world in the West. His demand for German national unity in a strong new Reich defied the humiliating Versailles Treaty. This clearly identified him to her as a champion of the old tribal principle. He stood against the degenerate capitalist and cosmopolitan order of the Allies. His adoption of racist ideas convinced her he intended to revive the Aryan caste system worldwide.

His anti-Semitism and the Nuremberg laws forbade intermarriage and sexual relations between Aryans and Jews. Hitler's ruthless use of military violence against his enemies in a resistant fallen world defined him.

His uncompromising plan to exterminate the Jews also defined him. The Jews were the age-old adversary and counter-image of the heroic Aryans. These traits characterized him as the essential Man against Time. Like a fiery comet from the heavens, he burst through the gloomy pall surrounding the earth in the Kali Yuga. He heralded the spreading sunshine of a new order of perfection, divine justice and righteousness. Savitri Devi is certainly the first Western writer to call Adolf Hitler an avatar.

She often quotes the Bhagavad Gita about him: "When justice is crushed, when evil is triumphant, then I come back. For the protection of the good, for the destruction of evil-doers, for the establishment of the Reign of Righteousness, I am born again and again, age after age." Her praise of Hitler's life and political career in The Lightning and the Sun (1958) starts with the divine collective Self of Aryan mankind taking human form.

It describes this incarnation as "the late-born child of light" in Braunau am Inn in 1889. Her account of his youth and growing sense of mission relies on August Kubizek's story of their teenage friendship in Linz and Vienna from 1904 to 1908. Whether she admires the ancient Germanic sagas and the magic of Wagner's music, or describes his plans for new cities, buildings, and monuments, Hitler is always her true friend of his people.

He is always inspired by an inner vision of a healthy, beautiful, and peaceful world. This earthly paradise reflects cosmic perfection. Savitri Devi was certain that Hitler had realized he was an avatar while still young. She found strong proof of this in August Kubizek's account of young Adolf's intense reaction to a performance of Wagner's Rienzi.

The two boys saw the opera together in Linz in November 1906. Both were swept up in the grand story of Rienzi's rise to become the tribune of the people of Rome and his later fall. When the show ended, it was past midnight. Hitler, who usually talked a lot after an exciting opera, was silent and withdrawn. He led his friend through the cold, foggy streets up the Freinberg hill on the western side of town.
Kubizek remembered how Hitler strode on, looking pale and sinister, until they reached the top.

The fog no longer surrounded them, and the stars shone brightly overhead. Then Hitler began to speak. His words burst forth with hoarse passion. Kubizek was completely amazed. Until then, he had always thought Hitler wanted to become an artist, a painter, or an architect. None of that mattered now. It was as if another Self spoke through him in a state of ecstasy or complete trance. "In sublime, irresistible images, he unfolded before me his own future and that of our people.…

He now spoke of a mandate that he was one day to receive from our people, in order to lead them out of slavery, to the heights of freedom." Postwar American neo-Nazis William Pierce and Matt Koehl would later pay tribute to Savitri Devi's revelation of Hitler's avataric illumination on the Freinberg. Savitri Devi returned to Europe in October 1945.

She carried a mix of Hindu-Aryan myth and Nazi belief. She felt deep regret and self-blame for missing the "great days" of the Third Reich. She decided to make a late contribution to German National Socialism. In London, she took a casual job as a wardrobe manager for a traveling Indian dance company. She came up with an idea to distribute pro-Nazi leaflets. She planned to do this while passing through Germany by train in June 1948.

She traveled through France and entered Germany at Saarhölzbach. From 7 September to 6 December 1948, she spent about three months distributing another six thousand leaflets. She worked in the three Western occupation zones and the Saarland. Before her third propaganda trip to enemy-occupied Germany, she printed a small German-language handbill in London. The handbill had a swastika at the top. In it, she urged Germans to stay true to their Führer.

She claimed he was still alive. She told them to rise up against the Allied forces stationed throughout the country. Her sense of mission, her Nazi devotion, and her claim to belong to a small group of Hitler loyalists are clear in the text: German People. What have the democracies brought you? In wartime, phosphorus and fire. After the war, there was hunger, humiliation, and oppression. the dismantling of the factories; the destruction of the forests; and now, - the Ruhr Statute!

[break]However, "Slavery is to last but a short time more." Our Führer is alive. And will soon return with power never heard before. Resist our persecutors! Hope and wait. Heil Hitler! S.D. This unusual appeal, combined with apocalyptic hopes that Hitler would return, was followed by a verse from a well-known Nazi marching song. Postwar Germany was in total defeat and despair.

Its industries were destroyed. Its workforce was depleted. Cities were hungry. The country relied more and more on the occupying forces. In this situation, such an appeal was at best symbolic. It mainly served Savitri Devi's strong need to show her support for Nazism. It showed her loyalty to Adolf Hitler. It showed her hatred of the West and its supposed superiority. She began handing out the handbill on the night of 13-14 February 1949 in Cologne.

She soon found a young ex-SS man to help her. She was caught a week later. In five months of secret work, she had distributed 11,500 leaflets and handbills in West German cities. At a hearing, officials decided that Savitri Devi had a case to answer. This was under Article 7 of Law No. 8 of the Occupation Status. That law forbade promoting militarist and National Socialist ideas on German territory under the Allied Control Commission. The maximum penalty for breaking this law was death.

She was held at the British military prison for women at Werl. Her formal trial was set for 5 April 1949. Hinduism gave Savitri Devi a style of worship for her Hitler cult, in addition to providing a non-Christian religious mythology for Nazism. While in India, she was always impressed by the mix of beliefs that let orthodox Hindus decorate their home shrines with photos of Hitler and Stalin.
They admired these figures in defiance of the British Raj, placing them next to familiar images of Vishnu and Shiva.

This bhakti form of devotion became the mark of her own Hitler cult. It included prayers, contemplation, and rituals. Her memoirs of the Aryan-Nazi mission to occupied Germany from 1948 onward show many examples of this devotion. At pious gatherings of hard-core Nazis in bare attics in ruined cities, she showed her unending loyalty to Hitler, the savior of a chosen race. They read Mein Kampf with emotion. They gave and received precious Nazi souvenirs.

They exchanged clandestine Hitler salutes and secret signs of recognition. They felt a high sense of community with fellow believers who awaited the vanished Führer's triumphant return. She expressed an intense spirituality focused on Hitler as a redeemer figure. She also showed her strong desire to be part of his congregation.
After her arrest, her sense of community with the Nazi faithful grew stronger.
She repeatedly told her amazed interrogators and patient lawyer that her Hitlerism was a matter of religious inspiration and conviction.

As her trial approached, her hopes of martyrdom soared. "I would walk to the place of execution singing the Horst Wessel Song.… Stretching out my right arm, firm and white in the sunshine, I would die happy in a cry of love and joy, shouting …the holy words that sum up my life-long faith: 'Heil Hitler!' I could not imagine for myself a more beautiful end." Back in her cell, she whispered fervent prayers to Shiva while holding a locket with Hitler's likeness against her breast.

She found further comfort in reading the Nazi Party program and the Bhagavad Gita. Once sentenced to three years' imprisonment, she felt she had truly joined the persecuted faithful. Her chief pleasures in prison were close friendships with convicted Belsen camp wardresses and overseers, and secretly writing her propaganda mission memoir. Savitri Devi felt deep affection and respect for the female war criminals in Werl.

After Nazism was defeated, the world condemned them. These Belsen convicts and other prisoners showed Savitri Devi the fearless, unflinching loyalty of committed Nazi women. These women dedicated themselves to creating a wonderful, beautiful Aryan world in the future, following Adolf Hitler's vision. Their disgrace, ill-treatment, and imprisonment only confirmed their status as martyrs to the Nazi cause in Savitri Devi's eyes.

She was proud to be associated with them and to share their hardships at Werl. In turn, the fanatical Savitri Devi enjoyed high regard among her fellow Nazi and SS prisoners. They admired her high-flown rhetoric, her insistence on the idealistic philosophy of Aryan rebirth, and her pious Nazi spirituality. She gave a more profound meaning to their cause. This cause had often been lightly embraced during the opportunist days of Nazi power. She sustained them in their present hardships.
The prison authorities regarded her as a firebrand. They later restricted her contacts with the other political prisoners. She was released early in August 1949.

Germany expelled her, so she went to stay in Lyons, her old hometown. In April 1953, she returned to Germany. This time, she traveled as a pilgrim on a personal tour. She visited places in the "Aryan Holy Land" that were most sacred because of their connection to Hitler and the National Socialist movement. Her pilgrimage started in Leonding and Linz. Hitler had spent his childhood and youth there. On 20 April 1953, she visited his birthplace.

That date marked the sixty-fourth anniversary of his birth. From there, she traveled to Berchtesgaden in Bavaria. She wandered on the site of the Berghof. This was Hitler's Alpine retreat on the Obersalzberg. In Munich, she paid respects at several shrines. These included the taverns where Hitler first held party meetings. She also visited the Feldherrnhalle for its memories of the 1923 putsch. She went to the site of the Brown House on Königsplatz.

She sought physical proximity to war criminals at Landsberg. This was the main prison for convicted Nazis in the former American zone. Her next stop for remembrance was Nuremberg. At the Luitpoldarena and Zeppelinwiese, she imagined the exultant party rallies of the 1930s. In a sombre mood, she visited the Palace of Justice. There, the International Military Tribunal tried the surviving members of the top Nazi leadership in 1945-46. Her pilgrimage ended on a wider mythical and pagan note.

She visited the prehistoric sun temple and the rock cliffs of the Externsteine. These are traditionally identified as an ancient Germanic sacred site. Here, she performed cultic rituals to speed the coming of the next Reich. In darkness, she experienced a spiritual death and rebirth in a stone tomb. At sunrise, she shouted the names of Vedic gods and Hitler from the top of the rocks. Her record of this pilgrimage was dramatic and emotionally charged.

Through her visits to the shrines of Nazism and ancient Germany, Savitri Devi dwelled upon the meaning of these places. She also considered their significance for her own lifelong allegiance to the pagan Aryan ideal. Together with the earlier memoirs of her propaganda mission and imprisonment, Defiance (1950) and Gold in the Furnace (1951), Pilgrimage (1958) has become a renowned example of Nazi devotional literature.
It is also a favorite in the neo-Nazi underground. Savitri Devi was isolated in India during the Third Reich.

She practiced intense underground fanaticism. These factors suggest that she and her friends celebrated their secret Nazi beliefs in postwar Germany. They acted like members of a persecuted sect. However, Savitri Devi was always outspoken. She also wanted to act and bear witness. This urgency eventually made her famous and influential in the neo-Nazi movement. First, she quickly became a confidante and companion to leaders in Germany's reviving nationalist scene.
The Allies stopped de-Nazification because they wanted to win Germans over for the Cold War against the Soviet Union.

New political parties then appeared in Germany. These parties drew much of their inspiration from National Socialism. The Sozialistische Reichspartei (SRP) was banned in 1952. The Deutsche Reichspartei (DRP) then became the most influential electoral force on the extreme right. It had about 16,000 paid-up members. It held a few seats in the Land diets. It received about half a million votes in federal elections across the country. Adolf von Thadden led the DRP.

The party boasted former celebrities from the Third Reich. These included Werner Naumann, a former Nazi secretary of state and Hitler's choice to succeed Goebbels. It also included SS general Wilhelm Meinberg. Several Wehrmacht generals were members. Colonel Hans-Ulrich Rudel, a Luftwaffe ace, was also part of the group. From the early 1950s, Savitri Devi often visited Rudel in Hanover.

She came to know him well. She finished her manuscript of The Lightning and the Sun there in March 1956. In 1945, Rudel fled to Argentina. He became a popular and prominent member of the country's large Nazi community. The Peron government protected this group. This wartime hero then focused on helping Nazi fugitives and war criminals escape Europe. He became the head of a rescue organization called the Kameradenwerk.

When Rudel returned to Germany in 1951, he publicly declared his undying admiration for Adolf Hitler. He also expressed his vision of a resurrected, strong Germany. This open loyalty to the Third Reich, backed by the legend of his Luftwaffe exploits, firmly established him as the idol of the reviving neo-Nazi movement. He became a committee member of the DRP. His nationalist views found a regular outlet in the Deutsche Soldaten-Zeitung (est.

1951). Former officials in Goebbels's propaganda ministry and SS officers edited this publication. When Savitri Devi first met Rudel, he was already perhaps the most popular and visible figure in the neo-Nazi scene in the young German republic.

He had extensive contacts among émigrés. This made him a key player in Nazi clandestine groups abroad. Along with his fellow conspirators Otto Skorzeny and Eugen Dollmann, Rudel played an important role in recruiting large numbers of former Nazi fugitives from Argentina. They took key posts in the new republican regime of Egypt. Rudel was impressed by Savitri Devi's praise of Nazism as an international racist movement.
This idea fit well with the clandestine and dispersed nature of postwar Nazi conspiracy. Thanks to Rudel's introductions, Savitri Devi entered the international die-hard network.

She then met leading Nazi émigrés in the Middle East and Spain. In the spring of 1957, she stayed for some time near Cairo with Johannes von Leers. Leers was Goebbels's former anti-Semitic propaganda expert. He was now the head of Nasser's anti-Jewish broadcasting service. He introduced her to many old Nazis and SS officers. These men had found a sympathetic refuge in Egypt. Later, in 1961, she was the guest of Otto Skorzeny in Madrid.

This famous commando leader masterminded Mussolini's escape in 1943. Since the end of the war, he had built up an extensive commercial and intelligence operation in Spain, South America, and Egypt. This operation involved American and German interests. Savitri Devi taught in Montbrison, France, during the 1960s. She spent her summer holidays in Berchtesgaden and kept up ties with her old Nazi friends in Bavaria.

She soon had a bigger impact on the international neo-Nazi movement. This movement began to grow from the 1960s onward. In early spring 1961, she made her first contact with British neo-Nazis. She was spending Easter holidays with an old friend in London. She quickly learned about the publicity the British National Party was getting. The party was attracting attention through confrontational stunts and demonstrations.

These actions protested rising levels of colored immigration into Britain. The growth of these fringe movements fired her enthusiasm. These groups were committed to racism, virulent anti-Semitism, and folkish nationalism. She lost no time in meeting Andrew Fountaine, the president of the British National Party (BNP). She soon became familiar with John Tyndall and Colin Jordan. After returning to France, she corresponded with Jordan.

Through this early contact, she followed later conflicts in the BNP. These conflicts were between Fountaine and Bean on one side, and the brazen neo-Nazi tendency of Jordan and Tyndall on the other. The latter group commanded her instinctive allegiance. In due course, she became their devoted supporter in the National Socialist Movement (NSM). In August 1962, Savitri Devi attended Jordan's widely publicized camp conference in Gloucestershire.

She was a founder-signatory of the Cotswold Agreement, which established the World Union of National Socialists (WUNS). Her work with the WUNS started her rise to prestige in international neo-Nazi circles.

She became close friends with Françoise Dior. Dior married Jordan in 1963 and joined NSM undercover activities in Britain. Savitri Devi lived in France, where Dior led the national section of the WUNS. Through the camp, Savitri Devi also met Lincoln Rockwell. He was clearly impressed by her Hindu-Aryan mythology as a basis for universal Nazism. When Rockwell succeeded Jordan as leader of the WUNS, he launched National Socialist World as the smart party magazine.

His editor, William Pierce, gave prime space to a condensed edition of Savitri Devi's The Lightning and the Sun. Pierce decided to publish her alongside Rockwell and Jordan, the leaders of the WUNS. He devoted nearly eighty pages of the first issue to her. For Savitri Devi, this publication marked her first major entry into international neo-Nazi circles. Before this, her books praising National Socialism were privately published in Calcutta in small editions.

She gave or distributed these books through personal contacts in England, France, and Germany. She relied especially on old Nazi contacts like Hans-Ulrich Rudel and Otto Skorzeny. She also used the many sympathizers and Nazi widows she visited regularly in the 1950s. Through Rockwell and Pierce, her ideas reached a much wider readership in Western Europe, the United States, South America, and Australia.

These ideas included National Socialism as a religion of nature, the Hindu cycle of the ages, and Hitler's world significance as an avatar. In the third issue, Pierce announced that the magazine received an enthusiastic response to The Lightning and the Sun.

He decided to offer readers more of her writings. Excerpts from two chapters of Gold in the Furnace appeared in 1967. Excerpts from Defiance appeared in 1968. Her reputation was then secure among American Nazis. Her devoted admirer Matt Koehl approvingly quoted her "religion of nature." He also spoke at length about Hitler's revelation on the Freinberg. After retiring from teaching in France, Savitri Devi returned to India to live on her small state pension.

She still had the friendship of her husband and his family there, even though they had long lived separate lives. She spent nine months working on her new memoirs at Dior's home in Normandy. In August 1971, she went back to live with Mukherji in New Delhi. Although she was far from the activities of European and American neo-Nazism, she kept up a busy correspondence with Colin Jordan, Matt Koehl, and other Nazi enthusiasts in Europe and America.

This is akin to the Kalki avatar or the mâhdi. Through this, Claudio Mutti assimilates Savitri Devi into his own neo-fascist war against the profane West. It is perhaps noteworthy that Mutti first encountered Savitri Devi by reading the fervent prose of Pilgrimage as an idealistic teenager. Further Italian translations of her work have been published in Arya, an émigré neo-fascist journal published by Vittorio de Cecco in Montreal.
[break]Matt Koehl invited Savitri Devi to lecture to New Order audiences in the United States. She died on 22 October 1982 while visiting an old friend in England.

Thus, Savitri Devi, a nomadic pan-Aryan Nazi and Hitler worshipper, entered the neo-Nazi Valhalla of the former American Nazi Party. It is ironic that she included Indians in her vision of a pan-Aryan world under Nazi rule.

Chief Nazi theorist Alfred Rosenberg believed Indo-Aryans had long mixed their Nordic blood with the indigenous dark-skinned peoples of the subcontinent. It is also clear that racist groups in Britain and America barely distinguish between Asian and black ethnic minority groups, viewing them all as unwanted aliens. Still, Savitri Devi's intense Hitler cult provides a global Aryan mystique for defenders of a threatened white world.

As noted earlier, this was exactly George Lincoln Rockwell's goal in founding the World Union of National Socialists. It is notable that her writings first gained prominence among American neo-Nazis. This universal Nazism offers a powerful mythic reason to resist colored immigration in the predominantly white nations of Europe, North America, Australia, and New Zealand. Her ideas reached a new generation of cultic neo-Nazis in the 1980s and 1990s through underground channels.

Miguel Serrano, a Chilean author and diplomat born in 1917, has been a key publicist of her work. His "Esoteric Hitlerism" blended the Hitler figure into a Manichaean cosmology of anti-Semitism (see chapter 9). Serrano praised Savitri Devi greatly as a pioneer of Esoteric Hitlerism and as "the priestess of Odin." He inspired a loose network of Nazi pagans and satanists in Britain, France, and New Zealand.

These groups used names like the Black Order and the Infernal Alliance (see chapter 11). A Combat 18 magazine for racist skinheads in Britain featured a eulogy for Savitri Devi. The Lightning and the Sun was republished in 1994 by a Nazi satanist press in New Zealand. That press also dedicated a special magazine issue to her as the "Priestess of Hitlerism."

Mystical fascists and racist pagans have hailed Savitri Devi as the "foremother" of international neo-Nazism. She has become an Evita-like figure for opponents of multiracial society. Her books are increasingly popular among racist pagans, skinheads, and Nazi metal music fans in the United States, Scandinavia, and Western Europe.
