6. The Nazi Mysteries. In the years right after the war, the terrible results of the Third Reich made its image very negative among the Western Allied nations. German militarism destroyed much of Europe, and the brutal killing of Jews made Hitler and National Socialism objects of universal condemnation and horror.

The German people quickly rejected their former beliefs in power and conquest. The shameful behavior of major war criminals at the Nuremberg trials completed the disgrace of Nazi Germany. However, the former worship of Hitler by Germans, the regime's dramatic but short rule over the continent, and the irrational and grim nature of its anti-Semitic racist policies set National Socialism apart from other periods in modern history.

Outside a purely secular view, people saw Nazism as the embodiment of evil in a modern twentieth-century regime. It was a monstrous pagan relapse within the Christian community of Europe. The total defeat of the Third Reich, along with the disappearance, suicides, and executions of its major figures, added a further uncanny aura to the image of Nazism. By the early 1960s, this quasi-religious view of Nazism had started to hold a terrible fascination for the Western mind.

Before, people felt simple revulsion and horror toward the Third Reich. Now, one could clearly see a mystique around Nazism. This mystique presented its figures and symbols in a sensational and fanciful way. The trappings of Nazism, stripped of all political and historical context, began to enter popular culture. They appeared in thrillers, nonfiction books, and films. Stories about Nazi fugitives became common.
These fugitives included Martin Bormann, Josef Mengele, and even a resurrected Heinrich Himmler or Adolf Hitler.

After all, they were survivors. These stories placed them in the Amazon jungles, in the desert capitals of the Middle East, or down obscure back streets of London and New York. Such tales became the standard fare of paperback fiction and speculative nonfiction. Like a monstrous and obscene survival from an earlier dreaded era, these paper Nazis lived a shadowy existence. They existed on the margins of the modern postwar world.

That world bristled with its own problems, conflicts, and political forces. Often, these fugitives became plotters. They sought to subvert our apparently safe liberal world. They wanted to restore their power in a Fourth Reich. They did this by means of a conspiratorial revival. The idea of unholy relics is closely tied to real and fictional fugitives. Soon after the war, Nazi symbols, uniforms, awards, and documents became collectibles.

They quickly fetched high prices. The highest prices went to items from the Nazi leadership. For these collectors, the Brown House dinner service has an eerie aura. It was used for many high-level feasts at the party headquarters in Munich. However, Hitler's paintings or his supposed personal diary have a talismanic quality. Journalistic successes and failures involving Hitler memorabilia show how fascinating these relics are.
This fascination peaked with the scandalous Stern magazine Hitler Diaries affair in 1983.

These magical tokens of a vanished order are joined by secret Nazi treasure. The leaders of the Third Reich were famous art lovers. They seized loot on a massive scale from all occupied European states. Much of it has been found and returned to its rightful owners. But stories of Nazi loot sunk in lakes or buried in mines or glaciers still abound. The fugitives, the unholy relics, and the hidden treasure hoards suggest that Nazism secretly survived.

By implication, this excited a shiver in the liberal but romantically tempted spirit about its dreaded revival. The idea that Nazis secretly survived and might return became a central part of the modern "Nazi Mysteries" myth. In this version, Nazism was turned into a neo-Gnostic religion. It was linked to Theosophy, secret centers in Tibet, cult rituals, and black magic. This trend started with the French bestseller Le matin des magiciens (1960) by Louis Pauwels and Jacques Bergier.

The book was later translated into many languages. From the early 1960s, many popular books in Britain, France, and the United States connected Hitler and the Nazis to secret societies, the occult, and magic. Interest peaked around the mid-1970s. This approach stripped the history of dictatorship, terror, war, and oppression of its real context. Instead, it presented these events as a mythic story of a demonic mission and global change.

This occult myth also claimed that Nazi objects and relics held magical powers for revival and restoration. Fictional stories, such as finding Hitler's ashes or a secret Nazi colony in the Himalayas, then mixed with older tales of Nazi survival. Although it began as a literary trend, the twisted theology of the "Nazi Mysteries" became a strong force in mystical neo-Nazism during the 1980s and 1990s.
[break]These popular books have consistently portrayed the Nazi phenomenon as the result of mysterious and evil influences.

They directly link Hitler's rise to power with supernatural forces. According to this belief, secular or material factors cannot fully explain the appeal of Nazism. No analysis of social and economic factors can account for its harmful irrationalism and early rapid successes. Instead, this modern mysticism explains the rise of the Third Reich through an absolute but secret power that supported and controlled Hitler and his circle.

This hidden power is described either as a non-physical entity, such as "black forces," "invisible hierarchies," or "unknown superiors," or as an occult elite from a distant time or place with whom the Nazis communicated. Common themes in this tradition include Hitler's possession by spirits, a Nazi connection to hidden masters in the East, and the Thule Society and other occult orders serving as channels for dark initiation.

All writers in this genre document a secret history of the Third Reich, unknown to conventional historians, which they claim was the tool of dark powers for achieving satanic goals. Hans Thomas Hakl has done pioneering work in identifying the early French sources for the idea that occult forces guided Hitler. In 1934, René Kopp, a Christian mystical author, looked for the secret behind the success of Napoleon, Mussolini, and Hitler.
He found it in "destiny," which he defined as "the totality of invisible spiritual forces which influence mankind.…

The masters of the world (especially Hitler) have been placed on earth by these powers with intent." Kopp analyzed photographs of Hitler taken over time. He concluded that Hitler's face had changed. He also saw signs of somnambulism. This suggested the possibility of "possession by a spirit of unknown origin." Another French writer, Edouard Saby, wrote in the spring of 1939. He also described Hitler as a medium, a magician, and an initiate.

Saby found proof of Hitler's magical activity in his vegetarianism, his self-discipline, his artistic development, and his magical gaze and gestures. Saby cited the history of the Vehm, a secret medieval court. He quoted an alleged member of the "order" who said: "We trained, encircled and led Hitler, we Brothers of the Holy Vehm; we, the Seven Commanders of the Rosy Cross of Bavaria; we, the High Initiates…." Here one finds the prewar seeds of the myth of Nazi occult forces.

[break]France is the largest Roman Catholic nation in western Europe and the birthplace of the Enlightenment. It has always viewed militant and nationalist trends in Germany through Christian teachings and the new religion of reason.

Hostile movements in its neighbor across the Rhine are often dismissed as irrational. However, if religious thought dominates, German motives appear evil and ungodly. French Christian and esoteric writers attribute potentially demonic inspiration to Hitler. This reflects that viewpoint. It is important to remember that Hermann Rauschning's book, Hitler m'a dit (1940), appeared in French just as the German Army invaded the country.

Air-raid sirens whined. Parisians panicked at the prospect of renewed occupation by the dreaded "Boche." These alleged conversations with Hitler aimed to show dramatically that the German enemy was more than a common foe. It was infernally inspired. Rauschning's book offered strong moral propaganda. One could think France would prevail because God was on her side against the devil.
[break]In this mythology, Hitler's demonic possession is directly linked to his Nietzschean vision of a new species of mankind.

This new species is the Aryan superman, who will become a god among mere mortals. National Socialism has the task of breeding this divine mutation. It is therefore not just a political movement. It aims to transform the very nature of life on earth. The original source for these ideas was Hermann Rauschning (1887-1982). He was a member of the conservative Prussian ruling class. He was also the former president of the Danzig Senate. He broke with the Nazis early on.

After leaving Germany in 1936, he wrote several books. These books exposed the vulgar leadership and base methods of the Nazis. They were published in English, French, and America. Hitler Speaks (1939) was allegedly based on a long series of personal conversations with the German dictator.

The book intended to reveal his nihilism, fanaticism, and warmongering ambitions. It also aimed to show his unstable and prurient personality. Recent scholarship has almost certainly proved that Rauschning's conversations were mostly invented. However, his record has an uncanny note of veracity. It records the authentic voice of Hitler through inspired guesswork and imagination. Rauschning's role in shaping the later myth of Hitler's demonic possession is clear from a few sample quotes.

He wrote: "Hitler was abandoning himself to forces which were carrying him away - forces of dark and destructive violence. He imagined that he still had freedom of choice, but he had long been in bondage to a magic which might well have been described, not only in metaphor but in literal fact, as that of evil spirits." This satanic pact connects to the blasphemous Nazi goal of breeding an Aryan superman.

In a chapter called "The Human Solstice," Rauschning reports Hitler's thoughts on the magical evolution of a higher human species. He also describes the opening of the Cyclopean eye as an organ of supernatural perception and other occult powers.

Hitler stated: "Man is God in the making.… Those who see in National Socialism nothing more than a political movement know scarcely anything of it. It is more even than a religion: it is the will to create mankind anew." Hitler added triumphantly: "The new man is among us! He is here! …I will tell you a secret. I have seen the vision of the new man - fearless and formidable. I shrank from him!"

Another episode records Hitler waking in the night, screaming and shaking with terror at the apparition of an unnamed presence, presumably a demonic vision of the superman. Rauschning's conversations strongly inspired the 1960s myth of a demonic Hitler, starting in France. With a lost war, collaboration, and Allied liberation still fresh in memory, this demonic view of Hitler and Nazism helped excuse the defeat at an unconscious level.

It also soothed wounded French pride. How could ordinary people have defended themselves against these monstrous powers of darkness? Pauwels and Bergier quoted Hermann Rauschning extensively to support their claim that Hitler had grand plans to change the human race. They cited his statements on magical consciousness, the fearsome new man, the cyclical development of humanity, the end of its "solar period," and the dawn of a new race during a planetary crisis.

These and similar passages from Rauschning often appear in books by Trevor Ravenscroft, James Herbert Brennan, and later writers on the new "Nazi Mysteries." These Rauschning quotes usually serve two purposes. First, they show Hitler's surrender to evil powers. Second, they suggest a Nazi satanic pact to magically transform consciousness and even the physical nature of life on earth, starting a new aeon.

[break]The literature of the "Nazi Mysteries" quickly mixed up such demonism with the myth of a Nazi link with the Orient. This myth had a complex pedigree of Theosophical and French provenance. The notion of hidden sacred centers in the East was originally rooted in Tibetan and Mongolian mythology. Helena Petrovna Blavatsky, the founder of modern Theosophy, first popularized this idea to Western audiences. In The Secret Doctrine

[break](1888), Blavatsky maintained that many similar centers of esoteric learning and initiation existed. She based this work on the "Stanzas of Dzyan," which she claimed to have read in a secret Himalayan lamasery. Magnificent libraries and fabulous monasteries were supposed to lie in mountain caves and underground labyrinths in the unexplored regions of Central Asia.
Notable examples of these centers were the subterranean city of Agadi, thought to lie in Babylonia, and the fair oasis of Shamballah in the Gobi Desert.

The divine instructors of the Aryan race were said to have preserved their sacred lore there. Other Theosophical writers later extended these speculations. Annie Besant and Charles Leadbeater described "Shambhalla" as a city founded c. 70,000 B.C.

by the leader of the Aryan race on the shores of a now-vanished Gobi Sea. Alice Bailey identified "Shamballa" as the seat of the "Lord of the World," again in the Gobi Desert. This Lord watches over the evolution of men until all have been saved.

[break]The legend of Agartha, another hidden sacred center in the East, was developed by French occultists writing from the late nineteenth century onward. Louis Jacolliot (1837-1890) was a French official at Chandernagore in India under the Second Empire. He wrote a trilogy on Indian mythology and its relationship to Christianity. In Le fils de Dieu (1873), he relates local Brahmans' stories of "Asgartha," a prehistoric solar capital.

This city was the seat of the chief priest of all Brahmans and the manifestation of God on earth. Invading Aryans later took the city. The Norsemen finally destroyed it around 5000 B.C. Joseph Saint-Yves d'Alveydre (1842-1909), a French occultist, greatly elaborated this mythology. He described the secret city of Agartha as an underground theocracy in the Himalayas that guided the course of world history. Agartha was originally on the surface of the earth.

It was transferred underground and concealed from the rest of humanity at the beginning of the Kali Yuga, dated to around 3200 B.C. A supreme pontiff rules a society of millions there. This society is technologically and spiritually superior. Once the surface world reaches a sufficiently advanced level of enlightenment, Agartha will reveal itself in all its glory. It will then complete the epiphany of mankind in a global transformation.

[break]After the First World War, Polish adventure and travel writer Ferdynand Ossendowski offered another version of the Agartha myth. In his account of a journey through Siberia and Mongolia after the Russian Revolution, he described local Buddhist beliefs. These beliefs spoke of a subterranean kingdom called "Agharti," where the King of the World reigned.

This utopian realm was said to have supernatural powers. These powers could be unleashed to destroy evil mankind and transform the surface of the entire planet. Apocalyptic prophecies suggested that the King of the World would appear when the time came for him to lead all the good people of the world against the bad.
However, in 1890, the King of the World was said to have appeared at Narabanchi monastery. He foretold a coming period of war, hunger, disease, and dreadful crimes.
At the end of this period, he would send a people, now unknown, to lead men in the fight against evil. These people would found "a new life on the earth purified by the death of nations."

Finally, in the year 2029, the peoples of Agharti would swarm forth from their subterranean caverns onto the surface of the earth. French esotericist René Guénon (1886-1951) was intrigued by Ossendowski's account. He later published his own book on the spiritual center of the world as Le roi du monde (1927). These ideas of a secret theocracy in the East were added to by the spiritual power of vril in the "Nazi Mysteries." In his novel The Coming Race

[break](1871), Sir Edward Bulwer-Lytton gave this power to a subterranean race of men, the Vril-ya. They were psychically far ahead of the human species. The powers of vril (likely from the Latin virile) included telepathy and telekinesis. Madame Blavatsky quoted this purely fictional notion in Isis Unveiled (1877). She called it just one name for the mysterious, all-pervading force known to man since the ancient theurgists.

People understood the vril to be a huge store of psychic energy. This energy existed in the world at large and in the human organism. Only initiates could access it. Some occultists believed that whoever mastered the vril force could enjoy total control over all nature. They would be like Bulwer-Lytton's underground race of Vril-ya. Willy Ley emigrated to the United States in 1935. Before that, he had a short career as a rocket engineer in Germany.

He wrote a short account of the pseudo-scientific ideas that found some official acceptance during the Third Reich. Besides Hörbiger's World Ice Theory and a Hollow Earth Doctrine, both of which had leading Nazi patrons, Ley recalled a Berlin sect. This sect did meditation exercises focusing on a bisected apple. They did this to penetrate the secret of vril. Pauwels and Bergier cited this article in their Le matin de magiciens.

They exaggerated the importance of this obscure Berlin sect. They did this to claim that Nazi leaders wanted to contact an all-powerful underground theocracy. They also wanted to gain knowledge of its power. They believed this power would let Germany conquer the world. It would also transform human life according to an apocalyptic vision: Alliances could be formed with the Master of the World or the king of Fear, who rules a city hidden somewhere in the East.

Those who sign a pact will change the Earth's surface. They will give the human adventure a new meaning for many thousands of years. The world will change. The Lords will emerge from the center of the Earth. Unless we have allied with them and become Lords ourselves, we will end up as slaves. We will be on the dungheap that feeds the roots of the New Cities that will rise. Pauwels and Bergier claimed that Hitler and his circle believed in these ideas.
In their account, the Berlin sect was called the Vril Society or the Luminous Lodge.

They treated it as an important Nazi organization. They quoted a French psychiatrist. He said, "Hitler's real aim was to perform an act of creation, a divine operation …a biological mutation which would result in an unprecedented exaltation of the human race and the 'apparition of a new race of heroes and demi-gods and god-men.'" This linked racism with the vril force.
It also linked racism with the occult mythology of an Eastern theocracy. This evoked a millenarian image of the Nazi future.

Pauwels and Bergier commented on the Nazis' religio-mythological thinking. They noted that this thinking was backed by science and technology. They described Hitlerism as "Guénonism plus tanks." The "Nazi Mysteries" give the Thule Society and some of its members a special role.

They see the group as the occult center of the Nazi movement. They also view it as a channel for black magical initiation for the mediumistic Hitler. Rudolf von Sebottendorff (1875-1945) founded the Thule Society in Munich in July 1918. It was a völkisch-racist group named after Ultima Thule. The Greek navigator Pytheas of Marseilles recorded this northern land around 400 B.C. Scholars tentatively identify it as Iceland.

Because Iceland is the homeland of the Eddas, Guido von List and other German nationalists saw it as the last refuge of ancient Teutons who rejected Christianity. At the end of the First World War, the Thule Society acted as an important focus for nationalist and racist circles. In the spring of 1919, it provided military support against the left-wing revolution in Bavaria.

It is fair to regard the Thule Society as a ginger-group and predecessor of the National Socialist German Workers' Party. Organizational and personal links went directly from the Thule Society to the German Workers' Party through a Political Workers' Circle.

The German Workers' Party was the precursor of the Nazi Party. Later leading Nazi figures such as Rudolf Hess and Hans Frank were members of the Thule. Dietrich Eckart and Alfred Rosenberg were guests.
[break]Pauwels and Bergier identified two specific people as Hitler's occult mentors in Munich in the early 1920s.

Dietrich Eckart (1868-1923) was a bohemian playwright. He gained some fame for translating Ibsen's Peer Gynt. He was also a fiercely anti-Semitic journalist. He was prominent in Munich's nationalist circles as the editor of his newspaper, Auf gut deutsch. He also attended the Thule Society in 1919. Eckart and Hitler likely first met in November 1919. They were working on the German Workers' Party program.

They became close companions throughout 1920 and 1921. Eckart was experienced and well-connected. He gave strength and direction to Hitler's growing anti-Semitism. He also introduced the young party leader to wealthy and influential social circles. Eckart's influence faded as Hitler's fame and self-confidence grew after 1922. He was not involved in planning the Munich putsch. He died shortly after on 26 December 1923.

Hitler remained devoted to his old friend. He honored him with various memorials within the party. He also dedicated the second volume of Mein Kampf to him. Pauwels and Bergier say that Karl Haushofer (1869-1946) was another alleged occult mentor of Hitler. They describe him as a powerful Thule initiate and the central figure in German geopolitics.

Haushofer served in the military during the First World War. He reached the rank of major-general in the Reichswehr. After his military career, he studied political geography. He then became the Chair of Geopolitics at Munich University. Rudolf Hess worked there as his student assistant. After the putsch, Hitler and Hess were imprisoned at Landsberg. Haushofer visited his former pupil. He also met Hitler. Hitler was reportedly impressed by Haushofer's geopolitical theories.
These theories claimed that the "heartland" of Eastern Europe and Russia gave its rulers wider dominance in the world. Haushofer spent 1908-10 in Asia.

He developed a lifelong interest in the Far East, especially Japan. As military attaché at the German Embassy in Tokyo, he also traveled in India, Burma, Korea, and China. These links with the East gave fuel to the "Nazi Mysteries" mill. In 1954, Pauwels wrote a book on George Ivanovitch Gurdjieff (1866-1949), a Caucasian thaumaturge. Pauwels claimed Haushofer met Gurdjieff in Tibet in 1903, 1905, 1906, and 1908.

Back in Germany in 1923, Haushofer supposedly founded the Thule Society. He modeled it on similar groups in Tibet. Its philosophy was based on the cities of Agarthi sic and "Shampullah" sic. Pauwels described the latter as a city of violence. The King of Fear ruled it. One could make an alliance with him to rule the world. Pauwels alleged the Thule group formed such an alliance with "Shampullah" in 1928. They did so through a colony of Tibetan monks in Berlin.

To rebut this legend, note that Haushofer never traveled outside Europe before 1908. His well-documented movements in the Far East also ruled out any visit to Tibet. Pauwels's only source for this alleged contact between Haushofer and Gurdjieff is Jacques Bergier. Bergier claimed to have received his information from German officers. He was imprisoned with them at Mauthausen camp.

[break]Pauwels and Bergier argue that Eckart and Haushofer mainly influenced Hitler by passing on secret knowledge from unknown powers. Just before he died, Eckart reportedly said, "Follow Hitler. He will dance, but it is I who called the tune. We have given him the means of communicating with Them. Do not mourn for me: I shall have influenced history more than any other German." This shows that Eckart's role as an occult mediator was directly tied to invisible hierarchies.
[break]Thule was believed to be the magic center of a lost civilization.

Eckardt sic and his friends thought that not all of Thule's secrets had died. Beings between humans and other intelligent beings from Beyond would give the Initiates [i.e., the members of the Thule Society] a store of forces. They could use these forces to help Germany rule the world. Its leaders would be men who knew everything. They drew their strength from the source of energy and were guided by the Great Ones of the Ancient World.

These myths formed the basis of the Aryan doctrine of Eckardt and Rosenberg. These prophets instilled them into the mediumistic mind of Hitler. The Thule Society soon became an instrument that changed the very nature of reality. Under the influence of Karl Haushofer, the group took on its true character as a society of Initiates in communion with the Invisible. It became the magic center of the Nazi movement.
[break]This false account also claimed that Haushofer belonged to the Luminous Lodge, a secret Buddhist society in Japan, and the Thule Society. Haushofer likely learned this legend in 1905.

René Guénon also told it in his book Le Roi du Monde. After the Gobi cataclysm, the lords and masters of this great center of civilization moved to a vast underground camp under the Himalayas. These masters were the All-Knowing, sons of Intelligences from Beyond. In the heart of these caves, they split into two groups. One group followed the "Right Hand Way." The other followed the "Left Hand Way." The first group centered on Agarthi.

This was a place of meditation, a hidden city of Goodness, and a temple of non-participation in this world's things. The second group went to Schamballah. This was a city of violence and power. Its forces command the elements and the masses of humanity. They also hasten the human race's arrival at the "turning-point of time." Haushofer told Hitler that humanity needed to return to its roots in Central Asia.

He made this argument as a follower of Eastern religious traditions, not as a geopolitical strategist. He supported the Nazi plan to conquer Turkestan, Pamir, Gobi, and Tibet. His goal was to give Germany access to the hidden centers of power in the East. This dramatic picture of the Thule Society and its members is mostly made up.

Hitler never went to a single meeting. Rudolf von Sebottendorff, the founder, was indeed interested in the occult. However, a detailed diary kept by secretary Johannes Hering records regular meetings from 1918 to 1925. It lists only two talks on such topics. On 31 August 1918, Sebottendorff spoke about dowsing. Hering did not like this. He noted that occultism sometimes brought questionable members to the Thule.
On 23 February 1919, a man named Wilde gave a lecture on occultism.

All other talks and trips focused on different themes. These included megalithic culture, the original home of the Teutons, Germanic myths and poetry, the Thule legend, Jews and Zionism, and current political issues. Eckart was only a guest. On 30 May 1919, he read from his plays Lorenzaccio and Ahasver. There is no evidence linking Haushofer to the group. The Thule Society did not grow into an important occult force behind the Nazi Party.

It was politically insignificant by 1920. It stopped all activity after 1925. During its peak in 1918-19 and later, the Thule Society was defined by its nationalist and anti-Semitic beliefs. It also had a solid membership from the Munich middle class. After Pauwels and Bergier offered this basic set of myths about the occult inspiration behind Nazism, other authors were drawn to this sensational field.

It promised clear commercial success. In Germany, Dietrich Bronder repeated the story of the link between Haushofer and Gurdjieff. This included Haushofer's initiation into Tibetan mysteries and a colony of monks in Berlin. In fact, the 1939 SS expedition led by Ernst Schäfer was said to have gone to Tibet. Its stated purpose was to establish a vital radio link between the Third Reich and the lamas. Bronder was the first to write about Sebottendorff in this way.

Pauwels and Bergier had not mentioned Sebottendorff, despite his occult interests. Bronder ended his account of the Nazi occult background with a fake membership list for the Thule Society. This list wrongly included Hitler, Mussolini, Goering, and Himmler. In France, many books about the mysteriosophy of Nazism came off the presses. These books busily repeated accounts of Hitler's mediumship.

They also covered Dietrich Eckart and a sinister link between Nazi Germany and a theosophically imagined Tibet. This link pointed to the Vril Society, the ill-used Haushofer, Sebottendorff, and the Thule Society. These themes appeared in Pierre Mariel's L'Europe païenne du XXe siècle (1964), René Alleau's Hitler et les sociétés secrètes (1969), Werner Gerson's Le Nazisme, société secrète (1969), and Jean-Claude Frère's Nazisme et sociétés secrètes
[break](1974). Pauwels and Bergier's book dealt with Nazi occultism in only one section. The rest of the work focused on prehistory, ancient science, and lost civilizations.

This mix has proven to be a successful market formula. Robert Charroux's popular books also explore the mysteries of ancient civilizations, including Egypt, Hyperborea, Atlantis, Mu, and the American Indians. Born in 1909, Charroux served as Minister for Cultural Affairs in the French Vichy government. From 1960 onward, he devoted himself to archaeology, prehistory, and a reinterpretation of ancient civilizations. This suggests a familiarity with Julius Evola's ideas.
In Le livre des secrets trahis (1964), he speculates on whether the Hyperboreans were extraterrestrials from Venus who became the tutors of early mankind.

His work includes the enmity between the Hyperboreans and the Hebrews, the myth of the Black Sun, the Thule Society, and Agartha. Originally published in France, the book was translated into many languages. By the 1970s, Charroux could boast of more than two million readers. He shares an international reputation with Erich von Däniken for literature about gods and ancient astronauts. Charroux extended the "Nazi Mysteries" into a wider mythology of Aryans and their semi-divine ancestors.
[break]The most influential "Nazi Mysteries" book in the English-speaking world was probably The Spear of Destiny (1972).

Trevor Ravenscroft (1921-1989) wrote it. He served as a British commando in the North African campaign during World War II. He was captured and held in a German POW camp from 1941 to 1945. After the war, he became a journalist for the Beaverbrook Press. He also worked for the International Publishing Corporation. At some point after the war, Ravenscroft claimed he met Walter Johannes Stein (1891-1957).

Stein was a Viennese Jew who moved from Germany to Britain in 1933. Ravenscroft falsely told Stein's story of Hitler's demonic inspiration. Before the Third Reich began, Stein taught at the Waldorf School in Stuttgart. This school followed the anthroposophical principles of Rudolf Steiner. While there, Stein wrote a curious and learned book, Weltgeschichte im Lichte des Heiligen Gral (1928).

It offered a spiritual view of history and its Christian fulfillment. This view relied on the legend of the Holy Grail. Stein argued that Wolfram von Eschenbach's Grail romance, Parzival (c. 1200), drew on the historical background of the ninth century. He claimed the epic's fabulous characters matched real people from the Carolingian Empire. For instance, he named the Grail king Anfortas as King Charles the Bald, Charlemagne's grandson.
He identified Cundrie, the sorceress and messenger of the Grail, as Ricilda the Bad.

He named Parzival as Luitward of Vercelli, the chancellor of the Frankish court. He identified Klingsor, the evil magician and owner of the Castle of Wonders, as Landulf II of Capua. Landulf had a sinister reputation because of his pact with the heathen powers of Islam in Arab-occupied Sicily. Stein understood the battle between Christian knights and their evil adversaries as an allegory. It represented their enduring struggle for possession of the Holy Lance.

This was the Spear of Longinus that pierced Christ's side at his Crucifixion. Ravenscroft built his own occult explanation of Nazism based on his possible contact with Stein and his knowledge of Stein's work.
This account centered on Hitler's supposed obsession with Grail mysteries and the Spear of Longinus.
In The Spear of Destiny, Ravenscroft described how the young student Stein found a worn, secondhand copy of Eschenbach's Parzival in an occult bookshop in Vienna's old quarter in August 1912.

The book contained many handwritten notes that commented on the text. These notes interpreted the Grail epic as initiation trials on a path to transcendent consciousness. Many quotations in the same hand supported this view. They came from oriental religions, alchemy, astrology, and mysticism. Stein also noted that a strong theme of anti-Semitic hatred and pan-German racial fanaticism ran through the entire commentary.
The name on the inside cover showed that the book's previous owner was Adolf Hitler. Stein became curious about the notes and allegedly went back to the bookshop.

He asked the owner if he knew anything about this Hitler. Ernst Pretzsche told Stein that the young Hitler was a dedicated student of the occult. Pretzsche also gave Stein Hitler's address. Stein then went to find Hitler. During their many meetings in late 1912 and early 1913, Stein learned that Hitler believed the Spear of Longinus could give its owner unlimited power to do good or evil.

The previous owners allegedly included Constantine the Great, Charles Martel, Henry the Fowler, Otto the Great, and the Hohenstauffen emperors. Since the Holy Roman Empire dissolved in 1806, the lance had belonged to the Habsburg dynasty.

It now sat on display in the Treasure House of the Hofburg in Vienna. Hitler was determined to get the lance to ensure his own bid for world domination succeeded. Ravenscroft also included the sensational story that Hitler sped up his occult development by using hallucinogenic peyote. Pretzsche had given him the peyote. Pretzsche had worked as an apothecary's assistant in the German colony in Mexico City until 1892. Much of this seems plausible.

Hitler knew the Grail romances and the Spear of Longinus. This knowledge likely came from his strong love for Richard Wagner's (1813-83) operas. Hitler idolized Wagner as the greatest interpreter of the Germanic folk spirit. The Grail and its knights are central to Lohengrin (1850). Hitler first saw this opera at age twelve in Linz. He saw it again more than ten times in Vienna between 1907 and 1913. Parsifal (1882) was Wagner's last work.

It is the only one to involve the Spear. Wagner based it on Eschenbach's Grail story. He fused the original Christian symbolism with the blood mystique of the Aryan racial myth. In this work, Parsifal is the chaste champion of Aryan manhood. Only he can retrieve the sacred spear that pierced Christ's side. This act preserves the Grail, the talisman of the German race. Hitler studied all the Wagner librettos. He would have known the racial overtones of Parsifal.

In the 1930s, he declared that this opera was the basis of his racial religion. A conversation with Rauschning refers to "the holy grail of pure blood." Ravenscroft's allusions to Hitler's occult reading in Vienna were already endorsed by Alan Bullock's masterly biography. Bullock referred to Hitler's appetite for books on "the Eastern religions, yoga, occultism, hypnotism, astrology." The only trouble is that Ravenscroft was lying about his source.

Stein never knew Hitler personally in Vienna or anywhere else. The figure of Ernst Pretzsche was plainly invented. Ravenscroft described a similarly fanciful social network of people supposedly involved with occult lore in Munich, Hitler's next stop in life. He described Dietrich Eckart as an occult initiate who traveled to Sicily to find the castle of Landulf II at Caltabelotta. This putative model for Klingsor was said to have performed satanic rituals of Arabian astrological magic there.

These rituals were said to have appalled the Christians of southern Europe. Landulf was supposed to have invoked the spirits of darkness through the torture and sacrifice of human victims. Ravenscroft suggested that the Thule Society, under Eckart's direction, performed similar rituals on Jews and communists. These people had unaccountably disappeared in Munich during the early postwar years.
Ravenscroft even recruited the person of Aleister Crowley (1875-1947), the notorious English magician, for his "Nazi Mysteries." Crowley established his antinomian Abbey of Thelema at Celafù in 1921.

Crowley was alleged to have hunted for clues at Caltabellotta. Meanwhile, Eckart made a study of Crowley's Gnostic sex-magic and its symbolical connections with Landulf's satanic practices. This jumble of links between twentieth-century occult Nazism and ninth-century Sicily was crowned by the claim that Hitler believed himself to be the reincarnation of Klingsor-Landulf. He was a modern vessel for the spirit of the Anti-Christ.

[break]Ravenscroft concluded that Eckart and Haushofer initiated Hitler into black rituals. These rituals were designed to establish contact with evil powers. Dietrich Eckart worked to develop and open the centers in Adolf Hitler's astral body.

This gave Hitler the ability to see into the macrocosm and the means to communicate with the powers of darkness. He used his memories of a past life as Landulf of Capua in the ninth century. By revealing The Secret Doctrine, Haushofer expanded Hitler's sense of time. He also awakened Hitler to the true motives of the Luciferic Principality that possessed him. This allowed Hitler to become the conscious tool for its evil intent in the twentieth century.

[break]The centers of the astral body, vision into the macrocosm, and the Luciferic Principality and its imminent manifestation as the Anti-Christ are all concepts from Anthroposophy. This shows how Ravenscroft softened the work of Rudolf Steiner and Walter Johannes Stein to create a near-Anthroposophical story about a demonic Hitler and the occult powers of Nazism. With the appearance of Eckart and Haushofer, one can see the influence of Pauwels and Bergier.

Their twin Eastern theocracies of Agarthi and Schamballah also appear in Ravenscroft's book. This time, they serve as demonic mystery centers representing the powers of Lucifer and Ahriman in anthroposophical doctrine.

Spiritualism also features in Ravenscroft's wild account of the Thule Society. People claimed that Eckart, Rosenberg, and Sebottendorff held obscene seances with a naked female medium. They did this to contact the spirits of the Thule hostages who were murdered by communist revolutionaries in April 1919. Both Prince von Thurn und Taxis and Countess Heila von Westarp spoke from beyond the grave. They said Hitler would be the next claimant of the Spear of Longinus.

He would lead Germany into a disastrous bid for global conquest. The Spear of Destiny has been translated into several languages. It has been in print for twenty-five years. It continues to inspire new authors and readers. The Spear of Longinus, the Grail romance of Parzival, and their key role in Hitler's idea of demonic world-rule have appeared in many other books. Francis King's popular study of how the occult influenced the rise and fall of Nazi Germany, Satan and Swastika

[break](1976), mentions the story. Dusty Sklar quotes Ravenscroft's account of Thule seances. He also cites Hitler's racist reading of Grail symbols. Sklar lists Haushofer as an authority on The Secret Doctrine. James Herbert, a best-selling British horror writer, entered the profitable "Nazi Mysteries" market. His grim thriller The Spear (1978) followed a plot by a modern Thule Society.

They planned a right-wing military coup in Britain. This was during the troubled, strike-torn late 1970s, when the National Front was winning votes. The spear served as the central talisman for satanic rites. These rites aimed to resurrect the corpse of Heinrich Himmler. The location was a replica Wewelsburg in North Devon. A ritual using the lance at the real Wewelsburg in Westphalia also marked the climax of Russell McCloud's Die schwarze Sonne von Tashi Lhunpo (1991).

Howard A. Buechner, a distinguished American physician, has written two books. They describe the transfer of the Holy Lance and Hitler's ashes to a secret Nazi shrine in Antarctica at the end of the war. They also describe their recovery in 1979. In this search for shocking mystification, Heinrich Himmler and the SS eventually outdid the Thule Society as a black order of satanic initiation.
Pauwels and Bergier had already hinted at Hitler's plans, as Rauschning described them, for Ordensburgen.

These were elite schools for the party's new leaders. Pauwels and Bergier mixed these up with Himmler's SS. At these medieval castle schools, the pride of young Aryan manhood would be trained in fanatical belief, loyalty, and self-sacrifice. They would make vows and start on an "irreversible, superhuman destiny." The SS itself would become an international order. It would sit at the top of a hierarchical society.

This society included overlords, party members, the anonymous masses, and, below them, the modern slaves of conquered foreign races. In their story, the concentration camps were a type of imitative magic. They served as a model for the future social order. The crematorium ovens of Auschwitz were just a ritual for a magical act of demonic creation. Hitler was linked to the Holy Lance, but the Holy Grail entered Nazi mysteries through the SS.
In 1960, Pauwels and Bergier claimed that Otto Skorzeny, a German commando ace, planned to steal the Grail.

The French adventurer and writer A. de Saint-Loup fully developed this legend. In a book about the Cathars and their mountain fortress Montségur, Saint-Loup told the story of Otto Rahn, a young German scholar (1904-1939). Rahn studied Grail traditions in Provence in the early 1930s. When Rahn joined the SS, Himmler encouraged his research. Himmler was impressed by the idea that Catharism was a Germanic dualist heresy of ancient Aryan origin.

Saint-Loup claimed that after Rahn died in 1939, Himmler believed the Grail still lay undiscovered in the Montségur area. Consequently, the SS returned to find the Grail. They succeeded in their mission and flew the priceless relic to the "Grail Castle," Hitler's Kehlsteinhaus, also known as the Eagle's Nest, at Berchtesgaden. At the end of the war, German commandos took the Grail and hid it in a glacier below the 3,000-meter Hochfeiler peak in the Zillertal, Austria.

This story combined all the essential ingredients of Nazi mystery, including religious heresy, the subversion of sacred symbols, and hidden postwar treasure. Saint-Loup was an SS member in the French Charlemagne Waffen-SS division.

That unit fought in the final stages of the Battle of Berlin. Born in 1908 as Marc Jean Pierre Augier, he spent the 1930s on overseas adventures. He crossed the Sahara on a motorcycle. He explored the Arctic. He visited the Soviet Union and Franco's Spain. After his SS service, he moved to Argentina for several years. There, he advised the government on mountain warfare. He also wrote a book about life in Tierra del Fuego.

His later books on Montségur and the legend of an SS mission to find the Grail sparked new French publications on the Nazi-Cathar connection. Michel Bertrand and Jean Angelini wrote a bestselling book on this aspect of Nazi mythology. They used the joint pseudonym Jean-Michel Angebert. The book is Hitler et la tradition cathare (1971). It was quickly translated into English as The Occult and the Third Reich (1971).

It was reprinted in 1974. Howard Buechner's fanciful book Emerald Cup - Ark of Gold (1991) reused the story of Otto Rahn. It also reused the SS quest for the Holy Grail and Skorzeny's successful mission to secure it, with new variations. Focusing on Himmler put the mythologists on firmer ground. Unlike Hitler, Himmler was deeply interested in esoteric traditions, Atlantis, and Aryan origins.
Pauwels and Bergier were among the first to find Heinrich Himmler's SS Ahnenerbe, or Ancestral Heritage, organization.

The Ahnenerbe was a key institution within the SS. In 1933, Himmler encouraged the creation of a new research group. This group included scholars in humanities, natural science, and medicine. The humanities covered prehistory, archaeology, linguistics, ethnography, and symbology. All this work aimed to support the Aryan racial worldview of Nazi and SS ideology. After 1935, the Ahnenerbe grew quickly. It came to include more than 50 departments.

It published two scientific journals. It also ran several publishing houses in Germany, the occupied Low Countries, and Norway. The organization planned foreign expeditions to exotic places in Asia, Africa, and South America. Scholars from German universities edited studies on Indology, Sanskrit texts, the Cathars, the Holy Grail, the Rosicrucians, and the mysteries of Tibet. Scientific research also covered biology, heredity, and genetics of rare animal breeds in Central Asia and the Caucasus.

[break]The SS expedition to Tibet in 1938-39 started as a private project. Himmler offered limited funding to put it under the Ahnenerbe umbrella. His occult ideas about the semi-divine origins of the Aryan race strongly motivated his interest in Tibet. The expedition leader, Dr. Ernst Schäfer, was the son of a wealthy Hamburg industrialist. As a student in 1931-32, Schäfer joined a Tibet expedition led by the young American Brooke Dolan for the Academy of Natural Sciences in Philadelphia.
After joining the SS in 1933, Schäfer went on the second Dolan expedition to eastern and central Tibet in 1934-36.

He was in charge of the scientific work. The success of this expedition brought Schäfer to Himmler's attention. At their first meeting in June 1936, Himmler explained his interest in the World Ice Theory. This theory held that primeval floods had submerged the ancient continent of Atlantis. Himmler also said he believed the Nordic race did not evolve. Instead, he thought they had descended from the heavens to settle on Atlantis.

He believed Aryan emigrants from Atlantis had founded a great civilization in Central Asia. Therefore, he was very interested in Schäfer's studies. He wanted to help Schäfer's next expedition to Tibet. Ernst Schäfer's third Tibet expedition ran from April 1938 to August 1939 under SS sponsorship. Schäfer was an expert in zoology and botany, with some background in geography and ethnology.
His report surveys the animals and plants of this remote land on the roof of the world.

It does not mention Himmler's esoteric interest in Aryan origins. However, the team took careful anthropological measurements of Tibetan nomads. Color photographs show the grand Himalayan landscapes and the lonely desert plateaus of the Tibetan interior. They also show fortresses, monasteries, temples, and the splendid Potala in Lhasa. The report includes rich documentation of Tibetan cultural and religious festivals.

These include portraits of the aged abbot of the Taschilunpo monastery, the seat of the Panchen Lama. They also show processions of Buddhist monks, masked impersonations of Tibetan deities and demons, and lamas summoning the gods with the strange sounds of their long horns and drums. Schäfer returned to Germany with many animal species and 108 volumes of Tibetan sacred scripture, the Kangschur, a gift from the Dalai Lama.

[break]However, a Nazi scientific expedition in the fabled land of Tibet could only lend credence to the imaginary occult links between Hitler, Nazism, and the eastern theocracy of Agartha. Pauwels and Bergier noted that Schäfer had made contact with a number of lamas in various monasteries.

He also brought back "Aryan" species of horses and bees to Germany. Bronder alluded to the German links with Tibetan Buddhism already made by Haushofer and Hess. A certain Karo Nichi, the ambassador of Tibetan Agartha in Berlin, was said to have led the Schäfer expedition. His goal was to deliver radio equipment for communications between Berlin and Lhasa. The perennial fascination of these tales of strange Nazi missions to remote destinations has remained a constant in popular culture.

Himmler's esoteric projects even feature in the highly successful Indiana Jones films of Stephen Spielberg. In Raiders of the Lost Ark (1981), the American archaeologist is assigned to find the Ark before the Nazis can obtain it for their own evil use. In Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade (1988), the race is on to secure the Holy Grail.

Images of uniformed Nazis pursuing such objects of power as the lost Ark of the Covenant and the Grail have created a worldwide awareness of the SS's interest in ancient and exotic traditions. Heinrich Himmler saw the SS as an elite military religious order leading an Aryan crusade to retake the East.
This view echoed his romantic take on medieval German history. On 2 July 1936, he held a special religious service over the tomb of Henry the Fowler at Quedlinburg cathedral.

That date marked the thousandth anniversary of Henry the Fowler's death. Henry lived from 875 to 936. He was a German king who founded the royal Saxon dynasty. He also pushed the Slavs eastward across the River Elbe.

In a mood of mystical pilgrimage, Himmler spoke of Henry as a model of Germanic valor and piety. He swore to continue Henry's mission in the East. Occultist writers later wrote at length about Himmler's interest in spiritualism. They also noted his belief that he was the reincarnation of King Henry. Himmler's castle, the Wewelsburg, gave the SS its reputation as an esoteric chivalrous order.
During the early 1933 election campaign, Himmler traveled through Westphalia, "the land of Hermann and Widukind."

He was deeply impressed by the mythical atmosphere of the Teutoburger Forest. Always inspired by romantic medieval models, he began to think about buying a castle in this region for SS use. The SS took over the Wewelsburg near Paderborn in August 1934. It first served as a museum and an SS officers' college for ideological education within the Race and Settlement Main Office. In February 1935, it came under the direct control of the Reichsführer-SS Personal Staff.

This change reflected Himmler's new plan to turn the Wewelsburg into an SS-order castle. He wanted it to be comparable to the Marienburg Castle of the medieval Teutonic Knights in Prussia. In the late 1930s, Himmler and the castle commandant, Manfred von Knobbelsdorff, held pagan wedding ceremonies at the Wewelsburg for SS officers and their brides. They also organized spring, harvest, and solstice festivals for the garrison and the village. Himmler's plans grew more ambitious.

Prisoners from a nearby concentration camp built to serve this purpose enlarged the castle's massive north tower. In the large circular upper hall, topped by a domed cupola, the coats-of-arms of dead SS-Gruppenführer were to hang.

The marble floor featured a large sun wheel made of twelve zigzag sig-runes. Below, in the vault, twelve pedestals lined the interior wall at regular intervals. They surrounded a paved circular recess in the stone floor. In the castle's wings, study rooms were named and furnished after figures from Nordic mythology. These included Widukind, Henry the Fowler, Henry the Lion, King Arthur, and the Holy Grail. Plans from 1940 to 1942 called for moving the village away.

They also called for building a huge complex of halls, galleries, towers, turrets, and curtain walls. This complex would use a radial layout around the hillside. The great northern tower of the medieval castle would be its center. At this early stage of the war, Himmler clearly saw the Wewelsburg as a future SS vatican. He intended to build it on a gigantic scale to represent the center of a new Aryan world order.
[break]The occult interpretation of the castle focused on its mythological and cultic features, rather than on the use of slave labor for its construction.

Raven-scroft spent time describing the interior design and symbolic decoration. The rooms were named after Germanic heroes, including Otto the Great, Henry the Lion, Friedrich Hohenstauffen, and Philip of Swabia. Others imagined the twelve top Gruppenführer meditating in high-backed pig-skin chairs. These chairs had silver plates with the occupant's name on them. They sat around a huge oak table in the great hall. The table resembled King Arthur's Round Table.

These figures were seen as modern-day Jesuit superiors. In the large stone crypt below, known as the "realm of the dead," people easily imagined symbolic ceremonies. When a top SS leader died, his heraldic device was ritually cremated in the central recess. The ashes were then placed in an urn on one of the twelve pedestals around the circular walls. By the late 1970s, the Wewelsburg appeared in thriller literature as Himmler's Camelot.

It was described as the mysterious ceremonial center of the SS. Himmler's organization spread terror across Nazi-occupied Europe, but in Occult Reich, J. H. Brennan gave it a different meaning: "With its runic doctrines, its inner circles, its ritual festivals and its Black Jesuit Grand Master, the SS was a magical order in every sense of the word."

The authors of the "Nazi Mysteries" focus on Himmler's occult whims and these mystifications. This approach lends weight to the pseudoreligious image of the SS. In contrast, they diminish the police and security services, the cruelty of their slave labor programs, and the terrible extermination camps. Romantic details tend to hide the brutal, violent nature of the SS behind an aura of magic and mystery.

These details include the alleged search for the Holy Grail, the meditations of the inner leadership, comparisons of the Black Order to the Jesuits of St. Ignatius Loyola, Arthurian and Germanic symbolism, and the strange ceremonies for the dead at the Wewelsburg. Alan Baker has recently tried to record and study this type of Nazi occultism.
The topic is complex because early, pre-Nazi völkisch and Pan-German racist groups before and after the First World War were clearly influenced by esoteric ideas.

The creation of the Aryan myth, which points to the polar origins of the Nordic race, had deep roots in European Romanticism and late nineteenth-century Theosophy. It also grew strong in movements like Ariosophy. Despite this ideological link, Baker accepts that the evidence for Hitler and other top Nazis practicing black magic is very weak. We again move through the tangled mythology of the post-1960 genre that gives the Nazis occult powers.

This includes Trevor Raven-scroft's The Spear of Destiny, the fringe cosmologies of Hanns Hörbiger's World Ice Theory and the Hollow Earth Theory, and ongoing stories about secret Nazi activities involving Antarctica and UFOs. As Baker argues, this is a valid field of study, even though this modern literature is dubious. The Nazis mythologized the history of their supposed Aryan ancestors to legitimize their claims to racial superiority.

In the same way, modern writers in the fields of occultism and conspiracy theory have mythologized the Nazis as a uniquely evil force. The Nazis won elections and later wars quickly. Their clear evil inspired esoteric writers in France to see them as demonic by the mid-1930s. Nazism's destructiveness and the Holocaust's dark irrationality called for a religious view. This view involved a war in heaven, satanic inspiration, and the use of dark forces.

Popular literature began exploring this idea in the 1960s. This fanciful demonization created and kept alive an occult image of Hitler, National Socialism, and the Third Reich. Authors of "Nazi Mysteries" write in a speculative spirit. Their readers are often less skeptical. When thriller writers borrowed these materials, the "Occult Reich" became even more common in popular talk. In this process, Nazism gained the status of a perverse theology.

It included doctrine, prophecies, rituals, and ceremonies. During the 1970s and 1980s, mystical neo-Nazis took over this sensational mysteriosophy of the Thule Society and Wewelsburg. They created new Nazi cults involving Gnosticism and satanism. The original labeling of Nazism as pure evil was thus inverted. It now celebrates the taboos of the liberal democratic world as the forbidden gods of a dark realm.
