7. Wilhelm Landig and the Esoteric SS. Vienna was a gray city after the Second World War. Its Habsburg glories, along with the charm and gaiety of its music and theaters, were a thing of the past. For about eight years since the Anschluβ, Austria had been just a province of the Third Reich. In the final months of the war, Vienna suffered heavy bombing, and the Red Army fought its way into the city. From 1945 to 1955, the Allies divided the capital into sectors.

Russian, British, American, and French military personnel handled administration, police work, and security in their respective sectors. The Four Powers took turns ruling the Inner City within the Ringstrasse for one month at a time. This area included its damaged statues and public buildings. Food, fuel, and medicine were scarce. Black market trading, prostitution, and espionage helped the local population survive. The gloomy, wintry atmosphere of Graham Greene's famous novel, The Third Man

[break](1950), hung like a heavy pall over the defeated and occupied city. Most Austrians now saw Hitler and German rule as a curse and the cause of disaster. Yet a large group of loyal Nazis could not accept defeat after Germany's power and expansion across Europe.

In the early 1950s, a belief in Aryan-Nordic myths took hold in Vienna. This stood in sharp contrast to the open worship of Hitler seen in post-war Nazi groups in Britain and the United States. Because Hitler and politics were painful memories, this new belief focused on ancient Nordic races, Thule, Atlantis, and Germanic religion. It also drew on the rediscovery of ideas and people from the Ahnenerbe.

This was Heinrich Himmler's SS office, which studied Aryan archaeology and anthropology from 1935 to 1945. Hopes for national rebirth and salvation centered on wild guesses about German miracle weapons.

These included flying saucers and secret polar bases claimed to exist at the end of the war. These ideas grew out of the bleak despair in postwar Vienna. They became the seeds of the neo-Nazi Black Sun myth, which has circulated in the far-right German underground since the 1990s. This mystique began with a small group of occult racists who first met to discuss ideas in 1950. They gathered at the studio of designer Wilhelm Landig (1909-1997) in the fourth district of Vienna.

Landig was born in Vienna in December 1909. He was a strong pan-German nationalist. As a schoolboy, he joined the youth section of the Freikorps Roβbach. He later fought in the Freikorps "Deutsche Wehr" in Vienna. These were two of many private armies formed after the First World War. They aimed to defend Germany's borders and suppress left-wing revolts. Landig served in the Third Reich.
From 1937 to 1938, he worked at the Labour Science Institute in Berlin.

Until 1941, he worked in a government department in Vienna. From 1942 to 1944, he fought with the Waffen-SS in the Balkans. He received German and Croatian decorations for fierce anti-guerrilla campaigns against partisans. In 1944, he was ordered from Belgrade back to Vienna for "special tasks" involving new military technology. In autumn 1945, he was automatically arrested as a former SS man.

He was interned in a British POW camp until 1947. After his release, he entered the world of inter-Allied espionage. He sold low- and medium-grade Soviet intelligence to Western security services. Another member of the circle was Rudolf J. Mund (1920-1985). As a teenager, Mund was an illegal Nazi stormtrooper in Vienna. He later served on the Russian front and in the Ardennes as a lieutenant in the Waffen-SS. He was also imprisoned and faced postwar disqualifications.

[break]These fighters turned to occultism and racist myths to rise above their defeat and the humiliation of the German Reich. They discussed a secret center in the Arctic called the Blue Island. They saw it as a starting point for reviving traditional life. This idea came from Julius Evola. His book Erhebung wider die moderne Welt [Revolt against the Modern World] (1935) became the Bible of the Landig group.

Landig's völkisch ideology of Ario-Germanic superiority fit within Evola's grand metaphysics of primordial Tradition. Only the Northern Atlantic races, especially the Aryan Germans, understood the sacred nature of regal authority.

They also understood the mystery of ritual, initiation, and consecration. They grasped the divine origins of patrician rule, chivalry, and a rigid caste hierarchy. Evola's polar mythology of Thule and his sharp anti-modernity were already common in German conservative and right-wing periodicals during the Third Reich. As a Waffen-SS officer, Landig may have met Evola during the war's final year. After June 1944, Evola worked in Vienna.

He helped recruit a pan-European army of Waffen-SS volunteers from across Europe. Their goal was to defend the continent against invasion by the United States and the Soviet Union. The Vienna group eagerly consumed the ideas and books of Herman Wirth (1885-1981), a Dutch-German lay scholar of ancient religions and symbols. Born on 6 May 1885, Wirth was the son of a schoolmaster in Utrecht.

He embraced pan-German ideas early and served as a German volunteer in the First World War. After moving to Germany in 1923, Wirth began to write. He published his major works on Germanic prehistory, Der Aufgang der Menschheit (1928) and Die Heilige Urschrift der Menschheit (1931-36).

By comparing the scripts of Mediterranean countries and the Orient, the symbols of North and West Africa, and the languages of North American Indians and Eskimos, Wirth argued that a former great civilization of the proto-Germanic Thuatas existed in the North Atlantic basin.

He found the oldest remains of this Nordic-Atlantean culture in the carved symbols of the Old Stone Age in southwestern Europe. Most university academics rejected Wirth's methods and conclusions. He attracted further controversy by editing Die Ura Linda Chronik (1932).

This is a Friesian manuscript generally regarded as a nineteenth-century forgery. Wirth presented it as a chronicle of Germanic life in the sixth to first centuries B.C. But these Nordic speculations brought Wirth the favor of Heinrich Himmler. In 1935, Himmler invited Wirth to found and direct the SS Ahnenerbe institute for anthropological and archaeological research. Wirth favored ancient matriarchy and archaic collectivism.

This showed his debt to the Swiss scholar Johann Jakob Bachofen. These ideas also seemed to support socialist ideals. As a result, he lost favor with the Nazis. He left the institute in 1937. However, his influence among German völkisch groups was strong from the start. He imagined an ancient high Thuata civilization. From there, Nordic sea peoples set out in swan and dragon ships. They colonized the Atlantic world. This vision offered a utopian imperialism.
It appealed to those who mourned the weakness and moral decay of the Weimar Republic.

Pessimists and critics of the present were drawn to his idea. They believed a revival of this Thuata-Atlantean culture would signal the rebirth of the Germanic race. It would also free humanity from the curse of modernity. Besides his major works and many controversial pamphlets, Wirth lectured widely in Germany. He wrote many articles for academic and popular press. He also led his own "Herman Wirth Society" in Berlin. He survived the Second World War.

He then carefully resumed work on Germanic prehistory. Wilhelm Landig was an early fan of his books. In 1958, Landig founded his own Volkstum-Verlag in Vienna. He began publishing new works by this prophet of the antediluvian age. Wirth lived in Marburg on the Lahn until he died at age ninety-five on 16 February 1981. The Landig circle cared about more than just cultural pessimism and longing for a lost golden age.

These men believed they could make spiritual contact with the Blue Island, a hidden polar center. Erich Halik, a Swiss engineer and another member of the circle, supervised the pouring of large plaster casts for mediumistic purposes.

The group also performed meditation exercises to try to tune in. Halik claimed that esoteric circles within the SS had sought the favor of this spiritual world center. These SS "heretics" were especially interested in the Cathar tradition. They directed their search toward the Arctic and Tibet. Halik cited the work of Otto Rahn, a Grail scholar whom Himmler commissioned to study the polar traditions of the Cathars in southern France. Halik viewed world history in deeply esoteric terms.

He said German bases on Greenland showed the SS "heretics" trying to reach the "Midnight Mountain" of polar tradition. He argued that the UN flag, with its blue polar symbol, showed the influence of rival Rosicrucian groups in California on the Allied side. Halik speculated that the SS "militant esotericism" was also inspired by Ossendowski's tales of Agharti and the mystical fascism of Julius Evola.

Halik was also the first to link the esoteric SS with the "Black Sun" roundel insignia carried by German aircraft in the polar region at the end of the war. Halik was particularly excited about modern UFO sightings after the war. In a series of articles in the Austrian esoteric magazine Mensch und Schicksal from 1951 to 1955, he linked flying saucers to the Black Sun myth.

He called the saucers manifestations of the Grail, which he described as "a cultic vessel used by the supreme hierarchy of Christian Gnostics." He studied the etheric nature of the saucers based on their glowing concentric rings.

Halik also believed that Germans had set up "polar empires" in both the Arctic and Antarctic. These empires operated under the signs of the "Golden Sun" and the "Black Sun." The Golden Sun represented a Luciferic, solar quest. This quest connected to Otto Rahn and the SS Cathars. The Black Sun was driven by Saturnine, satanic lodges within the SS. Halik saw the UFOs less as a technical invention and more as the use of a metaphysical and alchemical principle. The alchemical metaphor of sol niger

[break](Black Sun) meant occultation, blackening, and sinking into the mystery of self-discovery. This was the supposedly idealistic message of SS "heretics" working from the Blue Island. They were harbingers of a millenarian world transformation. Rudolf Mund's literary and intellectual interests reveal more about the occult-nationalist roots of the Landig group. In 1945, while held in an American prisoner-of-war camp at St. Avold, Mund was thrilled to find a fellow inmate in Edmund Kiβ.

Kiβ was an author whose books Mund had read eagerly before the war. A surveyor in Kassel, Kiβ wrote a series of novels. These books combined epic tales of life in prehistoric Atlantis, the Thuata culture of Herman Wirth, and the World Ice Theory of the maverick Austrian cosmologist Hanns Hörbiger (1860-1931).
First published in 1913, the World Ice Theory held that all stellar and planetary phenomena resulted from violent encounters between fire and ice.

Besides the origin and movements of heavenly bodies, the theory also explained earth history and prehistoric mankind. Hörbiger argued that the earth had captured several planets as moons before our present Moon.

These moons successively crashed onto the earth, causing geological upheaval and floods. He proposed that men existed in the Tertiary era. He also claimed that the oceans rose as the former moon approached. This led to the establishment of asylum cultures in Mexico and the South American Andes. The World Ice Theory attracted mythologists of lost continents. Its elemental cosmology seemed to mirror the Nazi ideology of struggle. The Brownshirts, (Sturmabeteilung, or SA), officially sponsored it.

[break]Kiβ was an early supporter of the World Ice Theory. In 1928, he traveled to Peru and Bolivia. He looked for evidence of a late-Tertiary asylum culture in the Andes. He worked with Arthur Poznansky, a German professor who had emigrated and long served the Bolivian government. Together, they studied the ancient ruins of Tiahuanaco on Lake Titicaca. Kiβ believed the carved relief on the city's sun gate was an astronomical calendar.
He thought it confirmed that prehistoric humans experienced the most recent lunar catastrophe and the flood that followed.

In the cordillera, he found a huge sculpture of a Nordic head carved from the rock. To him, this was strong evidence of earlier Atlantean migration and colonization. He believed this happened when the oceans surrounded this high Andean plateau. After returning to Germany, Kiβ wrote several scientific works. These focused on his speculations about Hörbiger's theories. However, his tetralogy of best-selling novels was even more influential. These books popularized the Nordic Atlantis hypothesis.
They also spread the idea of heroic-catastrophic events, including upheaval, inundation, and Nordic migrations, to a wide public.

In these works, Atlantis and its submergence became a political symbol. They represented the social chaos of the Weimar Republic. They also echoed Oswald Spengler's doom-filled prediction of Western decline. Kiβ argued that only the Germans could restore order in this disjointed world. He claimed they were the last people of the heroic Nordic race. He said they could achieve this through their powerful will to survive and prevail. His first novel, Das gläserne Meer

[break](1930), described the catastrophic earthquakes and floods that followed the fall of the first Tertiary moon. Glacial conditions and hunger drove the Nordics out. They migrated over an ice bridge to the hospitable climate of the southern continent. This blue-eyed, blond master caste of Atlantis kept its dark-skinned slaves in strict control. It secured the survival of the white race by plundering women from nearby lands. The novel Frühling in Atlantis
[break](1933) is set during the golden age of Atlantean civilization. The pure-blooded, Nordic "Asen" numbered only two million out of the state's sixty million inhabitants.

The rest were "darks" and partial citizens. The rulers' main task was breeding the Nordic type to guarantee their authority. However, the inferiors were restless. They eventually murdered the young leader, Baldur Wieborg of Thule. He was a hero of climatic disasters and eugenic policy. This ominous political note clearly reflected Kiβ's own anxieties about the threat that Slavs or other racial inferiors posed to German superiority. Kiβ's next novel, Die letzte Königin von Atlantis
[break](1931), is set against the sinking of Atlantis. This sinking resulted from climatic disasters caused by the capture of our current Moon about 14,000 years ago.

Remnants of the Nordic master race migrate to conquer the highlands of South America. This includes the Peruvian plateau of Atzlan. In this asylum, they practice strict eugenics to keep their blood pure. They condemn inferior races to menial labor. In this book, Kiβ brings the Nordic head he discovered to life as Godda Apacheta. She is the astronomer of Atzlan and the narrator. In the final novel of the series, Die Singschwäne aus Thule
[break](1939), all surviving Asen attempt to return to their ancestral Arctic home.

They fly under their blue banner with a silver swastika. But instead of the perpetual spring of former moonless times, terrible cold prevails. This cold hardens them anew. After many years, they swarm southward again to Hellas. There, they found the famous high Greek culture of the first millennium B.C. And so the cycle begins again. Throughout all history, the Nordic Germans will always send their supernumerary populations to colonize.
They will found new states and breed up the declining inferior races. Edmund Kiβ, known as the "poet of Atlantis," was recruited by Heinrich Himmler into the SS Ahnenerbe.

In July 1936, Kiβ and others signed the Pyrmont Protocol. This document agreed to official SS support for the World Ice Theory. The project became a meteorological section of the Ahnenerbe. Philipp Fauth, Hörbiger's prewar co-author, played a key role in it. In August 1936, Kiβ began planning a new expedition to the highlands of Abyssinia. He sought traces of human civilization from the Tertiary period and remains of the earlier moon.

Himmler quickly promised Ahnenerbe support. The Ahnenerbe also helped with Kiβ's plans for a research trip to Peru. This trip was scheduled for 1940 but was abandoned because of the war. The World Ice Theory received near-official endorsement in the Third Reich. Hitler's enthusiasm for it appears several times in his Table Talk. He promised to build an observatory at Linz.
This observatory would represent "the three great cosmological conceptions of history - those of Ptolemy, Copernicus and Hörbiger."

Kiβ then joined the Waffen-SS. He achieved the rank of SS Obersturmbannführer. Later, he served as commandant of the guard at Hitler's headquarters. At the end of the war, he hoped to lead a group of commandos to Tibet. The plan was to gather support from Mongolian tribes. This struggle would tie down Soviet forces in a Central Asian theater. That would relieve pressure on the struggling Reich.

[break]In the cold, dark nights of late 1945, Rudolf Mund listened closely to the old explorer's stories. The ruined cities on Marajo island in the Amazon delta, Tiahuanaco and Lake Titicaca, the mausoleum of Puma Punku, and the astronomical observatory of Kalaseseya appeared in his mind. Kiβ's skill at telling epic tales briefly drove away the misery of defeat in the wretched camp.

Nordic heads in the Andean mountains, wide-ranging SS expeditions to prove prehistoric high-Nordic civilizations in Africa and South America, and the huge timescale of Hörbiger's World Ice Theory created a world of ancient Aryan superiority.

Against this backdrop, the defeat of the Third Reich seemed a minor setback. The catastrophic nature of these distant events suggested a world of violent struggle and renewal that fit the Nazi view of nature. The fact that an ancient Nordic people had survived such upheavals, floods, and ice ages only confirmed the lasting heroism of the Germans when facing enormous challenges. In April 1946, Mund met Kiβ again in a camp at Augsburg.

Kiβ learned that the young Waffen-SS lieutenant planned to escape. The older Kiβ gave him a hundred marks. Fate brought them together again at Dachau. Kiβ was weak and ill. He said he intended to travel to Tibet after his release. Mund was deeply impressed by these meetings. They seemed to promise a future beyond the current disaster of Germany's defeat. Mund remained drawn to the esoteric Aryan mystique. He believed this mystique lay behind the SS.

As a young Waffen-SS soldier, he had no direct contact with mystical SS circles during the Third Reich. However, the comradeship, heroism, and sacrifice of his frontline experience in the Waffen-SS were the formative experiences of his life.

He believed the myths of this "first volunteer European army." The bravest young men of Germany and other Western nations had fought a crusade against Soviet communism. Defeat, capture, the shocking discovery of Nazi atrocities, and the disgrace of his SS uniform drove him to search for a noble SS. This noble SS had championed the utopian Aryan world against all that was dark, chaotic, and inferior. Throughout the postwar years, Mund pursued his occult-völkisch investigations.

He tried to make sense of his former ideals. These romantic studies led Mund to the works of Otto Rahn, a young SS-Unterscharfuhrer who was deeply interested in the medieval Cathars and Grail legends. Rahn originally planned to write a dissertation on Kyot, the Provençal troubadour whose lost Grail poem served as a source for Wolfram von Eschenbach's Parzival.

In 1931, he went to the Languedoc. He soon identified the Grail knights with the Cathars and Montségur castle as Montsalvat. He settled at Ussat-les-Bains. There, Antonin Gadal, a local neo-Cathar expert, encouraged him to explore the caves of Sabarthès, where the Cathar treasure was supposedly hidden. In his book Kreuzzug gegen den Gral (1933), Rahn fused the troubadour and Minnesang traditions, the Cathar heresy, and the Grail legends.

He posited an underground Gnostic religion of Aryan-Visigothic origin. Catholic authorities brutally suppressed this religion in 1244. Himmler was interested in Rahn's quest for a Germanic religious tradition based on heresies and legends. He sought Rahn's collaboration in SS-sponsored research. In March 1936, Rahn joined the SS. He undertook a research tour of Iceland under SS auspices.

He later published the travel journal of his quest for the ancient Cathar-Visigothic tradition across Europe as Luzifers Hofgesinde (1937). Rudolf Mund found evidence of the SS's mystical mission in Himmler's whimsical ideas and Rahn's passionate quest. In 1958, Mund joined the Order of the New Templars (ONT).

This was a racist chivalrous sect. It developed a heretical dualist Ario-Christian theology. This theology featured blond heroes in eternal struggle with inferior beast-men. Jörg Lanz von Liebenfels originally founded the ONT on Christmas 1900. The group gained some influence in Vienna before and during the First World War. At that time, Lanz was promoting his Ariosophy. This was a mix of Aryan racism, Gnostic Christianity, and Theosophy. He published this in his Ostara magazine.
People believe these mystical racist brochures strongly influenced the young Hitler.

The sect expanded from Austria into Germany and Hungary during the 1920s. It went underground in Vienna after 1945. Mund immersed himself in the archives of this Aryan cult. He studied the writings of the early Church fathers and the history of the Knights Templar. He later wrote a hagiographical book about Lanz von Liebenfels. In 1979, Mund succeeded Walter Krenn as prior of the ONT.

[break]Mund's research into the ONT also drew him to the mystical rune theories of Karl Maria Wiligut (1866-1946), known as Himmler's Rasputin. Wiligut claimed to possess ancestral memory and to have an inspired view of archaic Germanic traditions.

This made him Heinrich Himmler's favorite mentor on mythological subjects. Himmler gave Wiligut an official role in prehistoric research within the SS from 1933 to 1939. Himmler asked Wiligut for advice on many issues. Wiligut's influence reached the design of the death's-head ring worn by SS members. It also shaped the conception of Wewelsburg as the SS order castle.
He helped adopt other ceremonies meant to give the SS ideology of elitism, racial purity, and territorial conquest a traditional feel.

Wiligut's ideas resembled those of Guido von List, a runic occultist and Ariosophist close to Lanz von Liebenfels. Wiligut had links with ONT members as early as 1908. Richard Anders, an SS officer and ONT brother, introduced Wiligut to Himmler. Mund was pleased to find another source of SS esotericism. He wrote a biography of Wiligut, which Landig's Volkstum-Verlag published. Wiligut also gave another source for the Black Sun myth.

In one of his Halgarita mottos, a set of cryptic religious revelations he wrote for Himmler in the 1930s, Wiligut described an ancient sun called Santur. Wiligut's contemporary adepts, Emil Rüdiger and Werner von Bülow, saw this body as a second sun.

It shone 230,000 years ago on the Hyperboreans at the North Pole. It helped their spiritual growth. Santur still orbits near our planet today. It is an extinct star, so it is invisible. But as a Black Sun, it still sends out a powerful intelligence. Wiligut's rebuilding of a prehistoric Germanic "Irminist" religion drew partly from Guido von List's Armanism. Armanism was the ancient faith of the Ario-Germans. It reflected a Germanized form of Theosophy.

This happened in the völkisch-occult underground before the First World War. By tracing Wiligut's inspiration back to that time, we find an even earlier source for the Black Sun in Theosophy. Theosophy had strong influence in German esoteric circles since the turn of the century. In her major work The Secret Doctrine (1888), Helena Blavatsky occasionally mentioned a "central sun" in the Milky Way.

She called it "a point unseen and mysterious, the ever-hidden center of attraction of our Sun and system." As the energetic center of the galaxy or even the universe, this dark central sun represents the mass of potential energy before the Big Bang in modern cosmology.

The Jewish Cabala described its "black light." Eastern initiates of the Aryan tradition saw it as the source of "creative light" and the "center of Universal life - Electricity." Blavatsky thus emphasized a distinction between Semitic and Aryan cosmogony. The former materializes and humanizes the mysteries of nature. The latter spiritualizes matter. völkisch-theosophical authors in Germany took up Blavatsky's ideas before and after the First World War.

Guido von List wrote of an invisible "primal fire" as the ancient Ario-Germans' notion of the highest divinity. Peryt Shou (1873-1953), a German occult writer, described humanity's heightened receptivity to the ultraviolet spiritual light of the "central sun" in the Age of Aquarius. He related this to Germany's future in the troubled postwar era. Mund was mainly an esotericist, while Landig was a political activist.
In the mid-1950s, he served as the Austrian representative for the European Social Movement (ESB).

This fascist international group was founded in Rome and Malmö. It sought a German alliance with a global league of non-aligned nations, particularly Arab states, positioned between the two superpowers. In 1955, Landig kept in regular contact with Per Engdahl, the Swedish neo-Nazi leader. He also contacted Karl-Heinz Priester, a former Hitler Youth leader with wide connections in the German nationalist underground.

In 1958, Landig started his own nationalist publisher, Volkstum-Verlag. Its logo displayed an Ostrogothic eagle brooch from the fifth century, during the reign of Theoderich the Great. That same year, he began publishing his monthly international news service Europa-Korrespondenz.

This service took a nationalist and anti-communist stance. People speculated that Johannes von Leers helped fund it. Leers was a former official in the Reich propaganda ministry who had found refuge in Nasser's Egypt. In 1970, Wilhelm Landig became the Austrian representative for the World Anti-Communist League (WACL). This league was founded in Taiwan in 1967. It formed after the Asian People's Anti-Communist League merged with the Anti-Bolshevik Bloc of Nations.

This was arguably the most important far-right network in the world. It explains why Landig's international news service was so well informed. Wilhelm Landig's own novels kept occult-nationalist themes alive among younger neo-Nazis in the 1990s. The ideas and interests of the Landig group in the 1950s became permanent in his trilogy of Thule novels. The first, Götzen gegen Thule (1971), started in the late 1950s.

It uses the thought of Julius Evola and Herman Wirth. The book mixes theories of Aryan polar origins and Atlantis with new nationalist myths. These myths include "the last battalion," secret German UFO bases in the Arctic, alchemy, Grail myths, and Cathar heresies. It also features a Nazi-Tibetan connection involving Himalayan masters and an underground kingdom in Mongolia. In this novel, and especially in its successor, Wolfszeit um Thule

[break](1980), a global Jewish conspiracy always lurks in the shadows. It seeks to stop the revival of Nordic German rule. But its Judeo-Christian idols are powerless against the return of the Black Sun. The last novel, Rebellen für Thule (1991), is a wishful fantasy of right-wing radicalism among German youth.

A former SS officer, the hero of the second novel, is invited to lecture on the Atlantean heritage of the Aryans at a German secondary school. The pupils reject the liberal views of their despised left-wing history teacher. They eagerly embrace the new nationalist myths of Thule. Götzen gegen Thule is an allegory. It shows the Landig circle's attempts to contact an esoteric center of Nordic traditions.

This center is the legendary realm of Thule. Thule is the final bastion of the Germanic world in defeat. The story describes a world odyssey. A small group of SS soldiers and Luftwaffe airmen travel across four continents. This happens in the immediate aftermath of the Second World War. In the first part of the novel, two airmen are sent from Norway. Their names are Recke ("beserker") and Reimer ("bard"). They go to Point 103. This is a secret base.
The esoteric SS elite established it in Arctic Canada. The Allies do not know about it.

Most German authorities do not know about it either. Point 103 is a large underground complex. It has highly advanced technology. This includes flying saucers. Their apparent mission is to maintain the spirit of German defense. This happens after the final surrender of the Reich. Point 103 is also a combatant. It fights in a metaphysical war.

This war is between hidden forces on a spiritual plane. In this great power struggle, the secret base seeks proximity and support. It wants the support of the esoteric world center. This center has ethically positive forces. It is located somewhere nearby. It is at the Midnight Mountain of polar myth. Its symbol is the alchemical Black Sun. This is a round disk. It is not exactly black. It is the deepest violet.

[break]Like Landig's bloc of unaligned nations against the superpowers, Point 103 seeks to build an international alliance for the ideals of the Black Sun. Many foreign delegates attend a major conference in the base's assembly hall. The hall is decorated with astrological symbols and a huge image of Mithras slaying the Bull. The V-7, a German flying saucer, flew all the delegates to the conference. It travels at 4,000 kilometers per hour and has a range of 2,000 kilometers.
The group includes a Tibetan lama, Japanese, Chinese, and American officers, Indians, Arabs, Persians, an Ethiopian, a Brazilian officer, a Venezuelan, a Siamese, and a full-blooded Mexican Indian.

The Arabs speak darkly of secret Islamic brotherhoods. The Indians and Persians invoke old Aryan traditions. The Orientals allude to their occult orders and a mysterious world center. Wearing their uniforms or national dress, many delegates give speeches. They link their national myths and ideals to those of the Thule. They pledge full support when the time comes for action. Recke and Reimer are accompanied by Gutmann, an enigmatic Waffen-SS officer.

His name means "Good Man." He is a descendant of the German Cathars, or "perfect ones." Gutmann acts as their guide and mentor. He initiates them into Thulean philosophy. He quotes the Iranian Avesta. He also cites the theories of Edgar Dacqué, a Munich paleontologist. These sources serve as evidence of a golden age. During that time, the Arctic region was green and fertile. It was the primaeval homeland of the Aryans. Gutmann mentions the sinking of Atlantis.

He says a lunar collision caused it, according to Hörbiger's World Ice Theory. He also describes the forced exodus of the Aryans. Sinful egoism and climatic disaster drove them out. Kiβ's research in the Andes offers proof of these Aryan migrations. Kiβ discovered a stone head with Nordic features in Bolivia. Old annals called the Dogger bank area around Heligoland the "Holy Land." This is sure evidence of a sunken Aryan-Atlantean culture.

Wherever the Aryans settled in Europe, Iran, and India, they tried to re-create their lost paradise. They recalled its memory in their myths, legends, and place-names. Gutmann believes the Bible's flood myth comes from ancient Hindu texts and the Gilgamesh epic. This implies the Old Testament is merely a local Jewish adaptation of worldwide Aryan traditions. Following Herman Wirth, Gutmann claims the ancient Tuathas and Germans are blood heirs of the old Atlantean race on the European continent.
[break]After Germany formally surrendered in May 1945, the chief of staff at Point 103 ordered the removal of all German insignia from uniforms.

The Black Sun disk became the symbol of their secret, independent Reich. It replaced German markings on their aircraft and flying saucers. He followed this order with a speech that reviewed Thulean prehistory and destiny. This review was based on the works of Herman Wirth and Julius Evola. The Arctic and Atlantean Nordic races created the oldest German state. This was the Tuatha empire of Doggerland, which had Neolithic long barrows.

A solar deity and a belief in cycles of cosmic regeneration appear in the bull-slaying Iranian warrior cult of Mithras. This was the heroic religion of the Age of Taurus. The new Thuleans of Point 103 practice this religion. However, the virile horned son of God, the ancient revelation, gave way to the pale "fish head" of Jesus Christ: The Age of Pisces began the destruction of the aristocratic principle.
This happened through the revolt of slaves, the disinherited, and those with no heritage or tradition.

These groups held a grudge against everything that signified energy and leadership. Evola recognized that the poison of proselytizing fanaticism swept over ancient Rome in a barbarian Semitic wave. 8. Nazi UFOs, Antarctica and Aldebaran. After appearing in the early postwar years, flying saucers quickly became a major cultural icon in popular mythology. These futuristic disc-shaped aircraft could reach amazing speeds and perform complex maneuvers. They first entered public awareness after an incident on 24 June 1947. Kenneth Arnold was flying his private plane through the Cascade Mountains in Washington State.

He saw a formation of nine objects flying at about 9,000 feet. He estimated their speed at 1,700 miles per hour. This was an incredible figure before ultrasonic flight. He described the strange craft flipping up and down "like a saucer would if you skipped it across the water." Arnold's sighting was not the first. Nearly forty had been recorded earlier that year. However, this incident sparked a major wave of journalism about flying saucers.

That summer alone, reports came from forty-eight states. American fears of communism and Russian aggression fueled interest and anxiety. The Cold War was just beginning, with communist regimes being established in Eastern Europe. As saucer sightings increased across the Western world, people realized the saucers' performance far surpassed all known technology and human endurance. Belief in the extraterrestrial origin of the flying saucers soon became widespread.
[break]Public fear of Soviet superweapons or alien visits clearly required an official response.

The US government held a mixed view of the saucers. It tried to debunk them whenever possible. At the same time, it strongly denied that they came from Earth. In December 1947, a monitoring investigation called Project Sign began. Allen Hynek, then a professor of astronomy at Northwestern University, directed it. The project examined 237 sightings. In February 1949, the United States Air Force started Project Grudge.

In March 1952, it was renamed Project Blue Book. Hynek advised this project. It served as the official U.S. investigation of the UFO phenomenon until it closed in 1969. By then, "Unidentified Flying Object" was the preferred technical and more neutral term. Meanwhile, civilian investigation groups formed in America, Britain, and Europe. Waves of sightings continued without stopping.

Science fiction magazines and films grew rapidly in America and Europe during the 1950s. This genre reinforced the image of flying saucers and the idea of alien visitation. A new dimension appeared when people claimed direct meetings with extraterrestrial aliens. A new contactee literature developed after George Adamski told his story of meeting an alien in the Californian desert in November 1952.

[break]Fifty years of the UFO phenomenon have become a global mythology that crosses national borders. Stephen Spielberg's hugely successful film, Close Encounters of the Third Kind (1977), started a widespread belief in government coverups and conspiracies about their knowledge of UFOs and aliens.

A real UFO industry thrives today. Hundreds of books come out each year. They cover sightings, abductions, crash retrievals, and even alien autopsies. Many specialist magazines closely analyze data. This discourse is accessible to everyone. Esoteric Nazism has found a place within this powerful and universal mythology.

As early as the 1950s, rumors spread among certain German nationalist circles. They claimed that postwar flying saucers were actually German superweapons. These weapons had already been developed and tested during the Third Reich. When Germany surrendered in May 1945, this technology was supposedly shipped to safety in the Arctic, South America, and Antarctica. People attributed the many UFO sightings to a hidden Nazi presence in remote and inaccessible regions of the world.
By the late 1970s, neo-Nazi writers claimed that the "Last Battalion" held a vast tract of Antarctica.

This massive Nazi military force possessed highly advanced UFOs. At any moment, this fleet of Nazi UFOs could set out to save the world. They would free it from the control of the two superpowers and the postwar problems of democracy and liberalism. From the early 1990s, these myths of advanced Nazi technology mixed with ideas about alternative energy sources. They also included alliances with an extraterrestrial civilization in the remote solar system of Aldebaran.

Jan van Helsing, a notorious German conspiracy theorist and anti-Semite, now uses these myths. He combines them with the Black Sun in his best-selling books on secret societies and their power in the twentieth century. Nazi UFO mythology grew out of the closely related Hitler survival myth. Early myths of German revenge were tied to the idea that Adolf Hitler escaped the Berlin bunker in the war's final days and reached safety abroad.

Conflicting accounts of events in the bunker, circumstantial evidence, and early Soviet hints that Hitler was alive fueled widespread speculation about his fate. During the summer of 1945, stories of Hitler's last-minute marriage to Eva Braun and their flight to a new life spread through the international press. On 16 July, a sensational article in the Chicago Times claimed that Hitler and Eva Braun landed in Argentina and lived on a German-owned estate in Patagonia.

Every major American and European paper reprinted the story, including the New York Times, the Baltimore Sun, The Times of London, and Le Monde. The story likely stemmed from the late surrender of the German U-530 submarine at the Argentine port of Mar del Plata in early July. Several Buenos Aires papers had earlier reported secret landings by rubber boats along the coast.

However, on 17 July, the newspaper Critica stated that the Führer and Eva Braun had landed from the U-530 in Antarctica. It noted that the possible landing spot was Queen Maud Land, the destination of a German Antarctic expedition in 1938-39. The late surrender of German submarines in Argentina during the summer of 1945 drove press interest in Hitler's escape to the Southern Hemisphere.

The U-530 surrendered at Mar del Plata on 10 July. It had a crew of fifty-four men, which was too large. It also carried large food stocks and a strange cargo of over five hundred large drums of cigarettes.
On 17 August 1945, three months after the Third Reich surrendered, another German submarine, the U-977, surrendered at Mar del Plata. Captain Heinz Schäffer commanded only thirty-two men.
The logs of both submarines showed they left Kristiansund, Norway, on 2 May 1945. Like the U-530 crew, the U-977 crew consisted of exceptionally young, unmarried men.

A third submarine surrendered at Leixoes on the coast of Portugal on 5 June. The mystery of these submarines' long voyages, young crews, exceptional supplies, and unknown locations during the months before their surrender fueled speculation. People suspected the submarines were part of a "phantom convoy." This convoy allegedly brought Hitler and other top Nazis, along with auxiliary forces, to a secret hideout in Antarctica.

[break]Admiral Richard E. Byrd's large international mission to Antarctica in 1946-47 provided another clue about the Allies' concern over a possible postwar Nazi military presence there. On 2 December 1946, a United States fleet of thirteen ships left Norfolk, Virginia. It carried four thousand navy troops, amphibious tanks, helicopters, and two hundred airplanes.

The fleet sailed to join Anglo-Norwegian and Soviet task forces. They aimed to monitor Antarctica. The stated goals were scientific research and establishing territorial claims. The expedition quickly ran into trouble once it arrived. Byrd lost four airplanes and withdrew in a hurry. He abandoned the entire operation. A Chilean journalist, Lee Van Atta, quoted Byrd. Byrd said he worried about a threat to US security. Unidentified enemies in the polar region could fly from one pole to the other.

A Hungarian exile living in Argentina, Ladislao Szabó, wrote a book. It was titled Hitler esta vivo [Hitler Is Alive] (1947). The book described the failed U.S. Antarctic mission and the captured U-boats. It placed these events in the context of Hitler's escape to a secret Antarctic Nazi base. The book was immediately translated into French. It sparked a wave of sensational magazine stories from 1947 into the early 1950s.

[break]The next stage in Nazi UFO mythology linked postwar saucer sightings to the claim that German engineers had built flying disks during the Third Reich. In March 1950, Flugkapitän Rudolf Schriever (b. 1910) gave an interview to the German news magazine Der Spiegel. He explained that he started thinking about vertical take-off solutions in 1942.

He was working as a chief pilot at Eger (now Cheb) at the time. He designed a central domed cabin for the crew and controls. A circular plane of rotating turbine blades surrounded this cabin. Three jets mounted below drove the blades. The whole disk had a diameter of 49 feet (14.4 meters). The turbines could reach 1,650-1,800 rpm. They produced a thrust of 100 meters/second. Schriever calculated that his 3-tonne disk could fly at 4,200 kilometers/second.

It had a range of 6,000 kilometers. Once the Messerschmitt jet became available in 1942, he and his team began developing the project. They worked at the BMW works in Prague. He said his workshop was burgled in August 1948.

Thieves stole his designs for the flying disk and a model. He was convinced that Czech engineers had since rebuilt his flying disk for a foreign power. More details emerged later. It described the craft as a fantastic creation nearly 15 meters in diameter, with the plexiglass cupola of the control room glistening in the sunlight at its center.

A slight technical fault and an air-raid warning postponed the flight indefinitely. The works shut down on 9 May in the midst of a Czech revolt. Schriever and his colleagues blew up the flying disk. He then escaped by driving his BMW into the Bavarian Forest in the American zone. He repaired agricultural machinery there for a while. Eventually, his belongings, including the designs, were plundered.

Or they use these facts as proof of black disadvantage and white racism. Asian minorities do well in education and jobs. They are also less likely to end up in prison.

This shows that blaming white racism for black failure does not hold up. Focusing on white responsibility for failing race relations also ignores the high rate of crime and violence between different ethnic groups. Stopping white criticism by calling it individual or institutional racism, combined with a compensatory attitude toward black identity, has further fueled the racist far right. Aryan cults and esoteric Nazism create powerful myths to deny the decline of white power.
The cultural pessimism of Julius Evola, Savitri Devi, and Miguel Serrano shows their fear that white people will be submerged in a degenerate age ruled by social and racial inferiors.

They use Hindu chronology to map this decline into the Kali Yuga. They promise regeneration through a new golden age in the cycle of the ages. Francis Parker Yockey also presents a mythic view of history. He claims that alien Jewish influences temporarily disable European races. This prevents them from fulfilling their destiny in a powerful new Imperium or world empire. Wilhelm Landig speaks to a narrower German-speaking audience.

He develops a neo-völkisch mythology of Aryan origins in northern Thule. He uses this to predict the recovery and resurrection of Nazi Germany. The Black Sun and Nazi UFO myths serve a similar, though more local, function. They appeal to German neo-Nazis who mourn the loss of World War II and the victory of liberalism in the international order. George Lincoln Rockwell, Colin Jordan, Wilhelm Landig, and Ernst Zündel looked back to Nazi models and the epic story of World War II.

They used this to fight postwar liberalism and its supposed Jewish creators. Their recent successors, especially in the United States, tend to call on quasi-völkisch myths of white identity and destiny. Our review of Christian Identity groups, the Church of the Creator, and Nordic racial pagans shows a more diffuse defensive ideology than straightforward German National Socialism. Commentators have noted the rise of a new nationalism.

This nationalism acts as a culture of resistance to recent forces of globalization and immigration. It is highly significant that the Aryan cult of white identity is now most marked in the United States. This is where the challenges of multiculturalism and Third World immigration have been the greatest.

[break]Race relations based on the civil rights of Black Americans and the assimilation of New Commonwealth immigrants in Britain have long been overtaken by the rise of Third World immigration, refugees, and asylum seekers. The Immigration Reform Act of 1965 in the United States abolished the national-origins system of 1924. This law has arguably changed America more than any other legislation in the twentieth century.

It was initially intended to fix the imbalance in immigrant origins between northern and southern Europe. Racial quotas had previously kept immigration in line with the dominant north European immigrant stock of 1920.

However, by the mid-1970s, the south European backlogs were depleted. The economic reconstruction of Europe also reduced further immigration from that source. By 1980, only 5 percent of legal immigration came from Europe. Asians, chiefly Filipinos, Koreans, Vietnamese, and Indians, accounted for nearly half. Immigration from Latin America, chiefly Mexico, constituted about 40 percent. A family preference system fueled the new immigration pattern.

This pattern reached record levels in the 1980s. Meanwhile, a surge of illegal Hispanic immigration was perceived as a loss of control over the nation's borders. After the First World War, the American racial theorist Lothrop Stoddard saw a threat in immigration.

He viewed it in economic terms, arguing it forced wages down. He also saw cultural consequences, affecting religion, rules of conduct, laws, and customs. By 1940, during the Great Restriction of immigration, Time magazine mocked Stoddard's fear of the "yellow peril" as a delusion. Today, the same magazine predicts the inevitable eclipse of the white, Western world. The 1965 law supporting source-country universalism led to a sustained wave of Third World immigration.

Today, about 1 million people legally immigrate to the United States each year. This includes 100,000 refugees and 100,000 people applying for political asylum. An estimated 2 to 3 million illegal entries into the United States happen every recent year, overwhelming legal immigration. Conservative opponents of mass Third World immigration point out that this recent non-European immigration is already transforming U.S. demography dramatically.

Consider that southern and eastern European immigrants came from post-1870 immigration. This wave provoked the Great Restriction of 1924-1965. In 1930, these immigrants made up only about 13 percent of the total U.S. population. By comparison, post-1970 immigrants made up over 8 percent of the population by 1990, and the number was rising.
[break]Policies of bilingualism and multiculturalism in schools avoid the question of whether the United States can actually assimilate these immigrants.

Assimilation is further weakened by the expansion of affirmative action. This policy was originally meant to help Black Americans under civil rights laws. It has become government-mandated discrimination against white Americans, and in practice against Black Americans too, in favor of immigrants from the Third World. The rise of international human rights above national sovereignty has also eroded citizenship.
This erosion grants illegal aliens welfare, education, government subsidies, and even voting rights.

Conservative groups in the United States are deeply concerned about these issues. They see no reason to change the country's demographics, given the unpredictable consequences. Turning the United States into a "colony of the world" or a "universal nation" has no precedent in the modern world. Similar forces are at work in Europe, especially in Britain. There, left-wing and liberal political agendas promote multiculturalism to win the votes of growing ethnic minorities.

A recent report on the future of multi-ethnic Britain has even questioned whether the word "British" carries a racist taint. As we saw in the previous chapters, the far right in the United States and Britain has grown stronger since the 1980s.

This was surprising at first. The first generation of postwar neo-Nazi leaders was getting old. The memory of the Axis challenge to Western liberalism was fading into history. However, skinhead racist gangs, white power music, and the shift of neo-Nazi racism into new folkish religions of white identity clearly reflect rising immigration in Western countries. They also reflect the resulting pressure toward multiculturalism.
These latter trends lead me to compare them with völkisch German nationalist groups in multinational Austria before the First World War.

If fascism had not risen in the 1920s and 1930s, few people would care about tracing these precursors of National Socialism. We do not know what the future holds for Western multicultural societies. But the experiment did not go well in Austria-Hungary, the Soviet Union, and Yugoslavia. The multiracial challenges in liberal Western states are much greater. It is clear that affirmative action and multiculturalism are even causing a more widespread hostility toward liberalism.
Looking back from a potential authoritarian future in 2020 or 2030, these Aryan cults and esoteric Nazism may be recorded as early signs of major divisive changes in our current Western democracies.

[heading]About the Author.

[break]Nicholas Goodrick-Clarke has written several books on the Western esoteric tradition and ideology. These include Hitler's Priestess and The Occult Roots of Nazism: Secret Aryan Cults and Their Influence on Nazi Ideology.

The Times Literary Supplement called the latter "an intriguing study of apocalyptic fantasies." It has stayed in print since its 1985 publication. It has been translated into eight languages. Dr. Goodrick-Clarke has been associated with the University of Oxford since 1975. He is now a full-time author and historian. He lives in a farmhouse on the Berkshire Downs in southern England.
